I suggest you make peace with the past because back then, you were weak and didn't know how to protect yourself, and the other person shouldn't have bullied you. The past experiences are behind you now, and looking at them from a different perspective can bring us wisdom. Second, "acknowledge yourself and make friends boldly." You're now 20 years old, and you might feel worried and hesitant when it comes to making friends. You can only reap friendship if you take the first step. Don't worry about how others will react, whether they reply or not. Making friends depends on fate, and mutual attraction is what makes people friends. The prerequisite for mutual attraction is taking the initiative to look for it. OP, don't be afraid of rejection. Keep going! As long as you work hard, the season of harvesting friendship will come.

Hello: I saw a child who has been bullied for 7 years. During this process, he doesn't know why others bully him, and he has no way to resist. This is a direct "childhood shadow", I think it will have an impact on his future interpersonal communication and relationships. I'm glad that you are willing to face this problem through counseling. Let's analyze it together, don't be afraid, I will help you. Analyze and understand the problem: 1. When he was a child, he was bullied by a boy who had no intersection with him for seven years, from kindergarten to elementary school graduation. He didn't know why the boy always targeted him. The problem is that he never provoked him, but he always troubles him. (Seven years is very important for a child's growth, including the formation of his character in the future. We can't know the specific reasons now, but I am very clear that it is definitely not your fault, so you don't need to be afraid, right?) 2. He has always been a troublesome boy because of various insults to you. Until this year 2020, when you are 20 years old, you still haven't had a friend because of what happened in the past. (There are always some little boys who like to be mischievous, maybe he can also feel that you won't resist him. It is really uncomfortable to be oppressed in this way. Twenty years old is theoretically an adult, and you shouldn't be subjected to such bullying by children anymore. But that "shadow" has always been difficult to dispel. Thinking about this child, growing up in fear, with no one to help. From then on, he no longer believes in people, friendship, or anything. Although, I know you really want to find friends.) 3. No matter what kind of friends, you don't have any, really no friends. You have always wanted to break through, but you just can't. Every time you meet a new friend, you dare not send a message to greet or chat with them. You hesitate for a long time before sending a sentence, and in the end, you still dare not send it. (Hmm, I can feel your desire to make friends, it is really lonely to be alone. Assuming there is a person who really, really, really wants to be your friend, it comes from the bottom of their heart. What help will it bring to your life and friendship? What changes will it bring to your life? Or, you have sent out the edited message, and then they also replied to you. Think about it, is it not that scary?) 4. I long for good friends to chat with, but I am afraid of being rejected or ignored when sending messages. The reason is still related to the experiences of childhood. I really want to solve these problems, but I feel helpless. (Hmm, I can see your determination to face this matter. Don't be afraid, although there were childhood influences, people in the world are different. When we slowly face it, you will find that it is not scary at all. Don't be afraid, don't worry, I'm here to help you, teach you step by step how to do it, okay? Don't be afraid, everything can be explained with reason. You were young at that time, but now you have grown up. I will teach you how to make friends, how to say "no" to people you don't like, so you can gradually overcome this. Facing the problem of "childhood shadow" ~~~ Childhood indeed has an impact on people. However, the changes in the future are also very important. The past can only represent the past and cannot become the future. I believe you can do it. You need to try slowly, step by step. At first, it may be slow, but don't worry, this is a normal "speed". If there are details, we can also communicate about them. In short, when you slowly open your heart, you will definitely make friends and become your own best friend. Closing: I wish you happiness and joy! I hope you can be free from the influence of the past soon and confidently make friends. If you have any specific concerns, feel free to private message me!

Childhood psychological trauma, it is better to do more meaningful things to gradually dilute the negative memories of childhood, because you cannot erase these childhood memories, but you can find many meaningful things from them. In fact, as long as you find meaningful things to do every day, time will slowly fade some of the memories. If we volunteer every day, we can learn that being alive means being active, instead of staying at home all day, playing computer games and not doing anything productive. In that case, it is difficult to establish communication with others, let alone talk about meaningful activities. Only through communication with others, can you learn more from them and do more and better things. Therefore, being alive means being active. When you wake up every morning, it is better to do some exercise and let your body breathe in plenty of fresh air. People will naturally feel refreshed and have a good mood. Therefore, it is worth finding some things that can make you happy. The bad memories in life will fade away as a result. So, it is necessary to find something to activate the negative memories in your heart, let the memories fade away, and slowly forget the bad memories by finding things to do every day.

After enduring long-term bullying at school, you have been unable to escape the shadow and have projected your past experiences onto people and things in the present. This psychological response itself has a positive self-defense effect, protecting you from further harm. However, since the reality has changed, this reaction is not in line with objective facts and the disadvantages outweigh the benefits. It is necessary to make changes in order to avoid affecting normal interpersonal interactions. As someone who shares a similar temperament with you, as well as being a mental health counselor and someone who has overcome similar experiences, I would like to offer you some advice. Since I do not know about your childhood experiences and family environment, I can only discuss this issue within the scope of simple cognitive-behavioral therapy. First, establish accurate cognition. List out your triggering events and outcomes. Event: being with a few semi-familiar same-sex individuals. Outcome: feeling uncomfortable and uneasy. Then, list out the cognitive process: why do you feel uncomfortable, believing that they will dislike you? Thinking that they might talk behind your back? Thinking that they might plot against or bully you? And then what? If they do something behind your back, will more people isolate me? Will everyone believe them instead of me? Will everyone dislike me? If everyone dislikes me, does that mean I am a failure? Should everyone like me? Can we infer that if someone dislikes me, then everyone dislikes me? By critically reasoning, you will discover the flaws in your own logic. Write down each of your mistaken and correct logics. Next, implement behavioral correction. I suggest using rational emotional imagining techniques. When you are alone, imagine yourself in the situation of being bullied in your early years, experience the feelings of anger, fear, and helplessness, and then start trying to use rational thinking to gradually dissipate these negative emotions. After becoming familiar with this technique through repeated practice, you can then use it in reality. Whenever you encounter situations that make you uncomfortable, use accurate cognition to guide yourself. The aforementioned methods are only techniques to address symptoms. To fundamentally overcome this, it ultimately requires the tempering of a strong inner self.

The occurrence of campus bullying is not uncommon, and every time I hear about it, I feel deeply saddened and sympathize with the experience of the victim. It also makes me realize that there is not enough that I can do. The saying that "the unhappiness of childhood needs a lifetime to heal" is absolutely true. Childhood is a crucial stage for the development of one's character. The things experienced during childhood are deeply imprinted in our minds, becoming indelible memories. How can we stop this vicious cycle? 1. Learn to reconcile with our past selves. 2. Make ourselves stronger. 3. Break through ourselves and be more courageous.

question: Sometimes friends may say things that make you feel uncomfortable. What should you do?
description: I don't know if I am too sensitive, but sometimes friends say things that make me feel uncomfortable. It can make me feel like my beliefs are being questioned or even mocked. How should I face this?

answers.answer_text: First, you need to determine what type of friend this person is, whether they are just a casual friend or a close friend. When we feel uncomfortable with the things others say, we need to clarify whether their words are friendly advice or malicious insults. If it is advice coming from a friend with good intentions that makes us uncomfortable, we may understand logically that they are just trying to remind us, but emotionally it may feel like we are being blocked and that our whole being is being invalidated. In reality, we need to understand that they are only addressing this particular issue and not our entire person, and they are not denying our self-worth. However, if they are mocking or belittling you, that is unfriendly behavior and you can choose to attack back, because that is not about sensitivity but rather their incorrect way of communication making you feel uncomfortable, and it is not your fault.

question: Watching videos, browsing information, and listening to audio are all habitual at 2.0x speed. Information anxiety?
description: Watching videos, reading information, and listening to audio at 2.0 times the speed has become a common practice. It helps to concentrate attention quickly and saves half of the time. Personally, I don't think it is a big deal, but many people perceive watching at double speed as a lack of appreciation or disrespect towards the authors.

answers.answer_text: Everyone has their own pace, and broadcasters/authors need to consider the majority of people, so the speed should be moderately slow! So just enjoy it as you like. If you listen carefully to the content, why not respect the author? I have noticed that people have different voices. Some people can't understand the content at 1.5x speed, while others speak clearly and can understand the content at 2.0x speed. Everyone's pace is different, and the brain's response to information is different. everyone has different background knowledge, so the speed of listening to the same thing will definitely be different. I hope my answer can help you. Best wishes!

question: Who should be considered my friend, the one who contacts me or the one who helps me?
description: I usually contact some friends, but when I really have a problem, I think of other people instead. Although I feel like I could get help from the friends I usually contact, I don't want them to know for some reason. I don't know why, maybe subconsciously I don't consider them as real friends?

answers.answer_text: Hello, I think friends can be classified into many types. As you mentioned, those you regularly contact and think of when you need help, they are your friends. In our hearts, we probably have an understanding of each friend: what kind of person they are, how deep our relationship is, what we can do together, in what areas they can help me, and which friend I should turn to when I'm sad. Regarding the friends you mentioned that you don't want to share things with when something happens, I think there might be two possibilities: first, you feel that your relationship is not deep enough, and you don't want to show certain problems in front of them because you feel that your connection is not that strong. Even if you tell them, they would help you, but you might feel uncomfortable and think that you are bothering them. Second, it's also possible that your relationship is too deep, and you genuinely don't want to trouble them. You don't want them to worry about your issues. To figure out which one it is, you may need to ask yourself. In my opinion, it's best to find a comfortable way to interact with each friend. You don't necessarily have to worry about who is a friend and who isn't. Friends are originally a broad and complex concept, without a definite standard. Hugs to you, the world and I love you! (^_-).

question: 16-year-old girl, suffering from bipolar disorder, what to do if the family refuses to accept it?
description: I was diagnosed with bipolar disorder half a year ago. Every time my mom mentions it, she becomes silent and looks depressed. Initially, I was receiving treatment, but due to the pressure of studying in the third year of junior high, I didn't continue counseling after returning to school. Later, I stopped taking medication because the side effects were too severe and affected my studies. As my symptoms persist and cannot be relieved or controlled, I often feel very distressed. Besides the various negative impacts caused by the illness, I also face immense pressure and feelings of helplessness and fear when dealing with it alone. I have sought help from my family, but they always respond with questions like, "Why are you like this?" or "How did you become depressed?" without further discussion. I am currently in my first year of high school and live in the school dormitory. The school requires an investigation into students' specific physical conditions, with one of the items related to mental illness. I believe it is necessary for me to explain this to the school, but my mom is unwilling to provide the diagnosis report and does not want the school to know about it. She is concerned about the impact it may have on my future. I'm feeling tired now. I keep wondering if I shouldn't have had any hope for assistance from others from the very beginning. What else can I do?
keywords: Family, family relationships, communication between parents

answers.answer_text: Dear OP, hello there. From your description, I can feel your helplessness and feelings of despair. Firstly, why do parents resist or even ignore our illness? In the older generation's mindset, when emotions such as depression, bipolar disorder, and anxiety are diagnosed as psychological illnesses, they tend to associate it with insanity (what we call "crazy"). This is a cognitive error and prejudice. Parents temporarily cannot accept the fact that you have been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, they cannot accept that their daughter is different from others. This can be seen from their response every time: "How could you be depressed?" This shows it. Parents' love for their children is profound. Your mother worries that if others know about this, they might have a negative view of you, and it might even affect your future studies and campus life. If they were to accept the fact that you have an illness, to some extent, parents would feel that they have failed in their upbringing and they would feel a lot of pressure. Since you fell ill, your mother has been in a low mood all the time. Little sister, although parents have these various problems, they are all due to their lack of understanding. In their hearts, they love you. What can we do then? First of all, think carefully about the reasons why you have bipolar disorder and tell your parents. If it is not hereditary, then you have a greater chance of recovery. The onset of bipolar disorder does not happen overnight but is the result of a long accumulation. Think about the reasons behind your constant low mood, perhaps it is the family atmosphere, interpersonal relationships, or academic pressure. Once you have a clear understanding of this, tell your parents. Because your parents do not believe that you suddenly developed bipolar disorder for no reason, you want to not only understand the cause of your illness for yourself, but also to make your parents understand it in the future so that they can cooperate with your treatment. Let your parents realize that bipolar disorder is just like a cold or fever, it is just an illness that can be cured as long as you cooperate and receive proper treatment, although the recovery process may be longer. Give yourself and your parents confidence. Explain the situation to your teacher and ask them if having bipolar disorder will have any impact at school. Finally, please do not give up hope. Have confidence in yourself to overcome the illness so that you can recover faster.

Mom's non-acceptance is because many people associate mental illness with psychiatric disorders. Because of their lack of understanding, they may feel fear, anxiety, and a sense of unreality. Is it true? Does it really happen in our family? Therefore, Mom's acceptance will be a process, from not knowing to knowing to understanding. But this does not mean that parents do not love their children; it is precisely because of their deep love that they may be at a loss. As for whether the school should be informed, if it is a school survey, I think caution is necessary, especially if it is uncertain whether the confidentiality measures are sufficiently professional. This is because if the confidentiality is not done well, it may lead to many people knowing, but they may have limited understanding or even ignorance about this illness, and it may cause unnecessary harm to you. But if you are facing a counselor, you can talk about it. I believe that the counselor will provide safeguards in this regard. Mental illness, like any other physical illness, should not be avoided from seeking medical treatment. If there are side effects, you can discuss them with the doctor and adjust the medication in a timely manner. You should know that these illnesses have been around for a long time, and there have been numerous clinical trials. Compared to the illness itself, there is no need to be overly afraid of side effects. If certain medications have significant side effects, the doctor may adjust the medication or gradually increase the dosage after adaptation. In any case, do not stop taking medication on your own just because of discomfort. This could affect the effectiveness of treatment and prolong the duration of therapy. Meanwhile, psychological counseling should also be continued, and it is best if your counselor has a clear understanding of your medication usage. Overall, it is normal to rely on psychological support. There is no problem with that, especially with family members. Understanding that their non-acceptance is also due to anxiety caused by lack of understanding might make you feel a little better. We all may go from not knowing to knowing to becoming familiar with this. Acceptance from parents is just a reality for ordinary people. Let's all slowly learn about and face this illness, okay?

After carefully reading your confession, I deeply understand your pain. Sending you a warm hug. Here is my analysis: 1. "What else can I do?" As the saying goes, an idle person is prone to illness. The best thing you can do for yourself is to be diligent. Since you live in a dormitory, whenever you have free time, you can clean your room, wipe the doors and windows until they are spotless. Engage in more conversations with your roommates. Communicate more. 2. When people are not engaged in activities, they tend to overthink. Overthinking can lead to negative thoughts, followed by pain and depression. As long as you refrain from overthinking, your condition won't worsen. How can you prevent yourself from overthinking? By keeping busy. The more you keep yourself occupied, the less you will think. 3. Don't talk about your psychological illness with people around you. You can find an online psychotherapist as a confidant. If you don't have money, you can also find free psychotherapists. For example, the individuals who answer your questions are mostly offering their help for free. You can try seeking assistance from them, as they are usually willing to help. Whenever you experience negative emotions, confide in them, and nip the problem in the bud. This way, you won't suffer. Thank you for your question, may all the beauty in the world come to you as scheduled.

question: On the surface, they may appear happy, but deep down, there are many things going on, feelings of depression. How to regulate them?
description: Every day, I appear to be happy and optimistic on the surface, but only I know that many things in my heart have been suffocating me. My parents, husband, and even myself have their own difficulties. I don't want to burden them, and as for others, I don't like discussing my own issues with them. I have a high defense mechanism, so sometimes I don't know how to resolve my frustrations and end up forcing myself to suppress these emotions, creating a vicious cycle.
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, expressing emotions, healing methods.

answers.answer_text: If emotions are not released, they remain inside, making you feel repressed. Many emotions have nowhere to express themselves, and no one can understand you. Try opening up to your husband, when communication is established between the two of you, your inner suppressed emotions will be seen and understood by someone. Then you will gradually become happier in life. I'm not sure if my suggestion can help you, but you can also establish relationships with close friends, talk about your own confusion with them, and listen to their difficulties. Seeing how others live their lives can provide you with some inspiration and help. Wish you happiness and joy!

question: Despite knowing that one is doing something wrong, they still persist in their stubbornness and refusal to change.
description: I am a junior high school student, and I am a very self-insecure person. I have no sense of existence at school and have not felt love at home. Later on, I started getting involved in the internet and unknowingly cheated money. I used the money to buy clothes, but yesterday I encountered a big scammer who wanted to teach me how to cheat money. He told me how much money I could cheat in a month, and I was tempted and actually agreed. However, I did not cheat money with him, and I feel really uneasy in my heart. I feel like I am violating the law and I can't do this. So, I blocked all those people. I want to live a good life and achieve what I want through my own hard work. But I really don't know what to do now, how to return to a normal life, and I feel very bored. I don't know what to do.

answers.answer_text: OP, hello, don't continue to push the boundaries of the law recklessly, as the law will respond if you dare to test it. It's never too late to change course and avoid disaster. There are many paths in life, and those seemingly easy shortcuts may hide hardships and pitfalls that are not yet visible. From your description, I can sense your dissatisfaction and helplessness towards your current situation, whether it's your studies, family, or yourself. It seems like a negative and pessimistic state. It's clear that you feel remorse for your actions of deception and you deserve praise for refusing to engage in more significant acts of fraud. This indicates that you are well aware of your own moral principles and boundaries. Since you are beginning to question your own thoughts, it shows that you don't want to continue in this situation, torn between deceit and money, and instead, you wish to return to normalcy and focus on your studies. I advise you to promptly stop your deceptive behavior because your mental maturity is not yet fully developed, making you susceptible to temptations and vulnerable to environmental influences. What you should be truly wary of, is the possibility for your desires to escalate. It might start with just wanting to buy a few clothes, but later you may desire to upgrade your phone, purchase cosmetics, and buy more expensive items. These things you constantly yearn for are like bait, leading you unknowingly into deeper trouble. Acknowledge the actions you have already taken and shift your focus towards your future and tomorrow. Perhaps a dull and monotonous life can be tiresome, but we can create interesting and fulfilling experiences for ourselves. Don't slack off, take yourself seriously. When we make mistakes, besides stopping ourselves from continuing to make them, we must also accept the reality of our imperfections. Try to forgive yourself for the mistakes you've committed. No one is immune to making mistakes, and everyone has their weaknesses. Don't scold yourself excessively over such matters. It is unreasonable to treat anyone, even yourself, from a high moral pedestal. Strive to return to a normal life as soon as possible. Maybe you've never truly taken yourself seriously or loved yourself. Maintain good academic performance and find a sense of fulfillment and satisfaction through your studies. When you first laugh wholeheartedly because of your efforts and achievements, doesn't that become a different kind of desire? Your life doesn't have to be as dull as it is currently. You also have your own value and significance. Our sense of existence is something we give ourselves. It isn't tied to the lives of others. Take advantage of the opportunity to receive education while you still can, and while there are still options, opportunities for growth, and chances to change. Invest in and devote yourself to your own development. Every seemingly ordinary choice you make now may have a significant impact on your future. Therefore, from now on, take good care of yourself and think about how to make your life interesting and fulfilling. Every road you walk will not be in vain. Best wishes.

question: Personality disorder, self-blame a lot, sincerely repent, and reflect every day?
description: I enjoy joking online, but I'm not very good at speaking. When discussing things, I like to exaggerate and mock things and people I don't like. Sometimes I speak without thinking, saying whatever comes to mind without considering the consequences. I have many flaws, but I genuinely want to change. I won't comment on others' right or wrong anymore, and I won't argue or try to please others just to exist. I am really a simple person who wants to make others laugh through my abilities and talents. However, constantly giving without considering what the other person truly needs, and disregarding others' feelings, is really thoughtless. When I'm in a bad mood, I even get angry at my parents. I truly want to be a grateful and filial person who is not obsessed with the virtual world of the internet. I have genuine remorse, but I know that no one will give me a chance, just like this software says "the world is in love with you," I can't feel the world's love for me, all I feel is mockery. However, I have also mocked others in the past, so this is what I deserve. I hope everyone can calmly listen to the reasons why I became this way. I hope to give people with personality disorders and psychological trauma from childhood a little understanding, tolerance, and even a little care. I want to bring happiness to others, and it will be very fulfilling for me.
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, guilt and shame, panic and helplessness.

answers.answer_text: ~~Give the original poster an encouraging hug. From the original poster's description, I can feel the good intentions and understand the desire to make everyone happy. This is really a very nice idea, and I can sense that the original poster is a kind person. However, I also understand the frustration of feeling like one is always "doing harm with good intentions." Sometimes in life, even though we have good intentions, our actions may not turn out as expected. But the original poster doesn't need to feel guilty about it. As long as our intentions are good, we can always find other ways to change and improve our expressions, methods, and approaches. For example, we can learn how to express emotions more effectively, or learn how to be more humorous. Moreover, for the shortcomings that we have discovered in ourselves, we can firmly correct our mistakes instead of dwelling on self-blame. Because everyone has flaws, and it is not something to be ashamed of. What we really need to do is bravely admit and face them, and then work to correct them.

question: Feeling insecure and constantly thinking about getting a divorce, what should I do?
description: I feel insecure. He never confides in me, and when I talk to him, he often ignores me. Every day, I feel angry and want to get a divorce.

answers.answer_text: From the title owner's short words, I feel the frustration and suffocation of not knowing where to focus, the anger of feeling even more lonely when together, and the urge to escape by doubting oneself. I hope this answer can bring you some comfort. First, we don't need to quickly label ourselves as "lacking a sense of security." Let's first see what happened and feel it. Perhaps there are many causes behind it, not as simple as it seems. Perhaps we can try to see what our needs are behind this "sense of security." In the subsequent expressions, it seems that "sense of security" can be understood as the hope that both parties can communicate and communicate, listen and support each other. The relationship between people is interactive, and there is no interaction between individuals and objects. This is a very normal need, especially in intimate relationships. On the other hand, we also need to see that everyone's way of interacting with others is different. Some people may react quickly and casually, some people may think carefully and act cautiously, some people may respond with actions instead of words, and some people may respond with words but have difficulty implementing them with corresponding actions... Perhaps we can look back and see how we got together in the first place; when we entered into marriage, what expectations did we have; what changes have happened now; have we changed, have we shown ourselves more comprehensively, have we understood each other more broadly, or have our expectations changed, or something else? When marriage encounters difficulties or problems, divorce is the simplest and most direct choice, but it may not be the best choice. What we need more is to grow in these difficulties, understand ourselves, see our interaction patterns, and see our needs. Only in this way can we live better in the next relationship. Otherwise, it is likely to be another repetition or cycle. Best wishes.

question: Long-term on the verge of mental breakdown and suicide, just wanting to end everything as soon as possible.
description: During the years from 15 to 21, I have been on the brink of mental breakdown. I have had several attempts at suicide. In the last few months of this year, I have focused on my work and planned to go to the place I've always wanted to visit to escape from this world. In 2008, my mother chose to leave because my father attempted suicide. In 2009, my father went back to our hometown and became a farmer. He could have supported himself without relying on us, but he insisted on labeling our family as "poor." I remember one time when I received a subsidy for my studies, and as a beneficiary of this aid, I had to collect 100 yuan in front of the whole school. It was a blow to my self-esteem. The years in school were not easy, with classmates talking behind my back. I overheard someone say, "His family is so poor! We won't play with him anymore in the future." Elder relatives in the village would tell me, "You have a lot of pressure in your life. Sleep with a higher pillow." My father would spend money recklessly in our hometown. I started working at the age of 16 and still couldn't earn enough to repay the debts. Even my beloved grandmother passed away in 2019. Even my own aunt says that I'm a waste in this life! Now there is only my father left in the family, who only cares about money. I just want to end it all as soon as possible. I have been living with constant mental stress due to work, life, and family, and even good-natured people can push me to the edge.
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, panic, helplessness, fragility, tears.

answers.answer_text: "#A sentence for the disheartened# Have you ever stored memories in an object? For example, keep this beautiful memory on a train ticket. Preserve this ticket, and when you see it in the future, you will recall those days. You can also seal unpleasant memories in an item, like a small glass bottle. Write down the incident, put it in the bottle, and use a permanent marker to write 'Open again on November 25, 2029'."

question: 32 years old, unmarried, without a job, without any goals, what should I do?
description: As a single woman in her late 20s, I have been under a lot of pressure. My family constantly asks about my progress in arranged blind dates, even though the other party rarely contacts me. In the end, my family blames me for it. Of course, I am also resistant to the concept of arranged blind dates and find it extremely awkward. So, every blind date ends up without any progress. Besides my love life, my job situation is also the same. I can't find a suitable job, nor can I find something I am passionate about. I have tried various jobs, but none of them were what I liked. They either consumed my life or I couldn't handle them. During this year of unemployment, I have been struggling internally. I was never a confident person, and now I have become more introverted and resistant to social interactions. It feels like there's no hope in life. What should I do?

answers.answer_text: In your worries, including life, work, and relationships, everything is going wrong, which makes you feel helpless and desperate. These various frustrations and pressures make you doubt yourself, lose confidence, and become more withdrawn, resisting contact with the outside world and using avoidance as a psychological defense mechanism to protect yourself. Not being able to find something you love, a suitable job, or a suitable partner is because your inner self is unclear about what you want and lacks confidence in achieving those things. Therefore, you use avoidance as a way to cope. It can be said that you have extinguished your own hope. The ability to change yourself and regain hope can only be done by yourself, others cannot give it to you. Life is full of various difficulties and obstacles, and many times you have no choice but to face them and force yourself to accept and solve them. Avoidance cannot solve problems, and habitual avoidance will only lead to more and more experiences of failure, and also undermine your self-confidence. Feeling that the job is not suitable is because you lack the determination and effort to solve the difficulties at work. Feeling unable to find something you love is because you haven't tried to love. Not being able to find a suitable partner is because you treat blind dates and developing intimate relationships as a burden imposed by your family. Have you noticed? It's not that you cannot think and analyze various situations and difficulties, but you unconsciously resist and refuse, rejecting many opportunities and forming a mindset of "I can't do it". Only when you truly treat these things as things you have to face and problems you have to solve, accept their arrival, stop resisting, and bravely face them, can you possibly solve them, have the opportunity to gain some successful experiences, and become the motivation and source of confidence for your continued efforts. And hope often lies in constant attempts and experiences. Keep going!

Hello friend, first, let me give you a hug and I hope the following answers can be helpful to you. Based on the main reasons you described as "feeling like there is no hope in life," they are mainly as follows: 1. Emotional pressure: Being 32 and unmarried, you resist blind dates mentally. At the same time, you may face criticism from your family for not having results from these blind dates. 2. Work pressure: You can't find a suitable job. 3. Internal pressure: You lack self-confidence and resist socializing due to being unemployed. So, let's address each one: 1. Look at blind dates from a reasonable perspective. Overcoming psychological barriers is not just your problem, many people also find blind dates awkward. On the one hand, it may be because you are introverted and not good at dealing with strangers one by one. On the other hand, it may be due to stereotypes about blind dates, thinking that people who go on blind dates are usually "leftover" and even believing that blind dates are not about marrying for love like our parents did. However, in reality, with the development of society and open-mindedness, "blind dates" have become a healthy and popular way of socializing, which has indeed helped many people meet their emotional needs. Firstly, blind dates can help both parties save time on getting to know each other's family backgrounds and accurately match their needs, making it an efficient way of socializing. Secondly, you don't necessarily have to approach blind dates with the mindset of finding a life partner. But through blind dates, you can improve your ability to judge people. "The more you meet, the better you will know what you like and dislike." Without even having the opportunity to get to know people, it will be even harder to figure out what you want. I have seen many friends born in the 80s and even 90s who met their current husbands through blind dates, and their relationships are very sweet. Some even had whirlwind romances and quick marriages. When destiny comes, nothing can stop it. Therefore, if you approach blind dates with a rational mindset and change your own perspectives, you can naturally overcome the feeling of "awkwardness" and embrace the opportunity for happiness. 2. Consider this as a gap year for yourself, to get to know yourself better. Many people experience a bottleneck period after working for a few years. They can't see the prospects of their work, repeat the same tasks every day, and find it difficult to balance work and life, which can make one reflect and think, "Is this really the right job for me? Do I actually enjoy this job?" Since you are not a fresh graduate, I suggest taking advantage of this period of unemployment and giving yourself a gap year. During this time, you can "read good books, meet influential people, and experience the world." (1) Read books and autobiographies about personal growth. Learn from the experiences of great people for inspiration in facing life. (2) Look for different ways of living and find role models. Find people around you whom you admire, observe their lives, and bravely talk to them, finding our own direction from their examples. (3) Go out and see the world, embrace nature. When you're hesitant to interact with people, go out and explore the world, embrace nature. You will discover the vastness of the world and the greatness of nature, and realize that those trivial matters troubling us are really just small in comparison, as you have the whole world to experience. 3. Regardless of when, please believe that you are worthy of love. I believe that your lack of self-confidence is caused by the double pressure of emotional and work setbacks, and even more so when you are blamed by your family after failed blind dates, leading to self-denial and doubt. But the truth is, you are worthy of love! Always believe in this. Your family is actually just worrying about you, but they don't know how to express it better. There will certainly be someone who loves you, and the heavens have made you wait for a long time just to give you the best. Lastly, and most importantly, learn to love yourself. And the first step in learning to love yourself is accepting yourself, including your imperfections. Being 32 doesn't matter, you still have vitality and hope! I recommend you a wonderful autobiography called "Take Charge of Your Life," it will inspire you. I hope this can help you. Good night, friend.

Hello, being blamed by family, having difficulties in emotional development, and not being able to find a suitable job. I have become withdrawn, resisting contact with the outside world, and unable to see hope in life. I really want to find hope in life and find a way to integrate myself into society, but now I am very confused. Here, I want to give you a hug first and then ask you a question: Have you ever imagined what your future life will be like? Everyone has their own worldview and desires for life. What kind of life do you want? For example, do you have a very clear goal for your future spouse? If you don't have a goal, you need to think now: what kind of spouse do you want? After clarifying this question, you can have a targeted approach when dating. Similarly, have you thought about what kind of job suits you? In the process of past employment and job searching, have you summarized any experiences that can lay a better foundation for your future employment? When you have no job and no stable emotional state, people often cannot see what their future will be like. Your situation happens to be in such a period where you have not truly adapted to society and have not yet entered the waiting period for family life. I understand your confusion very well, and I suggest that you now start establishing your life goals and try to truly interact with society. Best wishes, the world and I love you!

Hello, I want to give you a warm hug, dear questioner! When it comes to work and family, as we reach a certain age, it seems like everyone around us is busy searching for another kind of stability. Those of us who have been "left behind" are pressured by others to find that stability. Just as you mentioned, family members are anxious to know the progress of blind dates and can't wait for getting engaged and married the next day. For women, age is indeed a criterion. According to medical research, 35 is the ideal age for fertility. That's why unmarried women around the age of 30 start getting pressured by family and friends to get married. It seems that you are currently experiencing this stage. Based on your description, you don't like blind dates and believe in your own romantic imagination when it comes to love. You hope to meet the right person on your own. However, you also need to face reality. Meeting someone requires a social circle. If you are not someone who actively participates in social activities and your circle of friends is limited, blind dates can be a way to get to know strangers. Keep a positive attitude, don't resist, and don't settle. As for work, your attitude towards work is similar to that towards finding a life partner. You may have certain standards and want everything to be perfect, but the reality is not always like that. It's important for you to have a clear understanding of yourself, your strengths and weaknesses, and your abilities. Analyze what kind of work you are more suitable for and what kind of work environment you can adapt to, and then look for a job that fits accordingly. Age doesn't represent anything, what really matters is your abilities and your efforts. Wishing you all the best!

question: I suspect that I have Asperger's syndrome, what should I do?
description: I recently came across an article about Asperger's syndrome, which led to the above suspicion. When I was very young, my parents described me as talkative. However, I didn't have any friends in kindergarten. I was also clumsy and had poor motor skills. I often fell down for no reason. I vividly remember one time when I fell and scraped my knees and elbows, but I didn't cry. A group of people said, "You're really brave." In elementary school, I didn't know how to make friends, and as a result, I was isolated by my classmates in second grade. I finally gathered the courage to talk to the teacher about this issue, but it didn't solve the root problem, so I ended up isolating myself until I graduated from elementary school. In first grade, I became interested in dancing because I thought it looked beautiful on stage, so I "developed an interest" and studied dance for six years. Nowadays, my motor skills aren't as bad. In middle school, I was isolated again, which led to depression (but I'm better now). I feel like I can't find the "right moment" to speak, and sometimes when I finish speaking, others look at me with strange eyes. Since I stopped dancing in high school, I often inexplicably bump into tables and chairs while walking in the classroom. Additionally, I have a tendency to collect things (from collecting dried ginkgo leaves in elementary school to now having a box full of used pen cartridges) and I lack basic empathy.

answers.answer_text: Give the OP a hug! Thank you very much for the invitation! I can feel the confusion in the OP's heart, unable to let go of the experiences on their own body, not knowing how or why they happened. Coupled with the stimulation from articles, the OP suspects that they have "an illness," which is both a denial and lack of trust in themselves, as well as a subconscious need for self, a subconscious "need" for this "illness" to satisfy their needs. However, this kind of need cannot be discovered, understood, accepted, or acknowledged by the OP's conscious self. Asperger's syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by social difficulties, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors. Asperger's syndrome and autism spectrum disorder belong to the autism spectrum disorders, but ASD does not have significant speech and intellectual impairments, and may even have abilities in certain areas that are higher than average, hence also being called "high-functioning autism." The prevalence of Asperger's syndrome is about 3.6‰-7.1‰, with a much higher incidence in males than females, and there is a tendency for it to cluster in families. Asperger's syndrome is a lifelong disease, but symptoms often improve gradually with development. Adults with this condition can recognize their strengths and weaknesses and improve their social skills. Currently, there are no effective measures for preventing Asperger's syndrome. Asperger's syndrome usually cannot be noticed until after the age of 3. The clinical symptoms of this disease vary greatly among patients. Clinical manifestations in children with Asperger's syndrome include: extreme difficulty in communicating with others. This does not mean that children with Asperger's syndrome are avoiding social interaction, but they lack the instinct and skills to express their thoughts, feelings, and pay attention to the feelings of others. Easily bothered by loud noises, lights, strong smells, or crowded patterns. They like routine and have difficulty making changes. They have difficulty recognizing verbal or non-verbal information and understanding social norms. For example, they may stare at others without making eye contact, or they may not understand the concept of personal space. They speak lacking in tone, intonation, and emphasis, and their speech may be straightforward and difficult to understand. They may have poor coordination, abnormal facial expressions, body postures, gestures, or be clumsy, and may have difficulties in writing or other motor skills such as riding a bicycle. They have only one or a few interests, or are strongly obsessed with certain things. For example, they may have unusual preferences for snake or star names, or they may be able to draw very detailed pictures. (The above information is from the Internet and is for the OP's reference only) The presentation of symptoms is only one basis for auxiliary analysis and diagnosis. In the analysis and diagnosis of psychological problems and diseases, it is also necessary to consider the impact of symptoms on normal daily life and the level of inner conflict and pain. From the information provided by the OP, it can be seen that there is a certain degree of repression in their heart, and social impairment is not very evident. They have the ability to lead an independent and autonomous life and have normal social skills, but they lack a sense of security to some extent, and after being stimulated by certain things, they may exhibit a certain degree of regressive behavior. At the same time, the OP mentioned that they often bump into table corners after not practicing dancing, which on one hand may be due to the OP's nervousness and anxiety, and on the other hand, it suggests possible damage to the OP's imagination and nerve-related symptoms. Emotional changes affect the circulation of Qi and blood in the body, thus affecting nerve reflexes. It is recommended to go to a local hospital neurology department for an electroencephalogram examination to further understand the detailed situation and rule out physiological abnormalities. Based on objective facts, a comprehensive analysis and diagnosis can be made. The OP can schedule an appointment with a suitable therapist or seek suitable counseling locally.

question: Can I analyze and correct my thoughts to recover from the sexual abuse I experienced at the age of 5?
description: When I was 5 years old, I entered an abandoned house under the pretense of playing hide and seek. They pinned me down, tore off my clothes, slapped me, and forced me to nod my head. It was so dirty and I couldn't bear it anymore. I went crazy halfway through and rushed out without considering the consequences. They were only 5 and 9 years old, but I managed to break free and run out. After coming out, I realized that if I could break free, it meant that this could have been avoided, and yet I compromised at the time. The fact has already happened, so what's the point of running out later? It would have been better to continue enduring the violation until the end, staying in the darkness without pain. It is painful to step out of the darkness into the light. I shouldn't have entered the house and I shouldn't have rushed out at the wrong time. It was my fault from beginning to end. One month later, I gathered the courage to confront him and said, "You should apologize to me!" He said, "Even if I pinned you down, didn't you nod your head? It was your own choice. You were asking for it, so what does it have to do with me?" I couldn't refute his words. Yes, even though he pinned me down, I didn't refuse, I nodded my head, it was my own choice. Even though I got hurt, I was also an accomplice with him. I harmed myself together with him, I consented to it, so what right do I have to demand an apology from him?

answers.answer_text: Hello, the subject. I really want to give you a hug first. Seeing you slowly open up yourself, it really takes a lot of courage. After reading your question, I can feel your guilt and self-blame. You blame yourself for not making the "right" choice at the time and for missing the opportunity to save yourself. Dear, what I want to say is, you were only five years old at the time. You didn't know what it meant to you, you only knew that the other person violated you and you felt immense shame. You shouldn't have to bear all of this. You were much weaker compared to a nine-year-old boy. Before you escaped, the other person used physical violence to threaten you, and you were forced to nod your head in agreement. When you ran out, you also felt despair because you felt that it had already happened and was irreversible. The reason you went back is because you felt too ashamed inside to face the light, and returning to the darkness made you less afraid. It was a desperate choice for a child. In my opinion, you did not make the "wrong" choice, in fact, you were always protecting yourself. The other person used physical violence against you, and you chose to nod your head to protect yourself. When you ran out, you found that it was more painful to walk from darkness to light than to stay in darkness, so you returned to darkness. These were the best choices you made for yourself at that time. When you confronted the other person a month later, they hurt you again and they said that you agreed of your own accord, and you didn't refuse. The other person used their "smarter" logic to refute you, leaving you speechless. But you need to see that the fact is that you didn't really want to agree to this matter, you were under the other person's violent threat and had no choice but to nod your head. You made that choice to protect yourself from further harm. In your response to me, you mentioned that another child involved, who was in the second grade when this happened, took it out and bragged about it, leading to the whole class ostracizing you and subjecting you to verbal abuse. I feel very sorry for the harm you have suffered. When I listened to your story, when I replied to your questions, I could feel that deep despair. So what else could you do at the time, facing a stronger force, you couldn't do anything. Your anger had nowhere to be expressed, so it turned inward towards yourself. Perhaps all these years, you have been extremely disgusted with yourself. Our greatest pain is the inability to accept the truth. We desperately want to change what cannot be changed and hope that the past can be rewritten. However, I believe that the choices a person makes at any moment in their life are the best choices. I believe a person's life inherently has this kind of strength. The child in you was the one who was hurt, the frightened and helpless child hiding in the corner of your heart has been there for many years, and now we need to use more love to nurture her, to accompany her so she can come out of that corner. I remember a line from the American author Tara Westover: "Who writes history? I think it is I." We are the ones who create history, and at the same time, we are the ones who write history. We are our own history. The past has become the history of the past, but our lives are not over yet, and we have the ability to write a new history, don't we? When that child from the past walked from darkness to light, she was scared, unable to bear the pain of stepping into the light. But today, I see you coming out of the darkness, exposing your wounds to the sunlight. Thank you for your courage, thank you for your honesty, from you I feel the power of life, a power that moves me. Today, in my article, I wrote this sentence and I want to share it with you: "What is pain? If you can accept this pain, it is a gift, a gift from life." That's my answer, I hope it helps you. Wishing you the best.

Hello! I feel sorry for your experience. Here's a warm hug for you! What really hurts me is your self-blame. You accepted their unreasonable logic and believed that you were complicit in hurting yourself. This way of thinking is what truly breaks my heart. After something happens, we look back and analyze the situation, only then can we make better judgments. So we blame ourselves, regret, and create countless "if...then..." sentences in our minds. However, these better judgments are based on knowing the outcome clearly afterwards. At that time, you didn't have the ability to predict. It's unfair to blame yourself using the information you gained later. If we all had the power to predict, we wouldn't expose ourselves to danger, deception, or take the wrong paths. But that's not how things work, many experiences are only learned after going through them. When they held you down, you didn't know if you had the ability to break free, it was only after you managed to escape that you realized you could. You regret why you didn't do it earlier, but at that time you didn't know! You said, what's the use of escaping now that the fact has already happened. It does matter, at least you made the effort to escape, you tried hard, and you succeeded. You think it's better to endure the violation until it's over, staying in the darkness without pain. If it were really like that, you would also regret it, regret why you didn't do anything and just endured it, you would hate your helplessness. So in this situation, no matter what you do, there will always be harm and regret. Since the event has already happened, try to accept it, imagine embracing that injured self, instead of blaming her. Later on, you had the courage to confront the other person, I think that was a very brave act, and you deserve praise for it. However, your courage only lasted for a moment and was immediately defeated by the other person's illogical argument. How can this be considered voluntary? It's like someone holding a gun and asking you to give them your money, and you comply, and then they say, "You gave it willingly." Is that considered voluntary? Of course not. It's just a form of self-protection in a dangerous situation. So, when you didn't resist, when you nodded under pressure, it was still coercion, not voluntary. Don't accept their illogical logic. Of course, you have the right to demand an apology, and you should even demand them to pay a certain price. So, don't blame yourself, you haven't done anything wrong, it is the people who hurt you that are wrong. If you find it difficult to overcome this incident, seek help from others, talk to friends, find a therapist, take it slowly, give yourself more time, and you will get better. Hugs to you, the world and I love you! (^_-).

Hello, after carefully reading the story you described in your question, although I can see your self-doubt and helplessness in the story, I believe you also see your courage and strength in this incident, just as you said in your question, a person does not suffer in the dark, but suffers when they move towards the light. I deeply understand this feeling, so I want to discuss a few aspects with you in the hope of inspiring your current self and helping your past self. [Your strong rebuttal hit the core of your "self-denial"] In the story, I can see that you have affirmation and complaints about your actions in the entire incident. As a young child, you were not sure whether you could break free from their control in that situation because you didn't know your own strength. This is a normal psychological state. Everyone is unable to measure themselves well when they are young, not knowing what they can achieve. Therefore, when they feel in danger, their instinct is to protect their own physical safety. Faced with a much stronger boy, choosing to comply is the best way to survive and it is almost an instinctive reaction. However, when you muster the courage to confront him, he refutes your claims and blames you. It's like a murderer holding a knife to someone's neck and asking, "Can I kill you?" This initial creation of fear actually makes people lose their rationality because the knife is already at their throat, and regardless of whether they nod or not, we would believe that he won't let us go. Therefore, this itself is a fallacy, based on the fact that he threatened you with force, forcing you to agree. So, all the fault lies with him, even in the face of the law, it is still his fault. [Growth always comes with pain, but life will eventually reward you] I understand the pain of feeling wronged and hesitant to move forward. Just as you said in your question, "One does not suffer in the dark, but suffers when they move towards the light." But do you know why people who stay in the dark do not feel pain? It's not because there is no pain, but because they are numb. They have numbed themselves in continuous pain and have given up on seeking sunlight. But fortunately, you are not the person who stays in the dark. You bravely chose to step out of the darkness and embrace the light, even though this process is accompanied by a lot of pain. But it is all worth it because growth inevitably comes with inner growth. In fact, all growth is such a process. The essence of growth is constantly breaking one's own self and then regenerating a completely new self. The process of breaking oneself is constantly self-denial, which is what you are currently experiencing and facing. Therefore, you will feel pain and find it difficult to accept yourself. When feeling pain, you will question your own actions, especially when you feel pain, you will want to retreat back to the shell that once numbed you. However, you still persist and continue to break through, change yourself, and I am very pleased to see your growth and courage. [Persist in your courage and confidence, be brave in protecting yourself] Now, you already have the ability to protect yourself. You can have many ways to protect yourself, and I believe you can think of these methods, such as promptly informing your parents and teachers, or even reporting to the police, all these methods will help you handle this matter fairly, rather than getting involved in a quarrel with him. Have you chosen to do this now? But I believe this incident is also enlightening to you, you should learn to protect yourself in life, learn to identify which invitations are friendly and which appointments are dangerous. At the same time, you should always maintain a firm determination to fight to the end and always believe that their actions are indefensible morally and legally. Of course, more importantly, I hope that after experiencing this incident, you can adjust your cognitive thinking through self-improvement. We need to understand that behind every event, there are two reasons: "ourselves" and "external environment". In this incident, the reason lies in the "external environment" or "that 9-year-old boy". Knowing these two methods of finding reasons, we should no longer shoulder all the problems by ourselves but instead analyze them from both perspectives. Because too much self-blame is not conducive to our own growth and will bring us a lot of negative emotions and psychological distress. I hope you, the brave one, can truly break free from distress and embrace the sunshine.

Hi, Lulu, nice to meet you. This is Aliang, a person who is willing to be your little sunshine. I'm glad that we can meet here, and I want to give you a big hug. After reading about Lulu's experience, Aliang also feels deeply connected. Aliang also understands this feeling very well because, like this kind of thing, Aliang has also experienced it before. It seems that in this world, treating women has never been so fair. When Aliang was very young, there were times when Aliang felt helpless about the world and even wanted to end it all, feeling that there was no brightness left in this world. In this world, some people always treat women differently. This is something we cannot predict because we are not others, and we do not know the "good and evil" in their hearts. Many times, the reason why we cannot get out of this shadow is because of our "disgust" towards this thing. These things are like a "brand" on our bodies, deeply engraved in our hearts, constantly reminding us, making us intensely conflicted internally. It took Aliang a long time to get out of these shadows. Here, Aliang knows that certain things have already happened, and when we reminisce about the past, they are of no use. Aliang wants to share how I have overcome these years, hoping that after Lulu reads it, there will be some answers. "Don't force other people's faults onto yourself." Aliang knows that Lulu has always been obsessed with the experience at the age of five, and even though he mustered the courage to confront him face to face, he was unexpectedly refuted and left speechless. This must have been a big blow for Lulu, but Aliang cannot give a strong suggestion like others, saying to "use the law" to punish him, because in a certain sense, Aliang is just as cowardly as Lulu. Here, Aliang can only provide some self-healing methods as advice because, when certain things are mentioned again, it is like rubbing salt on the wound. In this matter, we need to understand that the original "fault" lies not with you, but with that boy. The reason you can't get out of this shadow is that the harm he caused you cannot be repaired. Although you really want to go back to that moment in the past, we cannot turn back time in this world. It is precisely because time cannot be reversed that we become more obsessed with certain things. Because we care more, we cannot cross over. It is as if these "mistakes" would not have happened if we had refused at that time. This infinite loop of "possibility" stimulates our brain's nerves over and over, leaving us restless all day long. But if we think about it, if we keep caring about things in our hearts, doesn't that mean we lose too much of the "beauty and meaning" in our lives? Formerly, Aliang always saw the "terrible" version of myself from the past and always believed that such things were like a "stain" that existed, resulting in increasing self-doubt. And with self-doubt like a "stain," we constantly belittle ourselves in life, ultimately leading to the result of becoming more and more "terrible". I forcefully put the faults of others on myself, unable to get out of it, which led to encountering "terrible" people in those "terrible" days. If we want to truly move on from this, what we need is only one thing, and that is "courage" because only courage will make us fearless. We should not fear the bad things that have happened to us but rather strengthen our "inner self". How should we strengthen our "inner self"? Here, Aliang gives Lulu some advice: go out more, on weekends, plan something for yourself, visit nearby cities, and if you have extra time, travel further. After communicating with different people, your world will become brighter. At the same time, you will be more willing to face the "fragile" self inside you. We know our own shortcomings, but that does not mean we will be "terrible". We don't need to reach the level of "the world will kiss me with pain, and I will respond with a song." We can live a rich and colorful life. Find your own self-worth, do things you love in the fields you like, and achieve something. When our life is no longer based on the "stain," your whole world will become brighter. Read more. Maybe here, you feel that reading doesn't have much to help you, but often, we can find answers to the perpetual questions in books. Here, Aliang recommends that Lulu read books on how to overcome the limitations of life, how they strive to live towards the sun when encountering difficulties. Aliang recommends the book "When You Fly Like a Bird Towards Your Mountain." The above is only Aliang's personal opinion, a summary of Aliang's "unpleasant" experiences over the years, because in life, some things are in "equivalent exchange." When one door closes, another will definitely open, but this window needs us to find it ourselves. Finally, Aliang here wishes Lulu a happy life, and in the future, Aliang will encourage and support Lulu in life. Let's cheer together!

Give the original poster a hug! You can feel the OP's internal repression, anxiety, and conflicts. Anyone in this situation would feel a great deal of pressure, pain, and distress. However, the OP also shows us their confident, brave, and strong side. They can actively resist and protect themselves when they realize the danger, instead of allowing the tragedy of harm to continue. Even though the OP still experiences some harm, they at least have the courage to resist and protect themselves when faced with harm. And by doing so, they have achieved some success: they have prevented further harm to themselves and have demanded an apology from the perpetrators. The OP has done really well in these two aspects, and their courage deserves praise! For the OP, at the time, they were still young, just a five-year-old child. Their understanding of being stripped naked and what would happen next was limited. They may have regarded it as a "fun" game and didn't realize the harm it had on them. Moreover, there were more people on the other side, who were stronger, so the OP instinctively believed it would be better to not resist and that the risk would be smaller, without any life-threatening danger. This can be understood. It doesn't mean that the OP didn't want to resist at all; part of it was due to not knowing what was happening and how to deal with it, so they could only observe silently for the time being. The reason the OP eventually resisted was because their inner emotions could no longer bear it. It shows that the OP's inner suppressed emotions were very powerful, to the extent that they went beyond their conscious control and had to "erupt" in order for the OP to "break free" without caring about the consequences, and to protect themselves by resisting harm. From the OP's narrative, it seems that a large part of the repression in their inner emotions stems from a cognitive understanding of "dirtiness," or rather, their inner sense of morality is too strong. This also influences the OP's self-perception, which causes them to sink into the painful "darkness" even after successfully resisting and protecting themselves. The inner self has a rigid "bias" in its understanding and thinking, and external environmental stimuli only exacerbate these "biased" leaning, making self-perception even more "biased." Just like when the OP asked the other party to apologize, and they blamed the responsibility for the harmful behavior on the OP, saying that the OP nodded in agreement at the time, the pressure brought by these responsibilities also transferred to the OP, making their inner self even more distressed. Now, the OP wants to correct these thoughts, which is equivalent to "overturning" their self-perception and abilities to some extent. It will be difficult for the self to understand, accept, and recognize this. Therefore, the OP can try to accept these events that have already happened, accept their own ignorance at the time, accept the harm caused by the situation itself, accept and recognize the effort they put into protecting themselves, and accept the conflicts and confrontations in their own thoughts. In real life, they should do what they should do. The past is already gone, no matter how much we regret or suffer, it will not disappear. It's like a scar, maybe we can't erase it, but we can give it more careful and warm care, so that it won't be harmed in the future. We cannot choose the past, but we can choose how we live in the future. Putting our energy into letting go, looking ahead, can make us live more easily, freely, and peacefully. Dwelling on the past will only make us suffer, anxious, and afraid. Let go of the past and there will be a chance for us to carry on living the present and the future with ease, naturalness, and happiness.

Hello. I'm fortunate to give you some advice. From what I've read, I want to tell you that when you were 5 years old and experienced such an incident, you were not a co-conspirator. You were able to break free from their "clutches", and you were really brave! From your current perspective, you may think that your behavior at that time was "unbearable", or even "cowardly", or had some sense of "voluntariness". The reason for these viewpoints is that you have grown up, and when you look back on yourself at that time, you naturally think that your behavior at that time was so unbearable. Analyzing up to this point, I think you should have some doubts about your self-disgust thoughts. Next, we will analyze from your childhood experience. * The process of recalling memories can be painful and unwilling to face, but please believe that you will successfully heal. * Did your 5-year-old self understand the concept of sexual abuse? * When playing hide and seek with friends, why did you enter the abandoned house? * What did you see after entering the house? * After seeing these things, what was the first thing you thought of? * Was it fear? Helplessness? Confusion? * Or did you keenly feel that the other party would have inappropriate intentions, and therefore fear? * What was your initial reaction when they held you down? * Was your mind blank? Or...? * What did the sexual abuse mean to you at that time? Then, let's look at the things the other party questioned you about. * They were older than you and the ones who perpetrated the sexual abuse. For them, their own mistakes may not be a big deal, so they would question whether it was your consent. * Your brave escape from their "clutches" was actually something they did not expect. Deep down, they were also worried that the situation would be exposed. They wanted to confuse the situation and make you feel that it was your own problem and your own responsibility. * In this situation, the other party wants to minimize or even escape their own mistakes. Therefore, we don't have to shoulder the consequences of their mistakes, do we? Based on all of the above, I wonder if there has been some shift in your mindset. Experiencing sexual abuse is indeed shameful for oneself, but we also need to see our own "bravery" and our determination to "uphold justice" behind the shame, right? I believe this experience has provided you with great motivation to better protect yourself in the future and to see others clearly and face life bravely. I wish you all the best.

I don't know how old the questioner is now, but I guess they must be at least in their teens. In that case, I think the questioner should have this understanding: a 5-year-old child does not have the ability to act, so they cannot judge a 5-year-old child's behavior based on their current perspective. To exaggerate a bit, even if something happened when they were 5 and it was caused by the injured child themselves, it is not the 5-year-old's fault. Moreover, the 5-year-old child was being subjected to violence at the time. So, the problem that the questioner faces now is actually how to make themselves aware that the 5-year-old self did nothing wrong. The reason the questioner has this idea of "although they were also hurt, they were actually an accomplice in hurting themselves" is because this matter did not receive a proper resolution at the time, and the influence of people around them caused the unresolved aggressive feelings resulting from the incident to be internalized as self-attacks. The subsequent feeling of being "dirty" that the questioner has is actually a result of this internalized aggression. Under the constant impact of this aggression, the questioner consciously believes that they are "dirty". This is actually a form of self-punishment. If the questioner remains in this state of internalized aggression, they probably won't feel pain. However, now the questioner wants to break free from it, so the result is the pain of "staying in the darkness is not painful, but it is painful to step into the light" as the questioner described. This pain, however, is an inevitable part of personal growth, much like the pain of childbirth. Only through this kind of anguish can one experience the joy of rebirth. Therefore, what the questioner needs to do is to abandon their previous understanding and look at the behavior of their 5-year-old self from a different perspective. For example, in the process of the incident, they bravely managed to escape, which most likely saved them from more serious harm. This is truly remarkable for a 5-year-old child. For example, even though they were very afraid and worried after the incident, they were actually able to demand an apology from the person responsible face to face a month later, which is an even more remarkable action. You see, even adults, not many people would be able to request an apology from someone who has caused them harm, let alone do it in person. So, what the questioner needs to do is to find those inner strengths that have been constantly overlooked in the past and make themselves aware that the 5-year-old child, although they may have felt powerless in many ways, possesses even more internal strength. When the questioner is able to connect those neglected inner strengths with their present self, they should be able to complete the transformation from darkness to light. That's it. I hope it can be helpful to the questioner.

Hello, the title of the question, I feel very sad after reading your description. There is a saying that "an unhappy childhood takes a lifetime to heal," and it can be seen how much your childhood experiences have affected you even now. Actually, anyone will experience various problems during their childhood, but some are just minor issues, while others are major events that are not easily let go of. For you, it is the latter. Here, I have some suggestions in the hope that they can help you. 1. Don't engage in victim-blaming. As a victim, it was the right thing for you to escape from the house. You did nothing wrong, and you must remember that. In whatever we do, we often have thoughts like "If I had done this or that, I would have done better," "If I had another chance, I wouldn't be like this," or "Why did I do that back then?" However, no matter what, the past is already gone and cannot be relived. Therefore, don't always feel sad because you struggled too late. Struggling and escaping itself is a conscious resistance, and for someone so young, your actions were already great. The one who was wrong is the other person, so don't always blame yourself. Change your current thoughts and tell yourself that you were great back then. 2. Learn to practice self-psychological guidance. When you find yourself always thinking about these things, try to let go. How do you let go? For example, divert your attention and try to give yourself positive thoughts. Those things have already passed, and they will never happen again in the future. "I will become stronger in the future and face the future with a better attitude." Convince yourself more and strengthen your self-confidence. At the same time, when you are feeling particularly down, you can go out for a walk. Don't let past events limit you. If things become too overwhelming, you can also try talking to a friend to relieve the uncontrollable emotions at that time. 3. Read more books or practice meditation. Actually, if you read more books, you may find that there are many people in the world who have similar experiences to yours. Each person struggles and works hard in their own life and finds ways to overcome it. I think reading books is not only to learn from them but also to find strength in books. Since the past cannot be changed, find ways to make yourself stronger. Also, I recently discovered that meditation can help you understand yourself more clearly and separate yourself from your thoughts. You can try meditating to shift or change your focus on this matter, and thus find better ways to improve yourself. Finally, I wish you well!

Honey, I see that you are confused about personal development. You mentioned being forced and violated when you were young, but you discovered that you could escape, although you still compromised before.
