Even though my instructor said I was already doing well, I still bought it, and after purchasing it, the psychological burden was really minor. As for dealing with the instructor's criticism, have you ever read any online jokes? Which instructor doesn't scold people? Just take it in stride. Avoid interpersonal relationships and anxiety. You know you have to face them sooner or later. In fact, after you get your license, you won't have much to do with the instructor anymore, so it's better to end this experience sooner, right?

Hugging you, being picky and criticized in your overall evaluation makes it unbearable for you. Not just you, no one can tolerate such a coach. We didn't come here to listen to his criticism. Don't you agree? This coach is too extreme. There's no way to continue learning to drive, try changing coaches. Additionally, what I want to say is that maybe you have been living in an environment where you are constantly criticized, which makes you have a low self-esteem and always feel that nothing is good enough. Especially in such a critical environment, it further lowers your self-worth and makes you feel terrible. In this state, it's impossible to handle learning how to drive. In China, people have very low self-esteem, focusing on finding faults with themselves, but it's difficult to find their own strengths. Because no one has ever praised us, all they do is nitpick. Now, try to find three of your own strengths every day, love yourself, nourish yourself, and slowly you will start to feel better.

Hello, OP. It's clear that you are a very strong-willed person, and I can tell that you have put a lot of effort into learning to drive. I hope your instructor can see your efforts and progress, but unexpectedly, all you've received is criticism from them. Anyone would be affected by such a strong contrast and it would impact their motivation to keep going. In this situation, I hope you can give yourself a hug. It must be really difficult if you have put in all that effort and yet feel unseen. So, don't focus on external evaluations anymore. Pay more attention to yourself. You have enough strength to decide how you feel and not let external instabilities affect you.

Hello! I hope you're doing well. I have also been preparing for the driver's license exam recently. If something is causing you such severe anxiety, it might be a good idea to take a step back and give yourself some time to relax and recharge before attempting it again. Besides, learning to drive is not a "life-altering event," and many people choose not to learn at all. But if you decide to take the exam, don't let small failures or negative comments from your instructor affect your mood and confidence. If they say your driving is not good, you can say they're not teaching well. Show life that you're not afraid. It's not a big deal. I also have some tips to share with you: when you're feeling nervous, try blowing air onto your thumb. It might help calm your heartbeat and relieve some stress. When you're not practicing, you can read posts on Weibo or Zhihu about funny and relatable exam experiences. It's a great way to relax and realize that you're not alone in this. If you're interested, you can also mentally go through the driving procedures. Practicing is key to mastering this skill. (Not recommended) If you're feeling too anxious before the exam, you can ask your instructor or classmates for tranquilizers. Some exam centers might have them prepared, but it depends on your health condition.

question: Am I still considered a sadomasochist (SM)? I am a masochist, but I feel incredibly miserable when engaging in it.
description: I found that I have a sense of pleasure when I am slapped, and I consider myself to be a masochist. A few months ago, I found an sadist online and the initial conversations were fine, so I decided to meet up with him. The training went smoothly and he was gentle when we weren't engaging in that. However, after meeting in person, everything changed. I found that he would get extremely angry very easily, even if I just made a small comment (I believe that in an SM relationship, it should be a two-way street, so I also wanted to express my opinions). When he got angry, he would verbally abuse me, and it was really frightening. At first, I could accept it, but as our arguments became more frequent, almost every other day (and it was always him berating me), I gradually fell into a low emotional state. I feel a lot of pressure and anxiety, and I have nightmares at night and wake up early in the morning. Sometimes the disputes would last until one or two in the morning, and he would even make me do tasks in the middle of the night, guaranteeing a sleepless night. Now, I am afraid when he doesn't chat with me, but I am also afraid when he does. Because I believe that I have invested a lot in this dynamic and he also has a large collection of videos of me; however, when he does reach out, it's either to do online tasks or to argue (I am someone who is barely into feeling love, and most of the tasks he assigns are related to sex). I am very restless, but I cannot say a word of complaint, I have to pretend that I really like it, because if I contradict him, he will start arguing with me. Am I really a masochist, or am I just not a good one?

answers.answer_text: It is an honor to be invited to answer your question! From your description, it is evident that the current relationship is causing you a lot of pain and stress. The main source of this pressure is the difference in play styles between both parties. More specifically, each side has different points of excitement. Due to the specific nature of the SM relationship, your partner (the "s") may be focused on their own points of excitement and may overlook yours. Over time, the accumulation of these experiences may start to overshadow the thrill and pleasure you initially derived from SM, leading to increased pain. In actuality, in an SM relationship, although it may appear that the "s" is in control, they need to discover the "m's" points of excitement and the inner desires that they are hesitant or unwilling to surpass. This process helps the "m" break their own boundaries. Each breakthrough fully satisfies the threshold for physical pleasure. This continuous process of exploration and breakthroughs generates excitement and pleasure. Thus, it seems like the "s" has control, but in essence, the "m" is still in control, and the "s" suppresses their own desires. An "s" who disregards the "m's" preferences and solely seeks to fulfill their own desires is an inadequate "s." This may also be one of the reasons for your pain. As for your question about your answers, from a single sentence, it is evident that you desire contact from the other person, indicating that you lean towards being compatible. In conclusion, there is no qualification of being suitable or not, only whether or not it is a good fit. Lastly, I hope you won't be troubled anymore, and remember that the world and I love you!

Yes, that's right. I'm also not sure if I am an 's'. I haven't made any attempts. Girls have more opportunities to try it out. Every person can experience a slight pleasure in inflicting or receiving abuse. Girls should still be cautious because the other person has some information about you. You need to be alert. What you're struggling and caring about are these things. It seems like you are being passive and there is no secure SM relationship. This is my understanding.

I don't really understand why people feel the need to label themselves, to define who they are. Will it make them feel more secure inside? I just want to take a look at your relationship from a relational perspective. We met online, and when we met in person, I found that he gets angry easily and tends to take it out on you. If you can handle it, then your relationship might be okay. But if you can't handle it, you'll slowly get trapped in the emotions. So, have you ever asked yourself, what are you getting from this relationship? Is it what you initially pursued?

question: A sixth-grade girl returns home very late. My aunt is seeking help from me, how can I assist her?
description: My cousin is in the sixth grade. Recently, she often comes home around 10 PM. Her parents often argue, and my aunt turned to me for help. How can I help her?

answers.answer_text: Children in sixth grade have entered puberty and have their own resistance and challenges to their parents. This often manifests as a sense of alienation from their parents, especially for boys. If parents argue frequently, the child will be the biggest victim, surrounded by various negative emotions such as fear, anger, and worry. Therefore, it is normal for them to want to escape from this home, staying out late or not coming home at all. Girls growing up in such unloving families are most easily deceived by men. There are many difficult places for teenagers at night, and it is very dangerous for a girl to be outside late at night. They often make bad friends and can be harmed or corrupted. Your aunt is seeking your help and she can only see that the child is coming home late, so she can sense the risk, but she does not know about the mental torment the child is experiencing at home. You can first tell her to put herself in your cousin's shoes, experience the feeling of constant quarreling between parents, and help her understand the child's hardship in order to restrain their behavior as a couple, argue less, and create a harmonious and warm family atmosphere. When the family atmosphere is harmonious, the child will naturally be willing to come home. However, this alone is not enough because your cousin has grown up in an environment where their parents constantly argue and has already endured significant psychological trauma. You can tell your aunt and uncle to sit down as a family and have a meaningful conversation. The parents should sincerely express their inner feelings to the child and apologize sincerely for not providing such a nurturing environment, in order to earn your cousin's understanding and forgiveness. Then, talk to the child slowly about the danger of staying out late and advise her to come home early at night.

Many times, home should be a warm haven, but when it is filled with arguments, many people may slowly start to escape. The child is already in sixth grade and has his own judgment on some matters, such as coming home late. I wonder how the parents handled it when it first happened. If the child didn't say anything the first time it happened, and the parents just kept scolding and even argued with each other about it, blaming each other for not taking care of the child, the focus which should have been on where the child went, later extended to mutual complaints. We all know that when we encounter something that is troublesome and beyond our control, we often choose to escape. So when children see that their family is always full of conflicts, they may want to leave this family. If at that time we could sit down and talk with the child, telling them that although public safety is relatively good now, she still doesn't have enough ability to protect herself, so sometimes it's better to let the parents know in advance if she will be coming home late. Parents won't interfere with everything the child does, but hope that the child can inform them of her whereabouts, so that parents can pick her up in time. Sometimes we need to think from a different perspective, and children also need understanding and support from their parents. We can suggest that aunt first figure out what the arguments are really about. If the same problem has been argued countless times without a resolution, then both sides need to reflect and find the root cause of the problem in order to solve it. After both parties have stabilized their emotions, they should find a time to sit down and have a heart-to-heart talk with the child. If necessary, they can apologize to the child, letting the child know that adults also make mistakes, as long as both parties realize it and can correct it. If the child still refuses to communicate, we can also chat with the child and see what has happened to her recently and what we can do. The world and I love you.

Analysis from Tan Yang: 
1. Every problem a child has can be traced back to their parents, so when parents discover that their child is coming home late, they should first reflect on whether there is a problem with their family education. Are they too busy working and neglecting to accompany their child?
2. "How can I help her?" Tell your aunt not to just scold her child all the time, but to spend more time with and communicate with her child. Maybe because they are usually dominant, your cousin doesn't confide in them at all. At this time, find someone who gets along well with your cousin and have a deep conversation with her. Find out the reason for her late return, and that will be good.
3. Let your aunt and uncle argue less, or don't argue in front of the child. Parents' arguments, emotional discord, and domestic violence have a huge impact on children. So instead of scolding the child, it's better to reflect on oneself. Your cousin's biggest problem is lack of love. And companionship is the best love. Thank you for your question, and may all the beauty in the world come to you as expected.

Hello, first of all, it's best that you ask your cousin why she came back so late and explain the whole situation clearly. Also, advise your aunt not to blame her too much and clarify everything. Most likely, the main reason is still a quarrel. Anyway, ask your cousin first, and you should know what's going on. Do what you should do, speak nicely to both sides, haha, advising others to reconcile means running back and forth and saying good things about each other. If she has been frequently going out in the past year, do you know this frequently from her parents or did they tell you? Investigate this matter thoroughly before giving advice, don't believe everything from either side.

Hello, I hope this answer can give you some help. My advice is the same as other responders, first ask the child about the reason for coming home late. When asking, it is important to stay calm and composed, as sixth graders may have some rebellious tendencies. Additionally, the parents' arguments may be a significant reason why she doesn't want to come home. Home should be a safe haven, and nobody wants to come home to arguments. Therefore, helping to resolve her parents' issues is also part of the solution.

Don't let the child know that it was your aunt who asked you for help. In case the child finds out, they may not tell the truth. You can tell the child that it has been raining outside these days and they should come home early, or have the child's mother tell them in the morning that she has cooked their favorite dishes for dinner, and to come home early after school to shower and eat. Ask the child if they have a lot of homework lately, or if their grades haven't been good, which is why they are coming home late. Explain that going out at night with other kids also worries their parents. Try to prevent the child's parents from arguing.

question: Bought a small table to put on the bed, feeling anxious when seeing others studying, what should I do?
description: I have a small table on my bed that I usually use for studying. When my roommate started school, she bought a table curtain to block it off and then she also bought a table for her own bed. I can see her studying underneath from the gap when I go up and down the bed, and even hear the sound of her flipping through books after eleven o'clock at night when the lights are off. It feels like she's studying all the time and rarely engages in any leisure activities. When I see this, I start feeling anxious. Although my grades are slightly better than hers, I still feel defensive towards her. So now I study secretly as well, but whenever I hear the sound of her flipping through books on her bed at night, I can't help but feel restless. What should I do?

answers.answer_text: Hello, dear asker, sending you a comforting hug~ I completely understand your thoughts. Maybe you can show concern about whether studying for long periods without taking breaks is harmful to her health. Then find an opportunity to chat with her and listen to her perspectives on studying. Your care might break the cycle of not communicating and make your interactions more natural and harmonious. Suggestion analysis one: Suspicion caused by lack of communication. I believe it is normal for roommates to compare their grades because we all have a competitive spirit. It is the lack of communication that fills the relationship between roommates with suspicion. If we casually complain in the dormitory like, "Ah, I studied for a long time today, so tired" or "X, I'm feeling thirsty, going to pour some hot water, do you want a cup too?" or "I just found out that this study website has a lot of resources, I'll send you the link", showing appropriate concern will make roommates feel at ease. Many things are imagined solely by you, so the dormitory atmosphere becomes tense. I think your roommate is probably also startled, not knowing what you're thinking. Suggestion analysis two: Cooperative learning leads to further progress. According to your description, "I feel like she is studying all day long, so now I am secretly studying too." It seems that many people like to work hard on their own and silently move towards a direction. However, from elementary school to middle school to high school and college, the higher the level of institutions, the more open and cooperative the attitude towards learning becomes. For example, for scientific research, having a team is crucial. If you have high goals and want to pursue further education in a prestigious institution, learning to cooperate is the first thing you need to prepare for. When you and your roommate can help each other and progress together, your efficiency will increase. Then, you can discuss many things, such as not having to study day and night or avoiding conflicts between studying and resting time.

question: My boyfriend secretly went to the internet cafe to play games without telling me and lied to me saying he was working overtime. What should I do?
description: He has been going to play games constantly in the past few days, not just once. The last time he went to play games, he went to the internet cafe and played for half an hour before he couldn't resist telling me. Tonight, he finished work at six and didn't come home directly. Instead, he went to the internet cafe in the neighborhood to play games until 9:30 p.m. and claimed that he finished work at that time. I always thought he was working hard and prepared dinner for him, waiting for him to come back. Tonight, I saw his phone and got really angry. I feel like it's not about him playing games, but about him lying to me. Because I have never cared about him playing games, I just asked him to go to the internet cafe less often since we have a computer at home. Also, the reason I'm angry is that I worked hard to make him dinner, and he went to play games behind my back and came back saying he was tired from work. So how should I get along peacefully with him?

answers.answer_text: I am very angry. I feel like it's not just about him playing games, but I'm angry because I worked hard to cook for him, and he went to play games behind my back and came back saying he was so tired from work. So how can I get along with him peacefully? Hello! Can you try to think from his perspective? If it's possible to play games at home, why does he insist on going to internet cafes? Try to communicate with him and explain that you don't mind him playing games, but you do mind him going to internet cafes to play games. Promise not to interfere if he plays games at home. Make it clear to him that you are angry when he lies and deceives you, and that there will be food waiting for him if he comes home from work, but no food if he goes to play games. The best way to get along with him peacefully is to communicate well, express your thoughts and needs, and understand and meet each other's needs.

question: I am 16 years old and a sensitive and melancholic person. Do I have depression?
description: I am sixteen years old. Ever since I got a tablet, I always feel very down. I am a sensitive person and often have thoughts of suicide, wondering if I am worthless. I had an argument with my mom today and with my little brother yesterday. I feel very irritable and my tears always uncontrollably fall. I never seem to make progress in my studies, always being discouraged by others. I feel really bad, I think I have depression. I am losing a lot of hair when I scratch my head, but I'm too scared to tell my parents that I'm feeling very sad.
keywords: Emotion, depressive emotions, emotional intelligence, fragile and tearful.

answers.answer_text: Hello, dear reader. From your description, I can feel your emotions. You have bravely taken the first step by expressing your feelings on this platform and describing them in such detail. No matter how bad you are feeling right now, you are already moving towards a better place, and it shows that your inner strength and courage are sufficient. It seems that you have not reached the level of severe depression but are just unsure about how to deal with certain issues. At 16 years old, you have so much ahead of you. This age is something many of us wish we could go back to. Perhaps you can focus more on the things you like and are interested in. You mentioned that your mood deteriorated after getting a tablet, so perhaps you can consider putting it away and living as you did before. You mentioned that you think you are not good and lack confidence. This is called self-efficacy in psychology. At 16 years old, you still have countless opportunities to prove yourself. If you haven't even tried yet, how can you easily dismiss yourself? If you want to improve and become better, you should first become optimistic. Only when you are optimistic will you have the motivation to do things well. If you are not progressing in your studies, consider whether your study methods are incorrect or if you need to put in more effort. Believe that you can improve your grades. Lastly, regarding your relationship with your family, it is normal for teenagers to have some conflicts with their families during adolescence. However, no matter what, you must believe that parents do not want to harm their children, they are just trying to guide them based on their own experiences and help them avoid unnecessary mistakes. Try talking to them more and sharing your thoughts and feelings. I believe they will be willing to listen. There are many people in this world who love you, and many people waiting for you to love them back.

Hello, I hope my answer can bring you some insights. I understand your feelings very well because each of us has experienced such a low point in life. It's okay to allow ourselves to have these sad emotions, and at the same time, we should accept them. It's already great that we can acknowledge our emotions. Now the next step is to figure out what to do (#^.^#) Regarding hair loss, reducing anxiety and getting enough sleep may help improve the situation.

question: If I were to kill everyone who has wronged me, what would happen?
description: There are always people intentionally causing trouble, speaking in a sarcastic manner. What would happen if I were to kill all those who provoke me?

answers.answer_text: Hello, if you killed everyone who has wronged you, it would not only destroy them, but also destroy yourself. If this revenge requires you to sacrifice your own life, do you think it's worth it? At least in my opinion, it is definitely not worth it. If someone is causing trouble and speaking in a sarcastic manner, can't you just stay away from these people? Out of sight, out of mind. It's really that simple. If they really cross the line and disturb you, you can choose to call the police and let them handle it. Not everyone is like this, so stay away from unfriendly people and seek out those who you can get along with, who share common topics and interests. Go enjoy the beauty of life and stay away from these unpleasant things. Hugs to you, the world and I love you! (^_-).

question: A 15-year-old girl, after one month in high school, is still not adjusting well and is feeling depressed and anxious.
description: In the past, I was always happy and had an optimistic mindset. However, in high school, everyone around me was unfamiliar and the environment was unfamiliar. Moreover, it's far from home and I can't go home every day. Slowly, in this month, I feel very sad and uncomfortable. I also start to feel nervous when communicating with others. While they have happy smiles, I have no desire to smile at all. Every day, I put on a brave face and try to smile, but deep inside, I feel very sad and unable to control it. I also want to cry. I try to encourage myself to change the current situation, but I feel like I have more and more problems and I feel a bit hopeless. I feel like I don't frown, but my brow hurts every day. I don't know if it's a psychological effect, but I can't overcome this feeling. Slowly, even when I go home during the holidays, I can't be happy or cheerful. There is something weighing on my heart and it feels really painful. I want to know if the respondent has any solutions. Sigh.

answers.answer_text: Hello~~~ When I first started high school, I also went through a period of feeling sad because I wasn't used to it. This might be a phase that everyone goes through in life, and your friends might also be feeling the same way, so there's no need to worry. It seems like in an unfamiliar environment, we might not be able to do the things we want or say the things we want freely, and it's also difficult to immediately have close friends like we did in middle school. Everything seems different from what we imagined, and new challenges have emerged, challenges outside of our comfort zone. My advice is: realize that you are not the only one with these emotions, don't be nervous about communicating with others, everyone has just started high school, and we are all in a relatively unfamiliar environment. So, dare to make friends and be each other's warmth. You can also take the initiative to get to know others, maybe you will make lifelong friends in high school. And talk to your friends or family about your thoughts. Life is like a mirror, if you frown at it every day, you might find it difficult to see the beauty in life. So, it's okay to talk to your family about your troubles. And besides, it's time for holidays, you can go home and adjust your emotions during this time.

Hello young girl, first of all, congratulations on entering high school life. I can totally understand your feelings because I have also gone through high school and experienced the same worries and emotions as you. The world loves you and is with you. In this stage, you are embarking on a new learning journey, making new friends, facing greater academic challenges, and also preparing for college entrance exams, which undoubtedly brings more pressure than before. I think your current feelings may come from various factors. Firstly, the pressure of academic competition has increased. Maybe you performed very well in middle school, but in high school, you will find that there are many friends who are just as good as you academically, which gives you an inexplicable sense of competition. Secondly, you have a strong sense of self-esteem, and you hope to quickly fit into this new social environment. However, various invisible factors related to self-esteem may hinder you from fully integrating. Consequently, you cannot be completely happy because there is pressure when making friends and it's difficult for these friendships to feel natural. This uncomfortable feeling will also affect your learning state and academic performance, as well as your communication with friends, self-esteem, and confidence. My advice is to first focus on your studies and set aside the concern of making friends and fitting in. Concentrate on steady academic progress, which will boost your self-esteem and confidence. Once you have excelled academically, friends will naturally be attracted to you. For example, by seeking help and asking questions, your self-confidence will gradually build up. You can then slowly integrate into your friend circle without feeling burdened by excessive pressure. I wish you a wonderful and happy high school life! Go for it! ^0^~

Hello, minder! Here's a warm hug for you! Entering a new phase of life: high school, a new and unfamiliar environment, unfamiliar people, and being far away from home with no possibility of returning. On top of that, there are new courses. Right now, you are facing four challenges, which can cause feelings of sadness, discomfort, despair, and even physical symptoms like headaches. It's normal to experience these maladaptive symptoms. Don't worry or be afraid. Facing challenges is not scary. Let's conquer them one by one. You can analyze and find the areas where you can adapt and change the most. For example, if you are good at making friends, you can start by finding a good friend in your class. Both of you can support each other in studying and share your inner emotions. Similarly, if you have good study skills, pay more attention to the learning content and strive to complete your daily homework with high quality. It's normal to feel sad and want to cry during the adaptation process. Let's accept it together. Cry if you want to cry, laugh if you want to laugh. It's also a simple and effective way of release. Not being able to go home has pros and cons. It helps foster your independence, laying a solid foundation for better adaptation to society in the future. The cons may include not being able to see your parents or eat the food they cook. But you can do that on weekends. It's just a matter of waiting a few days, which can also help improve your patience. You can also call your parents when you miss them but can't go home. Talk to them about your performance at school and express your yearning for them. Don't worry, don't feel sad. Believe that you will soon become the happy and cheerful self you used to be. Keep going!

Hello, first of all, congratulations on becoming a high school student and entering a new environment. Although this environment may feel unfamiliar and uncomfortable, it is a fresh start for you. Here, you can make new friends. You are just adjusting to a new environment, and it's natural to feel a bit out of place. Some people naturally adapt quickly, while others, like you, may take some time to warm up. You need to regain your confidence and believe that you can adapt to the new environment. You can take the initiative to care about friends who have shown interest in you, and actively make new friends. Gradually adjust your mindset and tell yourself to smile every day. A girl who smiles often is never unlucky. I wish you a happy and quick adjustment to the new environment and making new friends.

Congratulations on strengthening another ability. You can now be independent. You have already persevered for a month. There will always be changes and challenges in different stages of life, and we must learn to adapt. If you can't adapt now, in the future, you will have to leave home for college, and there are also opportunities for studying abroad at Tsinghua University and Peking University. Do you want to keep crying all the time? Or perhaps being too sheltered by family. You must learn to be strong! Otherwise, even if you enter society, you will still be bullied by others.

question: Online self-evaluation scores indicate moderate depression. Should I go to the hospital? How should I talk to my parents about this?
description: In school, I am constantly dissatisfied with my parents' expectations for my grades. I can only talk to a few people, and sometimes I deeply regret what I have done. I feel nervous when interacting with people I don't usually have much contact with, and sometimes I feel very uncomfortable. I engage in self-harm behavior, have trouble sleeping, and I am currently disappointed in myself. Should I go to the hospital?

answers.answer_text: Hug the questioner ~ I think depression should still be seen in a hospital, but online tests may not be accurate. If you want to tell your parents, I have a few methods: Firstly, you can describe your symptoms when you are in a better condition, so they will know that you are really depressed and not just avoiding studying. (Speaking slower can make you appear more sincere ~) Secondly, if unsuccessful, you can explode without hurting yourself. Your parents may be very angry: "Why are you making trouble out of nothing? Did I mistreat you?" If your parents love you very much, they may tell you to cheer up, persevere, and say things like "We haven't mistreated you, what do you have to worry about?" The probability of your parents taking you to the hospital is very low because this world has a deep misunderstanding of depression. If seeking help from the outside world doesn't work and you still feel depressed, I recommend: * listen to music * practice meditation * exercise more. I hope this helps. Good luck~.

How to talk to parents? How to broach this topic? Honestly tell them that recently you have been feeling very low, uninterested in things, and have been feeling depressed. You took a test online and found out that it is moderate depression. You feel like you have lost the ability to be happy, like you have entered a low point in your life, and you feel very miserable, struggling every day in a quagmire. You searched online and learned that depression is not just a psychological phenomenon, but also a problem with the secretion of brain hormones that needs to be controlled with medication, so you need to go to the hospital to check if you are sick. If your parents don't believe you and think you're making a big deal out of nothing, then mention a few tragedies of people who have committed suicide due to depression. Make them realize the seriousness of the problem, that you are not joking, everything you said is true, and this is a very serious matter. Hope that they can also take it seriously, and if they still don't believe or refuse to take you to the hospital, then find a trusted relative. If that doesn't work either, then you have no choice but to secretly go by yourself. Show them the test results with black text on a white background, they can't possibly not believe it, they can't deny that your depression has nothing to do with them. Finally, there is a book, there was a movement online called "Happily Dead!!!" by Jenny Rosen (the following content is from the internet. Copyright infringement, delete). I am at a low point in my life, but now I am happily dead! Jenny, a depression patient, wrote her story of living with loneliness and pain in a book. She collects every moment of happiness crazily and uses them to fight against every bad day. In this book, there are funny conversations with her psychiatrist, interesting daily stories with her family and stuffed raccoons, as well as humorous and touching scenarios that exist in her mind. Since high school, Jenny has begun her long depression journey. During this time, she has experienced various tortures caused by depression - long-term insomnia and restlessness, making Jenny increasingly haggard; sometimes, because of emotional instability, she cannot get out of bed for a week; when there are many people, she cannot control herself and hides in the bathroom or under the table; she is simultaneously suffering from more than a dozen mental illnesses, all those mental illnesses you have heard of or haven't heard of, she has experienced them all - depression, anxiety disorder, impulse control disorder (which can cause self-harm), avoidant personality disorder (severe social anxiety disorder), self-loss disorder (similar symptoms to being high), and mild OCD. What is even more heartbreaking is that Jenny mentioned in the book that sometimes her small achievement is simply "not self-harming for the past three days"... This terrible state lasted for many years. Until one day, one of Jenny's friends unexpectedly passed away. But this time, Jenny did not feel angry or shattered. She wrote in her blog: even if it's purely retaliating against the world, make oneself "happily crazy!" So, Jenny launched a grand movement on Twitter: the globally popular "Happily Dead" also became the most popular philosophy of life at the moment. She encouraged all depression patients to collect every moment of happiness crazily and use them to fight against every bad day. Under Jenny's call, within a few hours, the "Happily Dead" campaign became popular all over the world. Whether it's depression patients in a low point of life or more and more ordinary people, they all joined this movement! The value of this book lies in the fact that the pessimistic tide of depression seems unable to flood Jenny's levee. Although we can faintly feel the surging undercurrent of emotions in her book, she is working hard to overcome it. She turns regular psychological counseling sessions into funny conversations with her psychiatrist, turns the fantasies caused by depression into humorous skits, and even turns self-harm into amusing daily routines. She tries her best to turn her tragic life into a happy version, despite the continuous bleeding and pain.

Hug you, feel sorry for you. The online test can be referenced, but if the result shows moderate, it means there are already some issues and you should see a doctor. Depression is actually like getting a cold or fever in our body. It's just that one is in the body and the other is in the brain. It means that the brain is sick, and there has been a small change in a certain part of the brain. Well, it's actually normal. Our bodies get sick, so it's natural for the brain to get sick too. Some hormone imbalances can cause a lack of interest and result in depression. Also, the negative impacts from real-life experiences affect the mind, causing depression. Psychology and the brain influence each other. Since there is a problem in the brain, which is a physical issue, it naturally needs a physical solution, which is seeing a doctor. Let the doctor take a look and determine if medication is needed. What medication is needed? Adjusting the hormone secretion will do it. Sometimes, when you have a cold or fever, you need to go to the hospital and get medication, right? Of course, after solving the physical issue in the brain, the negative impacts from real-life still need to be addressed. Parents care more about grades than they care about you. Because of this, you have generated anxiety and pressure, wanting to receive their love and care. You don't have many friends you can chat with, feeling like nobody understands you. There is a lack of friends with whom you can have deep conversations, and a lack of emotional support from family and friends. Both family love and friendship, these two important intimate relationships, haven't provided you with much positive emotional support. People are social animals, living in groups, and need emotional connections. But if there is a lack of it, a person will feel lonely and may even develop some issues. To solve the problem, we need to take action. The root cause of the problem is what? How does the problem manifest? What do you want but not get? Ask yourself these questions, and you should have answers. Speak out, let your parents know, let them know that their way of doing things has had a negative impact on you. If they love you and sincerely want the best for you, they will gradually change. Family environment is not something that can be changed quickly or easily. Long-established behavior patterns are not easily changed. But if efforts are made, both you and your family, there is a possibility of change. "Know yourself" is an eternal topic for us. What kind of person are you? How have your family and parents influenced you? Understand why you got sick. How can you get better? You can read articles on public accounts, books, watch videos, listen, etc. This step is about gaining more information related to yourself and helping yourself make behaviors that are beneficial to you in the present and in the future. And friends, you need to overcome your own obstacles. Depression can make you lose interest in many things, and this might manifest as a social anxiety. You need to overcome this barrier in your mind because nobody else can do it for you. A few days ago, I learned a lesson. When I wanted to retreat or give up, when I wanted to stay in the comfort zone and not come out, when I hesitated: think about what you truly want? Anything other than that is a trap. Don't let the trap deceive you, don't let the trap win. Both real-life friends and online friends can help. In fact, it's sometimes easier to confide in online strangers because there's no burden, unlike in real life. Precisely because they're strangers and because there's a screen separating us, neither party knows each other, so we can only perceive the person through their words, removing many real-life factors, and only seeing the version of themselves that they want to present online. Well, the Internet can also be deceiving, so don't be fooled. It's true that the Internet requires less effort compared to real life, but this only applies in the short term. Online friendships rarely last, which means that the provision of emotional support might not be as long-lasting. If you just want to vent for a moment, it's okay to find an online friend or use an anonymous platform. But the quality of the emotional support is what matters most, and it's best to have a long-term and stable relationship. In this aspect, real life is more likely to last than online relationships. Well, I have said so much just hoping to help you, even if it's just a little bit.

question: Should I expose my child who is in the second year of junior high school for cheating on the exam again tonight?
description: I discovered that my 8th grade child is copying answers for homework and cheating in online exams. I have talked to him, scolded him, and tried to reason with him many times, and he always promises to change. But tonight, I found out that he copied the answers for the physics test from the teacher's message in the parent group chat and wrote them on his notebook. I don't know if I should expose him now, and I don't know how to deal with him.

answers.answer_text: Hello, dear! Whether you catch your child cheating on assignments or exams "on the spot" or "discover it secretly behind their back" will determine how you approach and educate them about not cheating and make them aware of the seriousness of cheating. If it's the former, you can directly guide and educate your child not to cheat, helping them realize the gravity of cheating. If it's the latter, avoid direct confrontations or conflicts with your child. During their 8th-grade year, children are usually going through an adolescent rebellious phase, so generating emotional conflicts may not be conducive to resolving the issue of cheating or forming their personality during this period. First, try to understand why your child is cheating instead of criticizing them outright. If it is due to high expectations, many parents tend to have high expectations for their children, and in such cases, children may seek shortcuts in their studies. At times like these, parents can appropriately lower their expectations to avoid imposing excessive psychological pressure on their children's studies. Comparing children's academic performance is a good thing as it enhances competitive awareness among classmates and helps foster a desire to study. However, this should be based on a "formal" competitive system. Inform your child that the purpose of learning is not solely to achieve a specific result but that learning is an endless process. Encourage them to face problems rather than ignore them. Learning is a gradual process, building upon one step at a time. Positively guide your child about the seriousness of cheating, encouraging them to actively tackle the problem instead of attempting to deceive others by putting up a false display of "perfect scores." Solution: Regularly supervise your child's study progress If you notice signs of your child ignoring problems, you can allocate regular time frames to supervise their study progress. It could be checking their daily progress every evening or conducting weekly assessments, etc. Divide the semester into segments and conduct periodic assessments for subjects in which your child has cheated. Positively guide your child about the seriousness of cheating Engage in discussions with your child about the topic of "academic cheating." This topic is important for your child's growth and can be combined with real-life news cases to help guide your child to distinguish between cooperative learning and cheating. During conversations with your child, who is going through the rebellious stage of adolescence, they may appear irritable and impatient. Avoid emotional conflicts, control your own emotions, and calmly discuss these issues with your child. During the adolescent stage, children exhibit distinct characteristics and have their own thoughts and opinions. They do not want to be constrained by other people's thoughts, including their parents' advice, even if it is for their own good. It is difficult for them to listen carefully to their inner thoughts. Allow rebellious children to make mistakes, as this is a crucial period for them to form their own convictions. It is natural for them to make small mistakes. Do not overly restrict their freedom unless the problem is very serious or beyond your ability as parents, as long as it does not involve illegal activities. Let them face and solve some problems on their own instead of telling them what they "cannot do" or "should not do." Adolescents often realize the correctness of their own convictions through making mistakes.

What a coincidence, my child is also in the eighth grade and has had similar behavior, so when I saw your question, I wanted to share my experience. 1. Children of this age group are more sensitive, so it is not recommended to directly confront them. 2. Repeated preaching can cause children to rebel, and using physical punishment is even worse, it will only strain the parent-child relationship and make them less likely to listen to you. 3. Understand the reason why they plagiarized, whether it's because they are having difficulty with their studies or because they feel overwhelmed by academic pressure and are trying to escape. Once you understand the situation, you can find the appropriate solution. If it's the former, find ways to help them overcome their academic difficulties. If it's the latter, find ways to help them relax and take a breather. 4. Regardless of which method you choose, the premise is that parents should genuinely respect their children and establish a good parent-child relationship, keeping communication channels open. Of course, this is sometimes difficult to achieve in families with middle school students. My family also experiences frequent conflicts, but I always remind myself that caring for my child is not just about their grades, but also about their mental health. This is the most important responsibility as a parent. These are just my humble thoughts, I hope they can be of help to you.

question: Every time my father finishes drinking, he starts to mumble and say all sorts of nonsense.
description: My dad is fond of drinking alcohol. Every time he drinks, he ends up arguing like he wants to pick a fight. It's really annoying, and he can't quit drinking. I can't move out either. What should I do? Every time he drinks, I feel so frustrated, like something is stuck in my heart. The fights my parents had when I was young left a deep emotional scar on me. Now, whenever I see people arguing or speaking loudly, I want to run away, I'm afraid. When he's not drinking, he's actually a good person. Sometimes, I really want to leave this place, or even this world.
keywords: Family, family trauma, growth process, behavioral disorders.

answers.answer_text: Hello, if you're feeling really depressed, you can go out for a walk and relax. From your words, I can tell that you're frustrated, and I can also feel your love for your dad. You must be a very kind person, shouldering a lot of responsibility. But don't put too much pressure on yourself. You only need to fulfill your duty of taking care of your parents when they are old. If there are things you can't change, just let them be. Sometimes life can feel difficult all of a sudden, and I feel the same way as you. But when I think about how young we still are, I feel that we shouldn't give up on life. We should live well and live with purpose, because one day we will also meet someone who loves us and experience the happiness of life. Keep going, things will definitely get better.

Hello ~ Thank you for the invitation ~ I understand your feelings very well, as I have had similar experiences. Hugs to you ~ I remember that whenever they argued, someone would be intoxicated and not in their right mind. When things were normal, they were able to negotiate calmly, but when they were drunk, they would say a lot of inexplicable things. It wasn't until later that I realized it wasn't his fault, it was the alcohol's. I once tried to persuade my father to quit drinking, but failed time after time, and eventually learned to accept this fact. Occasionally, he still says a lot of annoying things when he's drunk. My way of comforting myself is very simple and rough - I secretly decided that when he's drunk, I will pretend not to know him. I won't care whether he's arguing with someone or what he's saying. In that moment when he's drunk, I see a stranger with a flushed face, talking about things I'm not interested in, and I just focus on doing things I enjoy. The result is that at least I don't feel anxious. Perhaps drinking really is a source of happiness and importance for them, so it would be somewhat selfish to try to deprive them of this right. When he's drunk, it is best and simplest for both of us to keep some distance. Best wishes ~.

question: Liked the boss and set boundaries due to misunderstandings, how to balance emotions and work?
description: I am bisexual and have a liking for my boss, so there is a certain level of ambiguity between us. Due to some issues and misunderstandings, we have set boundaries between us. However, we still have to work together, which makes me feel uncomfortable. How should I face her without being too affected by my emotions? I can't be purely professional, and I can't leave or resign from my job. I keep thinking about the feelings we have developed over the years. But facing her suddenly becoming distant, I feel abandoned. It's hard not to bring my emotions into it, and I often feel sad as if I have been let down. Going to work every day feels burdensome. How should I face her, adjust my mindset, and deal with work? (I hope to receive a rational answer)
keywords: Emotions, healing methods, anxiety, emotional regulation

answers.answer_text: Hello, dear OP. First of all, hugs to you. 🤔 After trying to set boundaries with your boss, it seems like you still can't completely face her, indicating that you still care about her. You mentioned that there were misunderstandings and issues that caused the need for boundaries, but have both parties explained their sides clearly? If not, I suggest having a serious conversation with her. After all, you don't know what kind of emotions she still has towards you, and there might be a chance for a different outcome.️ If this approach still doesn't work and you can't quit, can you consider transferring to another department? It's not easy to quickly let go when you have to face her every day, so I recommend adjusting your mindset at work. After all, she is your superior, and you have to interact with her. If she can be cold towards you, you can also try to be a little indifferent, treating her like you would on any regular day. 🤗 To let go of past feelings, the best way is to start a new relationship. After work, you can try socializing and meeting new people. Hope this can help you. Best wishes.

Growth is about finding breakthroughs, changing paths, spiraling upward, and becoming a better self. My journey: I developed a romantic relationship with my superior. Certain events and misunderstandings shattered the ambiguity that existed before. The subsequent work had a profound impact on me. Faced with my boss's indifference, I felt abandoned and it greatly affected my work with my emotions. Trying to return to the previous relationship with my boss within my social circle caused emotional turmoil, making it impossible for me to focus on my work. Resigning is not an option for me, so I need to overcome this inner struggle with my boss and return to how things were before. Changing paths: Fully accepting the reality: I am still primarily unwilling to accept the fact that I have to separate from my boss. I must let go of these thoughts and not hold onto any fantasies or feelings of being abandoned or betrayed. Love is between two people and not about following someone. Therefore, I need to see through all of this and only when I fully accept this reality can I focus on my work. Focus on work: Since my boss is still my boss, I need to place my focus on my work, do it well, and approach my boss with a professional attitude, not a personal one. Fully accepting - Focus on work - Changing paths - Spiraling upward - Becoming a better self.

Since we have already set boundaries, let's first reflect on our own emotional paths. Due to the ambiguity between us and the other person, many things have not been truly discussed, and some boundaries have never been crossed. So we need to consider whether there will ultimately be a result between us and the other person. If there won't be a real result in the future, then it's better to be straightforward. It's better to let go of something we can't hold onto. Sometimes giving up is a kind of happiness, although it may be a bit reluctant in our hearts. But since it's no longer possible, we might as well be generous. As for work, although it can be awkward to meet sometimes, it's best not to mix work and personal life. The other person did not betray us, nor did they deliberately abandon us. It's just that misunderstandings have arisen and our relationship has reached an impasse. So we should focus more on other aspects, like going out and relaxing. If the other person is really unwilling to communicate with us, then there's no need for us to keep chasing after them. If they have lost their feelings, then let's focus on our own job and not burden ourselves too much psychologically. We can also talk to other friends. The world still loves me.

question: 29-year-old female, unable to stop crying when thinking about childhood memories, what should I do?
description: During the process of growing up, I was often criticized, blamed, suppressed, and belittled by my father. I was also frequently overlooked. As a result, I developed an introverted, sensitive, and insecure personality. I tend to be more pessimistic, and sometimes, when I think about my past, I can't help but cry. I feel very unjust and unable to move on from the childhood trauma. How should I adjust my suppressed emotions, release the burden of the past, and let it go???
keywords: Family, family trauma, growth process, family control.

answers.answer_text: Being able to be aware of and feel the injustice experienced in childhood indicates personal growth and strength. Firstly, we should accept such feelings and allow them to exist, even though they may be painful. It is the feeling of hurt that we experienced in the past, and if we suppress the pain and deny it, it becomes a form of torture. There are parents who wrongly accuse or punish their children, causing the children to feel wronged. However, these parents do not allow their children to express anger or sadness, even forbidding them from crying, thus depriving the children of the ability to express and feel. Secondly, we should continually learn and grow, identify the problems and root causes of negative emotions, love and care for ourselves, and prevent ourselves from being hurt again. If the negative emotions are too severe and cannot be reduced, professional assessment, treatment, or psychological counseling may be needed from a specialized institution.

Hey, the questioner! Hello, sending you a hug~ After reading your description, it seems like you have been remembering some unpleasant things from the past recently, especially the unhappy experiences from your childhood, which are related to your father's "oppressive education." I truly sympathize with what you have been through. You mentioned that your childhood experiences have had a great impact on you, causing you to often feel overlooked, introverted, sensitive, and insecure. It's evident that your family environment has had a significant influence on your personality. Your current unstable symptoms are largely due to the unpleasant and overlooked experiences from your childhood. So, if you continue to feel persistently troubled by sad emotions, you may need psychological counseling and seek help from a psychologist. Based on your description of how you sometimes can't help but cry when you think about your childhood experiences and feel unjust, it is possible that you haven't been able to forgive your father for mistreating you in the past, and every time you think about it, it overwhelms you with sadness. However, I suggest that you shouldn't engage in such negative rumination that harms both your body and mind. If you want to break free from this state, you need to change your mindset and stop repeating the experience of painful memories. You describe your childhood misery as a "traumatic" experience, indeed, this kind of psychological trauma deserves our attention. If you want to escape from the pain and regain a sense of normalcy in your life, it's necessary for us to heal the trauma. You can choose to seek help from a psychologist for psychological counseling or confide in the person you trust the most, allowing the suppressed emotions to be released.

question: An 18-year-old high school senior boy often gets teased by his classmates at school, and it's really exhausting.
description: Classmates always call me by my father's name and constantly mock me, but I haven't done anything to provoke them. They started bullying me only after a male student in our class who was often targeted by them transferred to another school. They always tease me, and a few days ago, they found out my family's phone number and started making harassing calls to them. I'm really tired and scared to fight back. I feel so helpless, isn't this considered campus violence? I really don't know what to do. I just want to peacefully finish the remaining 190 or so days of my senior year.
keywords: Interpersonal relationships, conflicts, roommates, classmates, interpersonal boundaries.

answers.answer_text: Hey there, the subject. Hugs to you~ After reading your description, it seems like some classmates in your school have been mocking you. Not only that, they have also been bothering your family. It is clear that you are really troubled by this situation, and I truly sympathize with what you are going through. Based on your description, as a high school senior, you are being mocked and teased by your classmates during a time when you should be focusing on studying. Instead, you are being distracted by other matters. Considering that their actions have already significantly affected your studies and personal life, you have every right to hold them accountable. You can seek help from your parents and teachers. If we do not take this matter seriously ourselves and instead hope that those people will suddenly come to their senses, it will be difficult to resolve our problems. You mentioned that your family is being harassed with phone calls. You can take this opportunity to explain the situation to your family and let the adults handle it. Perhaps your individual efforts alone are not enough to help you break free from this predicament, and seeking external support will greatly improve the situation. You also mentioned feeling really helpless, and that this can be considered a form of campus violence. Indeed, this level of harassment can be classified as bullying, and it is something that deserves our attention.

question: Should college students not accept expensive gifts from friends due to their lack of financial independence?
description: I feel so tired recently. It's about some things regarding friends and studying. In a couple of days, it's my birthday, but actually, I have never received a birthday gift from anyone since I was little. Now that I'm in high school, my friends found out about my birthday and they want to give me gifts. As someone who has never received a gift before, I really want to receive one. So, I told my friend what I like, and a good friend of mine said she wants to give me a set of dresses. I was very happy at that moment because I really like dresses, and also because I have never received gifts before, so I agreed. But later on, I started feeling a bit sad and even scared. So, I asked another friend about it, and she said that we are all high school students now, and economically, we are not yet independent. It's still like using our parents' money. She told me not to accept it. I didn't know how it felt at that moment, maybe it was a mixture of fear and sadness. I feel like I'm strange. Receiving gifts is supposed to be a happy thing, but I feel sad and even scared about it. So, when the friend who wanted to give me the gift came to ask me about my dress size tonight, I suddenly didn't want it anymore, and I said I don't like it anymore. She was originally very happy, but then she suddenly couldn't speak and left. I don't know why I am scared. It's just tiring between friends. I really rarely receive things that others give me.

answers.answer_text: OP, hello~ First, let me give you a warm hug. I totally understand how you feel. It's great that your friends want to give you a gift, and it makes you happy. However, another friend's comment has left you feeling anxious and self-blaming. Actually, it's not true that you can't spend money on gifts just because you're not financially independent. If the price is not too expensive, it's acceptable. After all, not every birthday gift has to be expensive. Also, parents would understand if you spend some money to buy a gift for a friend. They would probably want their child to have good friends, as long as the price is reasonable. But the most important thing is the intention behind the gift. In the future, you can make handmade gifts, which will show even more thoughtfulness. Additionally, I guess your previous words hurt your friend. I suggest talking openly with your friend, explaining your thoughts, difficulties, and concerns. Let her know that you didn't actually dislike the gift, but rather you were trying to protect her from spending money and getting scolded by her parents, which led to the lie. Lastly, I want to tell you that everyone has different perspectives. Don't let a few words from others hurt you. Of course, what your friend said also makes sense. She cares about you. However, you should still have your own beliefs and thoughts. It's best to discuss and clarify things with the people involved before making any decisions. I hope you and your friend can resolve the conflict and misunderstanding soon~ Best wishes~

question: 13-year-old girl, in recent years, always wants to escape from life, escape from the world?
description: I used to be a very innocent and naive little girl, but after entering junior high school, I came into contact with all kinds of people. I don't know why, but I started to become insecure. However, later on, I learned to face others in a seemingly carefree and cheerful way. Maybe my behavior was annoying, so many people started to criticize me. By the eighth grade, I wasn't as carefree anymore and became slightly quieter than before. But sometimes I still use a mask to cover myself, it's very painful. I once thought of ending my life, but I care about my parents. However, another thought came to my mind, that I would wait for them to pass away and then I could go too. Eventually, I gave up because of my older sister. I feel so tired, and I want to escape from life, to escape from the world. So I started thinking, can I create a second personality, someone smarter than me, to replace me and live on?
keywords: Growth, personality traits, developmental patterns, and the meaning of life.

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP, I'm glad to answer your question. Based on your question, I understand that: 1) You were innocent before junior high school, but developed a sense of inferiority in junior high school. 2) You started wearing a careless mask, and later became quiet. 3) You had thoughts of wanting to die and wanted to escape from reality. According to the perspective of psychology, a person's fundamental personality is largely stable. In your description, the different aspects of yourself before and after junior high school actually indicate that your fundamental personality has not changed. It is your innocence that led to the distress of being afraid of being disliked. How should we understand this kind of innocent personality? Actually, we can say that you have a kind and pure perspective, expecting others to behave in a kind and pure way towards you. However, due to the complex reasons of personality and environment, others did not respond to you in the same friendly manner, which eventually led to the frustration and development of your inferiority complex, and the thought of wanting to die as a way to escape. Your fundamental nature is innocent, but because you care about others' opinions, you put on two different masks for the purpose of gaining positive evaluations from others. Therefore, overall, what you need to improve at this stage is not living for others and suppressing your own true needs to meet others' expectations. Actually, at this stage, you need to adjust your mindset and experience positive and optimistic emotions, in order to face the present and future difficulties. You also need to restore self-identity, be confident in yourself, in order to feel your own thoughts and needs, and put yourself first, thus completely breaking free from negative evaluations from others. Now, let's talk about the issue that is troubling you, whether or not your past behavior of wearing masks is right or wrong. Actually, this question makes you feel like you can't find the real you. First of all, according to psychology, people will wear different masks in different situations and environments in order to meet the needs of the environment and social interactions. So, wearing masks to face others is actually a normal and acceptable behavior, and not just for you, many people in reality also use masks. Therefore, you don't need to deny yourself because of this and deepen your sense of inferiority. Before, you used a careless personality which was disliked by others, and then you learned to be quiet. You need to have a clear understanding that none of this is your fault. The careless and quiet personality traits you exhibited were actually efforts made to have friendly interactions with others. However, for students of the same age as you, their minds are not yet mature enough to understand these efforts made for friendship. They only see the surface phenomena. So, you don't need to spend energy blaming anyone; this kind of blaming is not meaningful. What you need to do is to appreciate yourself and affirm your past behaviors. This will generate positive emotions to face future interactions and have a good mindset for future friends and classmates. The dilemma you are currently facing is whether or not to find a smart personality to replace yourself. In fact, what you imply is that you currently feel less intelligent. Perhaps this thought stems from failed interactions while wearing different masks. However, it can be seen that at this stage, you still have a strong need for companionship. This is something that should be encouraged and affirmed about yourself, and it further illustrates your innate kind and pure personality. Do you need to live with a smart personality? For the sake of your current psychological comfort, try not to create a personality that is significantly different from your innate kind and pure personality, as the discomfort caused by this difference will affect your mood. However, since you still want to have friendly interactions with others, a conclusion can be drawn: you can build upon your fundamental innocent personality and learn to face different environments by adding other personality strengths. In other words, you can still have a careless personality and a quiet personality, but you need to learn to differentiate the appropriate environment and the people you interact with, in order to experience positive emotions in interpersonal interactions. Generally speaking, when two individuals who have similar personalities first interact, they are more likely to get along well. Therefore, once you understand the general personality of the other person, learn to use your personality strengths. Moreover, according to psychology, sincerity is a quality that is more attractive in interpersonal interactions. Therefore, your innate innocent personality can be a resource for genuine interactions. Finally, I hope you are treated gently by the world!

Tired, just press the pause button for yourself, take a rest, take a break for a while, go home, and don't push yourself too hard. Dear, you started off feeling innocent and pure, but later on in middle school, you started feeling inferior. This is related to interpersonal relationships. As we gradually grow up, we will come into contact with more and more people, and we will encounter all sorts of individuals. If we don't adapt well to our environment, we need to adjust our mindset and adapt better. Based on the description, the choice of being carefree in order to adapt seems to have ended in failure and resulted in others criticizing you. Regarding the above description, as we grow up, our ways of thinking, abilities, cognition, and social skills all undergo changes, but what is the direction and nature of these changes? It varies from person to person, but overall, it should be about becoming more adaptable to our environment and more harmonious. However, if these changes suppress and make you feel inferior, then there is a problem with this direction. Suggestions for the questioner: 1. Communicate your confusion with your family and seek their help. 2. Communicate more with your good friends. 3. Find a psychologist. It is necessary to find a psychologist during this crucial phase of your life. You have your own worth and strengths, and you don't need to listen to others' evaluations. Keep up the good work!!!

question: Afraid of hurting my roommate who comes from a less privileged background by what I say, but also feel it's unnecessary and too sensitive?
description: I am a freshman girl and this is my first time living on campus. During high school, I was very focused on studying and didn't have much social interaction. Today, my roommates and I went out to eat together, and during the meal, we talked about each other's hometowns. My hometown is a city in a relatively unknown province, and one of my roommates suggested that we all visit each other's hometowns and stay at each other's houses. Although my hometown is a small city, my family's financial situation is relatively well-off, so I agreed. However, another roommate's family is not very well-off, and she has been quiet the whole time. I'm worried that our conversation might hurt her self-esteem. But then I feel like I'm being too sensitive. Later, we talked about the Western food we have eaten, and this roommate still didn't say anything. After returning to the dormitory, I isolated myself for a long time, not wanting to do anything. When I was younger, my family wasn't very well-off either. My parents borrowed money and didn't give me much pocket money, so I have been looked down upon and verbally hurt by others. Therefore, I am very sensitive in this regard. In the dormitory, whenever there's a money-related issue, I always try to take care of that roommate. I feel like I'm being too sensitive. I don't know why I was so upset when I returned to the dormitory, and I stayed upset for a long time, wasting a lot of time.
keywords: Interpersonal relationships, roommates, classmates, interpersonal boundaries.

answers.answer_text: I think it's not autism, but rather silence. Everything you talk about is too far from her world. It's great to share your knowledge, but her family is not well off, and she is afraid of spending money and not fitting into your circle. Speaking of which, it's not a big deal to come from a poor family. She may have many interesting stories, but she just doesn't dare to speak up. She fears loneliness and going out, because she doesn't have money, and she's also afraid of being ridiculed. Maybe you just give a friendly smile, but these anxieties make that kind expression different. In fact, you don't always have to consider her feelings of not having money in conversations. Actually, being broke can also bring happiness. It's not necessary to go out and play together to get along well. If you can find other topics, she won't be so sensitive, and it seems that she dislikes you paying attention to her lack of money. We focus on different aspects of life, but there will always be common qualities. I think she comes from a poor family, but what she lacks even more is love. A child who lacks love wouldn't easily feel inferiority like this. In fact, good friends are easy to get along with. You can study together, take care of her in group orders, share your embarrassing stories, open up your hearts. Perhaps you will gain her trust and forming a close-knit group together is meaningful. Money will never hinder true friendship at any time, as long as both of you are willing, maybe you will be the best friends.

You have strong perceptiveness, sensitivity, and kindness. You project your emotions onto your roommate because you have been hurt by similar things or remarks before, so you wonder if she might also be hurt. Many people have suffered, but you have transformed that suffering into energy. Others may be naturally privileged and not pay attention to your roommate's distress at all, but your sensitivity has created your kindness. Whether in your daily life or in this conversation, you have shown enough respect and attention to your roommate, which is excellent. Why blame yourself? Moreover, material wealth or lack thereof is not the standard by which to judge a person. Do you think your roommate is pitiful? She definitely doesn't want sympathy like this, what she needs is respect. There are many people in the world who have never taken an elevator, eaten western food, traveled abroad, or even owned a cellphone or received an education. Are they pitiful? Think about the logic behind it. Our upbringing is beyond our control, so don't use the outside world to judge a person too much, and don't impose those values on yourself. This may be a criticism of contemporary society. I hope you can see more, be inclusive, and respect others. If you have the ability to do something, don't trouble yourself anymore. People who love life will eventually be rewarded! I hope both you and your roommate are people who love life. Good luck!

question: 16-year-old girls may resist others showing their liking and confessing their feelings towards them, and may want to avoid it.
description: From childhood to adulthood, I have always had good interpersonal relationships. Perhaps it is because of adolescence, but in the past few years, about 6.7 male friends who I had a good relationship with have confessed their feelings to me or made advances. I have resisted and even avoided many of them intentionally. Some I have directly blocked and deleted as friends. I don't know the reason, but I just can't control my emotions. I don't even know how to refuse, and all I can think of is how to escape. What should I do?

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP! Give you a big hug. I can really understand how you feel because I have had similar experiences. Resisting and avoiding when someone confesses their feelings to you may have the following reasons: difficulty expressing yourself and rejecting others. Perhaps you are not good at saying no and expressing yourself, so you don't know how to reject others. Sensitivity and self-protection. When someone tries to enter your world, you activate your self-defense mechanism and fear others' invasion. Afraid of feeling guilty if someone unilaterally invests in you. If the other person pursues you and makes efforts, you may feel indebted to them and unable to reciprocate. This is a self-defense mechanism and common behavior when dealing with interpersonal relationships. Here are some suggestions: Avoiding won't solve the problem, you can hint at the other person to make your stance clear. If you like someone, you can try to develop the relationship; if you don't, give the other person some indications and reject them tactfully. It's better to have a short-term pain than a long-term one. Avoiding is actually a vague response that can lead to misunderstandings. Don't drag it out for too long. The longer it takes, the harder it may be for the other person to move on, and it may also become more difficult for you to speak up. It wastes both the other person's time and your own, and the future relationship may become more awkward. Lastly, if someone likes you, it means that you have qualities that attract others and deserve their admiration. From this perspective, being liked by someone is actually a good thing. I hope you can face it boldly.

question: When in psychological counseling, not daring to speak out about one's trauma can make one feel very ashamed.
description: Feeling ashamed of childhood trauma, every time I consider sharing it during counseling, I am too afraid to speak up. I know the therapist will keep it confidential and I trust them, but I just can't bring myself to say it. After sharing, I feel like running away and never coming back. What should I do?
keywords: Treatment, trauma therapy, and the opportunity to express and be heard.

answers.answer_text: Hello! After reading your description, I have gained some understanding of the question you want to ask, and I want to give you a virtual hug. From your description, I can see that you are feeling a bit anxious and conflicted. Your anxiety may stem from wanting to seek help through counseling to better resolve your issues, but also being afraid of exposing yourself too much.
