Although I've had a terrible upbringing, I still think about it when she goes crazy, but I have learned to control this thought because we are educated people. At fifteen years old, you should be in high school, right? High school is very stressful, not just for you, but also for your parents because they want you to have a bright future, even if it may not align with their understanding of the times. You say you can't let things go in one ear and out the other, so let's not do that. But we should try to understand that her behavior is shaped by her upbringing, and she may not be able to change instantly. So we should try to communicate with our mother. If she doesn't listen, father can help, or you can write a letter expressing your desires. After all, where there's a will, there's a way. If you really don't want to communicate, you can reduce contact. Our biggest concern should be our studies. We need to enrich our knowledge to achieve the future we desire, so we should try to avoid unnecessary arguments. If she starts scolding, let her vent. What you need to do is force yourself to look at your books during this time and suppress the urge to argue. There are many ways to solve problems, but there is never a reason to take away a life. Adjust your emotions, even if it means finding a place to cry loudly, to release your stress. Life must go on. Best wishes~.

question: My friend is always telling me how to get along with other friends. It makes me feel uncomfortable.
description: I have a friend whom I have been friends with for about ten years, and in recent years, she always feels like she's teaching me how to get along with other friends. For example, sometimes when I'm not at home and a package arrives, I would @ my friends in the group chat and ask if anyone can help pick it up. She would then privately message me and say that it feels like others should help me as a matter of course, and then tell me what I should say. Another example is when I don't reply to messages in the group chat, she would privately message me and say that others are unhappy because I didn't reply, and I should apologize and express gratitude. Others don't owe me anything, and it's natural to have emotions... Although it feels like she has good intentions, I feel uncomfortable. When I follow her demands, I always feel like I'm being educated. If I don't do as she says, she will tell me how my interpersonal relationships will be affected. It feels like a threat to me. In short, I want to confront her. - PS: I also have a question, sometimes when I post something in the group chat (for example, when the street comes to check something and I help out, or when something is missing at home and I have already bought it), sometimes no one replies, including her. Nobody says what she taught me, at least expressing gratitude or something. How should I interact with her? Every time she teaches me, she always thinks my interpersonal relationships are very poor.

answers.answer_text: Hello, the title sounds great! After reading your question, I can sense that you must be a very popular person with many friends who care and help each other in life. This kind of status is actually the goal of many people in pursuing interpersonal relationships. However, in this group of friends, although you initially felt that you were handling your relationships well, under the criticism and guidance of your friend, you felt worse about yourself. Hugs to you, I hope my answer can give you some inspiration. You have been with this friend for nearly ten years, and I believe you both know and understand each other very well. However, it seems that in this friendship that should have been equal, there have been some subtle changes in your relationship. Why is that? You've known each other for ten years, and it seems that she has considered you a very important person in her life. I don't know if she does similar things with other people, but clearly you are the special one. She expresses her concern in her own way. She pays attention to your interactions with others in the WeChat group, always private messaging you, telling you how to get along with others. In your description, she seems to have taken on the role of a mother in this relationship, and you have gradually become the child in the relationship. This is why you feel uncomfortable. Because parents always stand in a higher psychological position to discipline and criticize their children, and the children are the objects of criticism and discipline, they will naturally experience emotions and dissatisfaction. In her eyes, everything she does is to make you better, but in such behavior, all you can feel is pressure and restrictions. Feeling threatened is also due to the excessive pressure she puts on you in this relationship. How to solve it? Honest communication may be a good approach. You can honestly tell her that both of you are adults who have their own preferred ways of communicating and living attitudes, and you can handle your own interpersonal relationships well. At the same time, we should also recognize the positive intentions behind what the other person does. Thank them sincerely for their care, and believe that they will gladly accept your opinions and suggestions. Establish appropriate boundaries. No matter how close the relationship is, whether it is a friend or a family member, we should establish appropriate boundaries. When the other person touches your psychological boundaries, you can bravely say no. If you felt uncomfortable in the beginning, you could have expressed your feelings to the other person in a timely manner, and maybe the situation would have been different. The establishment of every relationship requires both parties to test and constantly adapt in order to find the most suitable boundaries and the most comfortable state of interaction. Being able to maintain a friendship for ten years with enthusiasm is really precious. I believe you will find better ways of communication to solve the small problems you are currently facing. Wishing you a long-lasting friendship and best wishes, the world and I love you~

Hello, let me try to answer this question. When I read about the situation you described, it reminded me of the "robber logic" of good people. Many people use the excuse of "doing it for your own good" to manipulate others' personalities. It feels like a form of personality coercion, making you feel unable to express your anger and causing frustration and confusion. I can empathize with your situation. From a psychoanalytical perspective, I can provide some directions and possibilities: your friend exhibits a very controlling "motherly" behavior that can feel suffocating. "Motherly" refers to someone who likes to teach others how to live, often displaying their greatness as a mother and seeking to dominate various relationships. They not only act as their children's mother but also as mothers to others. They can be caring and warm when it comes to taking care of others. However, their desire for control and expression can also bring a sense of repression. It may be difficult to say that she is suffocating, as it represents the traces of years and life. Her words and actions are also repeating past experiences and traumas, which bring her a sense of satisfaction. She constantly educates you in interpersonal relationships, perhaps due to her own inability to cope with setbacks and traumas in previous relationships, projecting them onto you through an educational approach. People who have not experienced love can only prove that they are still worthy of love by getting rid of their past selves, denying their weaknesses, and showing their strength and greatness. Many people who have experienced childhood traumas become overly dependent and clingy in adulthood. They no longer want to taste the bitterness of rejection, abandonment, or being ignored, so they use stronger ways to showcase their "deep suffering" and love. People who like to control others like a mother actually have an out-of-control life. They dare not face their own lack of control and helplessness, so they create a "false self." This "self" is tall, dominant, and gives a sense of control. The reason it feels oppressive is because of the gentle wrapping, making it both loved and hated. Try discussing these explanations with her, as well as your true feelings, and show care for the emotional trauma and sense of control she may have inside. At the same time, express sincere refusals when necessary. Explore the reasons why you can't resist the idea of "doing it for your own good" in your own personality, and I believe you can find a suitable way. Thank you for sharing, and I look forward to your acceptance.

Isn't this the so-called "stickler"? :) It feels like this friend is excessively invading your boundaries, even giving off a parental vibe, always trying to educate us and impose their values on us. She doesn't understand that your life is yours to decide, and it has nothing to do with her. She is not obligated to correct your life. Even if you did something truly wrong, what does it have to do with her? What responsibility does she have to correct you? So if you feel uncomfortable, if she is overly interfering, be brave and speak up. Tell her that you know she cares about you, but this care has turned into pressure, and you are no longer enjoying your relationship as before. You want to have your own space and thoughts, and how you interact with others is your own business, not hers. Hopefully, she can respect your wishes. If she is your friend, she will consider your feelings, give you freedom. If she continues to act like before, lecturing you and even thinking that you are wrong or immature, then I think you can distance yourself from this friend. No one has the right to make you feel uncomfortable, even if they have been friends for ten years. You have not done anything wrong, you don't need to endure this unpleasant feeling. But I'm not sure why she knows about your interpersonal relationships. If this happens again, don't mention it in the group chat, just privately message the person you want to talk to. That way, good friends won't know. It is indeed painful to interact with someone who dislikes, doesn't know how to respect, and appreciate oneself. I suggest that the questioner maintain reasonable boundaries and avoid excessive interaction with the other party. It will help improve their mood.

Hello~ I totally understand how you feel, sending you a hug~ It can be really irritating when others constantly give their opinions and make you feel like your life is being interfered with. Especially as adults, we really don't like having our lives directed by others. Considering you've been friends for ten years, I don't think he's intentionally trying to meddle in your life. So, this issue can be analyzed from two perspectives. On one hand, you can pay attention to whether the small issues he mentions actually exist and if they genuinely need improvement. For example, when a package arrives and you're not home, you mention it in the group chat and ask if someone can help, and he privately messages you, saying it feels like others should naturally help you, and then tells you what you should say. Or, in the group chat, if you don't reply to a message, he privately messages you, saying that others are upset because you didn't reply and you should apologize and express gratitude because others don't owe you anything, and it's only natural that they have emotions... He's not referring to any major issue, it's just his perception. Of course, I also think he's being overly detailed. Everyone behaves differently, and everyone has their own habits, so there's no need to adhere to any specific standard. So, you can take what he says into consideration if it applies to you, but otherwise, you can ignore it. On the other hand, you can communicate with him and make your stance clear. You can directly tell him that you don't want him constantly teaching you how to do things and that you think you're doing just fine as is. Of course, you can also express appreciation for his guidance, because I believe he means well. Then, politely decline his advice. I think this is a small matter and there's no need to strain your relationship over it. Just stick to your own attitude, how you speak and how you handle things, because ultimately, you have the right to make those decisions. Wishing you well~

Hello, I saw your concerns and hope I can help you. It seems that your old friend often tries to guide you in your social interactions. Occasionally reminding is fine, but too much can make you uncomfortable. From your description, I can see your obedience and tolerance. We can try to make some adjustments in the following aspects: Firstly, understand good intentions. From your description, it seems that you also know that your friend discusses this topic repeatedly out of good intentions. Maybe she thinks that her way and pace of social interaction are the right ones. She may not realize that everyone has their own coping mechanisms and she doesn't have any malice. It's possible that she just wants to express her views. Once you clarify this, when she brings up this topic, you may not feel so resistant if you approach it with a listening attitude. Secondly, set boundaries. Even with friends you've known for over a decade, there need to be boundaries. From this perspective, your friend's excessive interference with your social interactions has crossed the line. You can establish boundaries in various ways, such as expressing your thoughts and feelings tactfully, or not participating in common group conversations. On one hand, let the other person feel your gratitude for her good intentions, and on the other hand, make her understand your desire for understanding and respect. Thirdly, find a common path for mutual progress. Because I don't know your friend and can only understand from your description, it seems that in the topic of social interactions, you always find yourself in a passive position. You can try to explore new topics that both of you find interesting, bypassing topics that may trigger negative emotions. By subtly refusing the other person, you can truly empower each other and create a positive cycle in your relationship. Friendship thrives in mutual growth, so cherish it as it progresses. Wishing you new discoveries every day.

Hello, a friend of mine that I have known for about ten years has been constantly trying to teach me how to get along with other friends in recent years. Her teachings make me feel like my interpersonal relationships are poor and make me uncomfortable. Although it may seem inappropriate, I need to ask you a question. Before she started teaching you, how did you feel about your interpersonal relationships? Behind every situation, there is meaning. If you observe every situation around you carefully, you will see that there are things we need to pay attention to. For example, a person who needs to renovate suddenly notices a lot of renovation information around them that they had never noticed before. Or a new mother suddenly notices other pregnant mothers and pregnancy-related information everywhere, feeling like there was never so much before. These phenomena are determined by our cognitive selectivity, not that the information suddenly appeared, but that we chose to let them appear. The amount of information surrounding us is enormous, so in order to prevent our brain from being overloaded with information, our cognitive mechanism selects only the information our brain needs. You noticed that your friend suddenly started teaching you how to get along with friends, and you also followed her advice. At the same time, you also realized that your interpersonal relationships did not change much. You understand that the other person means well, but you feel somewhat uncomfortable. Have you ever expressed these feelings to the other person? Just like sometimes we want to help others, we tell them what we think is helpful, but it is difficult for us to know how they feel unless they tell us, right? Maybe you can express your feelings and your wishes when both of you are in a calm state of mind, for example, you can handle things on your own and don't need this kind of advice. Best wishes! Karen.

Hello, constantly receiving advice can be mentally uncomfortable. In a sense, advice is a form of negation. Frequent advice can make oneself feel like they are doing things wrong, always being invalidated. It's really distressing. Let's change our perspective. When a friend frequently offers advice, is there any hidden message behind it besides her good intentions? It might be worth trying to communicate and ask if your behavior has made her feel bad or if someone else has said something about you to her... If it's the former, you can consider adjusting your behavior. You have the final say in this matter. Adjusting your behavior in a timely manner doesn't mean admitting you were wrong, but rather caring about your relationship with your friend. If it's the latter, it could be your friend's well-intentioned reminder, but her approach may not consider your feelings. There's a story about a father and son leading a donkey... No matter what you do, someone will be dissatisfied. Instead of that, it's better to peacefully coexist with your friend of ten years. There must have been happy times, as well as conflicts. Your friend's frequent advice makes you uncomfortable, but you haven't expressed it to her. Often, the more we care, the easier it is to overlook our own emotions and accumulate resentment towards our friends without expressing it, which can also affect the friendship. Ask yourself why you feel uncomfortable and haven't expressed it. What are you worried about? What would happen if you expressed your emotions? Can you not accept the worst-case scenario? If it seems like there's no big deal, does that mean you know what to do now? I believe you will handle your relationship with your friend well and no longer be influenced by their advice.

Hello! It can be seen that your friend is quite caring towards you, but her good intentions went a bit too far, which makes you feel uncomfortable and that's perfectly normal. For you, she is just a friend, not your elder, so repeatedly telling you how to socialize in a instructive tone is really inappropriate. The status between friends is equal, no one can act superior. Your way of socializing is your own choice. Of course, if you do something inappropriate, others can kindly remind you, but it shouldn't be a demand. Of course, her intention was indeed for your own good, but her approach was indeed inappropriate. Friends also have their own sense of self and boundaries. What should you do? You can express to her that you have your own way of making friends, thank her for her reminder, but there's no need for her to constantly lecture you, and be sure to be polite and tactful. I wish you well!

Hello! After carefully reading your description, I sincerely feel your warm-heartedness and the desire to help others. I believe you must be a person who radiates warmth in your daily life. However, it is natural to feel disappointed when our helpfulness is not understood and we are criticized, especially when it comes from someone we have long considered a trusted companion. In your description, I noticed that you have attempted to express your discomfort to your friend, but unfortunately, she did not receive it. Despite facing her criticism, you were still able to respond patiently, which is a great coping mechanism. I genuinely applaud you for that! However, such a response is not a long-term solution as it can drain a significant amount of energy and may not be beneficial for both of you. I would like to offer two suggestions: 1) Try sincerely reminding her about the issue of "boundaries". Even the best of friends need to have certain boundaries in their relationship. If you feel that her concerns are exceeding the boundaries of your relationship, this reminder can serve as a "relationship lubricant" that is relatively necessary. 2) Express gratitude to her more often, and then act according to your true needs and handling things in your own way. I hope this understanding will be helpful in resolving your confusion. The world will surely treat someone as kind-hearted and warm as you with gentleness!

question: Found someone who likes each other and then got scared, do I have a mental illness?
description: Encountering someone that both parties have feelings for each other, we could have been together, but I got scared. I don't know what I am afraid of, maybe I'm afraid of losing, or I have concerns. After things cooled off, it was clearly me who rejected being together, but I still feel upset. I feel like a terrible person, unworthy of saying that I like them. Since we can't be together, we shouldn't continue to have contact. But I miss the old days, the pleasure of chatting with them. I'm really messed up, criticizing myself while still thinking about them. Do I have a problem?

answers.answer_text: Hug the topic creator, through your words, I can see a person in the fog, not knowing what to decide, nor where to go. First, I want to affirm your question, you are not sick, maybe just a little lacking in confidence. But it doesn't matter, this is a normal psychological feeling that most people have to some extent. You don't need to see it as denial or attack yourself. 1. Here are some of my thoughts, maybe there are some inaccuracies, but you can always express your true feelings. Your understanding of why you feel "worthless": I also liked someone before who I couldn't be with. At that time, they said we could be friends if we couldn't be lovers. I didn't accept it, I didn't think I could be content with just being friends, and I even criticized them. But now, I seem to have become just like that person back then, and I feel ashamed of it. Maybe it's because I haven't resolved and healed from the pain caused by that unclear attitude, and instead I have inflicted that kind of hurt on the current 'them'. I feel worthless because after expressing mutual interest, I realized that there was a barrier in my heart, so I didn't agree to be together, like taking back a move in a chess game. And then, we agreed to be like before, but it seems like it's not possible anymore. And later, I realized that my requirement was very unreasonable and I regretted my behavior, but I didn't know how to express the guilt, so I used an external evaluation - "worthless" to balance and rationalize my inner shame and guilt. You have experienced being treated poorly, so you know the pain it can cause the other person, but you don't know what actions to take to remedy the situation. Because in your past experiences, the injured version of you also never experienced successful help/love. I can understand your confusion. But I also miss the past, the joy of chatting with them. I don't have the face to contact them, and they haven't contacted me. I don't deserve to say that they like me. From your words, I feel that reason cannot stop you from still having feelings for them, but you hesitate to express those feelings and believe that you don't have the right to contact them or say that you like them. What is the barrier between thoughts and actions? I think perhaps it stems from your "inferiority complex". Since we couldn't be together, we shouldn't let ourselves sink deeper. But it still feels a little uncomfortable, it's all my fault. And if we continue to communicate, who knows if it will make them sink deeper? This is probably why we don't contact each other. You think that perhaps the reason for not contacting them is to prevent them from sinking deeper. It is based on your own experiential judgment, limiting yourself to an environment you can control, but it does give you a sense of security. I think maybe it's because this sense of security compensates for your uncertainty when faced with deep-water relationships (such as deep, long-term commitment relationships), and you haven't yet acquired the ability to handle deep intimate issues. So you hope that the development of the relationship meets your internal psychological expectations, and you may not be able to accept the unknown in a real relationship. I think, perhaps in previous relationships, you lacked a bit of self-affirmation. When a partner shows kindness, you feel pleasantly surprised; when a partner points out discomfort in the relationship, you may find it difficult to bear. Insecure individuals crave recognition from others, care about other people's needs, but are also prone to self-sacrifice. Your choice of friendship also reflects this point. Because in a friendship, you feel safe within certain boundaries. It doesn't require commitment to the relationship, nor does it involve the responsibility of an intimate relationship. In theory, avoiding the pain of commitment should make you happier, right? But I'm hesitant, I don't know what I'm afraid of, maybe I'm afraid of losing, I have concerns. Even though I rejected being together, I still feel uneasy. Since we can't be together, we shouldn't continue to stay in touch, but I miss the past, the joy of chatting with them. However, from your self-description, I can see a heart that hides its vulnerability and sensitivity underneath layers of armor. Lost, outside the door of love. I really want to hug you. 2. If you want to grow from this experience, I hope you can give yourself some time and stop to face your own inner self. Here, you can think about why your current view of romantic relationships has become a friendship-style relationship without commitment. Why are you afraid of commitment? For example, is it because of underlying self-esteem issues? Or is it due to unresolved past experiences? Or is it the influence of social environment that causes the "alienation" of people? (Such as the "fast food culture" and "functional social relationships" in society) Or is it the fear of dealing with failed relationships in the past that is causing you to avoid it? ...If it's because of self-esteem, I can share a method that has been useful to me. We can write down the moments when we feel insecure, to understand ourselves better. (It's from a book called "Healing the Injured Self-Confidence"). For example, transform the thought that blocks your expression: "But I'm hesitant, I don't know what I'm afraid of" into a thought that helps you express your needs: "I admit I feel afraid, I'm afraid they will ignore me or even be disappointed in me, maybe I can ask if I will disturb them?" Transform the thought that blocks your expression: "Maybe I'm afraid of losing, I have concerns" into a thought that helps you express: "I feel a little scared, my inconsistency might harm them and I don't know how to explain it. But only I know my feelings best, maybe I can try to express my conflicting emotions." Transform the thought that blocks your expression: "Even though I rejected being together, I still feel uneasy" into a thought that helps you express: "They might not trust me anymore, they might also reject my request, I have to admit I don't know their thoughts and attitude. But if I can articulate my doubts, that is also worth affirming." To summarize the core idea of this method, it is to concretize the behavior and needs behind your emotions, and assess the difficulty of implementation. We can start by trying to accomplish the tasks with the least difficulty. However, you know that the most important thing is taking action after making a firm decision, and in this aspect, I can't help you. If you only want to reconcile with them out of guilt, but you haven't prepared yourself for how to deal with deep-level commitment in the relationship. Then perhaps this kind of problem will occur repeatedly in your relationship's cycle. At the same time, in Adler's "Understanding Human Nature," it also mentioned that people with an inferiority complex tend to focus more on past failed experiences when facing failure. They lack a sense of belonging and social interest. They doubt that these issues can be solved through cooperation. In my opinion, the interaction of intimate relationships is also a form of cooperation. A good intimate relationship is characterized by equality, respect, honesty, and love. I think you can try to trust them and trust the relationship. Trust that the other person is an independent and mature individual. We can reveal our vulnerable and even conflicting thoughts to each other, believing that the other person has the ability to choose responsibility for us, and we are willing to respect their choices and respect this complex and special emotional state. I think maybe they can feel your sincerity. 3. About two months ago, I asked a question on having a "commitment-free" romantic relationship, can it last? How to maintain it? (If you're interested, you can try searching for it.) A user named @wo s  zui w ux  rén responded to me in the comments, and I'm very grateful to her. She said, "Life is about experiences, being a child, being a spouse, being a parent... different roles, tasting the sour, sweet, bitter, and spicy flavors, different tastes." Love, in its usual sense, isn't just sweet. It's also mixed with suspicion, pain, jealousy, and grievances. Love doesn't only have a bright side, it's because of this that our life experiences are so fulfilling. Real relationships have immeasurable power. May the topic creator find someone in their future that is worth cherishing, loving them while loving oneself. 🧚‍️

Give the OP a warm hug. The OP has met someone they have strong feelings for, and they enjoy their time together. However, due to certain concerns, they don't want to take things further. After rejecting their request, they feel that they shouldn't continue to enjoy the rewards in their relationship. But they realize that they still crave those rewards, so they find themselves in conflict, causing them a lot of pain and making them feel bad about themselves. Before answering, I hope the OP can consider a few questions: what is the standard for determining whether someone is bad? Do you meet that standard? Are there better ways to solve your current problem? I've seen many men online saying that girls like to string them along and they end up being backup options. I don't understand how these people view friendship between men and women. Perhaps in their eyes, there shouldn't be friendship between men and women. Men and women are different; men are more likely to exaggerate signals in their interactions with women, it's their nature. When a man thinks a girl is interested in him, he will most likely take action, but if a man thinks a girl has no interest in him, he probably won't take action. This is beneficial for the survival of the species and is a male reproductive strategy. But women are different. Women's reproductive resources are very precious, so they tend to be more conservative in heterosexual relationships because those who are not conservative are often eliminated. Women fear marrying the wrong man and in the past, they would suffer greatly from food scarcity and lack of protection if they did marry the wrong man. Even in modern times, pregnancy, miscarriage, and widowhood can cause women great distress. This tendency often manifests in male-female relationships as girls not showing interest, but boys thinking they are interested. Added to this is the conscious use by many women of their gender advantage to gain resources from the opposite sex, which is why backup options and "green tea" lovers naturally emerge. However, from your description, you haven't wrongfully used your gender advantage to gain anything, so naturally, there is no "bad" in this situation. What seems to be bothering you is that he pursued you and you rejected him, which is why many good friends who like each other don't dare to confess their feelings; once one side rejects the other, it becomes difficult to return to the way things were before and everything becomes awkward for both the man and the woman. Therefore, responding to such situations requires utmost caution and requires deep communication and soothing, rather than just leaving it at that. You have to understand that your friendship is still important and he is still worthy of being your friend. Beyond romantic love, there can be friendship between men and women, but you must decide where this is going at this point. If you also have feelings for him but have some obstacles or concerns right now, then the two of you should try to overcome them together. Let's be honest about the potential difficulties and make a decision together. If you truly don't want to pursue this romantic relationship, then you should make it very clear to him and in your future interactions, try your best not to owe him any emotional debts and maintain a good boundary. That should be enough.

Although simple, this description truly allows us to see your contradictions, inner struggles, self-blame, and a bit of melancholy... "Clearly rejecting the other person, but finding it difficult to completely let go and continuing to stay in contact," this contradictory behavior seems to indeed perplex the other person, thinking, "What exactly do you want?" The OP also mentioned feeling angry when they were treated this way in the past, thinking that people who do this are "scumbags". Regarding this, I would like to respond with two points: 1. Regarding this issue, let me ask you a question: because of this contradictory experience, can you now slightly understand the person from the past? Perhaps it wasn't because of your character or how you interacted, but maybe they were afraid of something, or they had their own unspeakable reasons...? 2. The desire to contact someone and the act of continuing to stay in contact should be distinguished. Having the desire to contact someone is very understandable, wanting to reminisce, feeling sentimental... However, whether or not to actually do so depends on consulting the other person's opinion. If the other person also agrees to remain friends, then there is no problem. If the other person feels hurt and cannot accept further contact, reaching out to them again might truly become a disturbance... Lastly, I would like to remind you of one thing: What are you afraid of? This is a question worth exploring and contemplating. Are you afraid that something good cannot be lasting? Are you afraid that getting close will reveal the other person's flaws? Or that the other person will discover your own flaws? Or is it something else...?

Hello, questioner. 1. I suggest that regardless of whether it is the person you currently like or someone you will meet in the future whom you like but are afraid to interact with, you should have the courage to take this step: that is, be honest with the other person about your thoughts. Let the other person understand your thoughts or concerns as much as possible. Give yourself a chance, and also give the other person a chance. Perhaps the other person will choose to leave because of your hesitant and distant attitude, but that's okay. You have bravely faced your own heart. Wait for the next person. Or perhaps the other person is willing to accompany you through the obstacle in your heart. In the process of getting along, your feelings will be more firm because of the obstacles you have gone through together, and you will also open your heart. Isn't this a happy thing for both parties? 2. I suggest that you still be honest. Inexplicable inconsistencies can make people who know you understand your situation, but those who don't know you can easily form negative opinions about you. Of course, it's not to say that you should care too much about what others think. But this is also likely to leave an impression on the other person. 3. I suggest that you work harder to build your self-confidence in daily life, so that you won't be so afraid of failure. To be honest, only after experiencing countless failures do many people know what their true selves are like, where they need to pay attention, and where their shortcomings lie. Relying solely on being afraid of failure and not trying will never lead to answers. Make yourself more calm in facing everything outside. Keep going.

Hmm, it is possible that "there is really an illness." People who we like often do not have the courage to pursue them. It's not easy to meet someone we both like. How many people go their whole lives without meeting that person? It is fate given to you by the heavens, so hold on tightly and don't let go. It's a pity that you are thinking of giving up on them. You both get along so well and have such a perfect love. It seems like it will slip away from your hands. What a shame. Clearly, you still think about them, miss them, and have the courage to love. There are only a few people in a lifetime worth loving, so don't have regrets for a lifetime. Why hesitate? Being hesitant won't bring you happiness. It will only ruin the good things. Rather than feeling like a scumbag, try to actively cultivate a relationship. Only by courageously pursuing love will you avoid self-torture. Whether you are scummy or not doesn't matter. What's important is whether you dare to accept the love that is in front of you.

question: Why have I been crying for no reason sometimes at night in the past two years?
description: I have always been fine, nothing has happened, but I always feel inexplicably upset and want to cry, and I always have thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
keywords: Emotions, depressed feelings, panic and helplessness, fragile and tears.

answers.answer_text: Hello! You've been doing well all along, and it's comforting to know that! Sometimes, when your emotions are unstable, you inexplicably feel uncomfortable and want to cry. Please carefully analyze what exactly triggers your discomfort. Is it a person or a situation that makes you feel uneasy? Once you have sorted it out, take a closer look at which issues that puzzle your mood you can handle yourself, which ones require help from others, and which ones you don't need to waste energy dealing with at all. After clarifying these questions, you may find the real causes and methods, and your emotions will naturally calm down. When you feel like crying, feel free to cry freely, release the pent-up sadness and discomfort, and you will experience a different feeling.

All tears are the result of unfulfilled needs in the heart. You can find a piece of paper and a pen, and write down the things that stress you and make you feel regretful. At the same time, write down your feelings about each thing to help you sort out psychological stress and find the root causes of the problems. I wish you find the unfulfilled needs in your heart and be happy soon.

question: Does my husband's explosive and easily irritable behavior, and inability to control his emotions, classify as a mental illness?
description: My husband has been very irritable in the past two months. He gets angry and loses his temper easily over trivial matters. When he's not angry, things are fine between us. Yesterday, we had a dispute about mopping the floor. I wanted to do it, but he didn't allow me to. I ignored him and started mopping anyway. In response, he kicked the mop several times until it broke into pieces. He also kicked and broke the bucket. When I saw this, I felt scared and angry. I complained a bit, but before I could finish speaking, he punched the wall next to him. It was really terrifying. He shouted at me with a fierce and aggressive look, as if he wanted to harm me. He said hurtful things and insulted me. I started crying and he cried too, breathing heavily and tightly clenching his fists. This scene seems to repeat itself every time we argue. We fight almost every day. He gets angry over trivial matters, and he never acknowledges when I do something right. If I make even one mistake, he will verbally abuse me, treating me as if I were a dog. Is my husband suffering from a mental illness? How can we make things better? I'm desperate!

answers.answer_text: OP, hello~~~ Give the OP a warm hug. First of all, from the OP's description, we cannot simply conclude whether the other party has a mental illness, but we can provide some suggestions for the OP to consider: First, I would like to ask if the OP's husband's irritable temper and behavior have been long-term? Have similar situations occurred before? We need to first determine whether the behavior with violent tendencies is a long-term existence or is caused by certain things in a short period of time. In addition, the OP mentioned that the husband's temper has become particularly irritable in the past two months. Is it because the husband has encountered some unpleasant things in life or work during this period? We can try to find the "trigger" for the husband's mood changes in these aspects. We can also communicate with him when his emotions are stable to see if there are other reasons. One more important point is to hope that the OP takes care of themselves and pays attention to their safety. When faced with the husband's irritable mood, try to temporarily separate from him and avoid confronting him head-on if the situation becomes more difficult to control.

question: When my boyfriend watches me from a distance, when he talks on the phone, I reject him in my heart.
description: My boyfriend came from a different city to visit me. He brought me my favorite food. However, when he was on his way back, he answered a phone call and didn't explain it to me when he called me back. I started doubting everything about him in my mind.
keywords: Love, attachment, and a sense of security.

answers.answer_text: Share a little story with the thread starter: A good person did many good things in his life, but one day he made a mistake. The people around him criticized him because they believed he shouldn't make mistakes, and they considered his mistake unforgivable. However, the truth was that his mistake was only a small one, but people deliberately magnified it. On the other hand, a bad person did many bad things in his life, but one day he suddenly did something good. The people around him called him a prodigal son, but the truth was that this good deed wasn't sincere. Therefore, in many situations, we shouldn't only look at the surface, but rather look at the inner meaning. When a boyfriend takes the initiative to visit us, it shows that he still cares about us, and when he takes us to eat our favorite food, it shows that he wants the best for us. It's just that during a later phone call, he couldn't answer our call immediately because of something unexpected, and when he called back, he didn't explain why he didn't answer the call earlier. In fact, we don't really deny him, we just feel that he doesn't genuinely care about us because his behavior overlooked us. So in that moment, we think he doesn't love us that much. If we calm down and think about it, did he really not care about us in the previous moments? If he genuinely didn't realize it, we can take the initiative to remind him instead of harboring silent resentment and he won't know where he went wrong, causing unnecessary misunderstandings. We can give him a chance to give us a reasonable explanation, and we can also proactively express some points that we care about to him, so that in the future we can try to avoid similar issues. Love sometimes requires a little understanding. The world and I love you.

Dear, your #insecurity# is causing you to become anxious and disrupt your thoughts~ From the information provided by the post owner, it can be understood that the post owner and their boyfriend are in a long-distance relationship, right? Can I ask if you have always been in a long-distance relationship from the beginning until now, or did you initially start out not in a long-distance relationship, but due to some reasons, you temporarily needed to be in a long-distance relationship? How long have you and your boyfriend been dating? How do you view this relationship? The post owner mentioned that the boyfriend brought things that they liked to eat when he came to visit from a distance. In fact, the post owner is a very easy-to-please girl. When the boyfriend brings things that he likes to eat, does the post owner feel full of happiness? The post owner mentioned that when he was leaving, he called me while on the way, and when I called back, he didn't explain anything to me. The boyfriend finished seeing himself and needs to return to his own work and living place. Here, the post owner deeply feels #reluctance#. While on the return journey, the phone shows that the call is in progress. How does the post owner view this matter? What does the post owner think the boyfriend is talking to someone about? Apart from this incident, in the normal course of interaction, are there any other aspects where the post owner has a suspicious attitude towards the boyfriend? The post owner mentioned that when I called back, he didn't explain anything to me, so I started to negate everything about him in my mind. If the boyfriend explained everything to you, would you still deny him and doubt him? So, did you directly ask the boyfriend for confirmation? From the information provided by the post owner, one can feel the post owner's lack of self-confidence and caution in this relationship. Don't you feel very tired, post owner? If it's tiring, I suggest that the post owner consider sharing their thoughts with the boyfriend, listen to what the boyfriend has to say, and see how the boyfriend behaves. I think a healthy and high-quality intimate relationship requires both people to work together to operate and maintain it. Especially for long-distance relationships, this is definitely the biggest test in an intimate relationship. I'm not sure about the specific situation of the post owner and the boyfriend's interaction, but I suggest that the post owner communicate with the boyfriend in a timely manner, reserve some personal space for both parties, and learn more to enhance their own confidence. I believe that your future relationship can be more relaxed and happy. The world and I love you. Best wishes to the post owner, Quiet Ting.

Hello~ Thank you for inviting me. From your brief description, I can sense a bit of your "stubbornness" or maybe you were feeling a little emotional at that time. It seems like your long-distance relationship with your boyfriend is not very stable, and you have a lot of insecurity or lack confidence in him. How long have you been together? How do you get along with each other? Or what kind of love do you feel for your boyfriend? Do you love him more than yourself? Or maybe you don't love him that much? Only you know that in your heart. Because this also determines the quality of your relationship and how you get along. Actually, if you really care about it, you can directly ask him who he was talking to just now and tell him your current feelings and thoughts. What do you think? Having grudges, creating barriers, and even suspicion towards each other will not benefit your relationship, right? I don't know if you have a tendency to be a perfectionist. If you really reject your boyfriend completely because of this, is it fair to him? Getting along between lovers requires tolerance, understanding, and consideration - it is also an important foundation for a relationship, especially since you are in a long-distance relationship. You need to jointly manage and protect this relationship. I believe that you love each other. I hope you can face each other's inner thoughts openly, communicate more, have more confidence in yourself. Wishing you both the best~~.

After carefully reading your confession, I deeply understand the small emotions in your heart. I offer you a gentle breeze to smooth out the little bumps inside. Here is my analysis: 1. "I started to invalidate everything about him in my mind." Women are capricious, like ever-changing little princesses. And a little princess should be cherished by everyone. How immature of your boyfriend, to have such a great little princess as his girlfriend and not treasure her. He doesn't even answer calls or explain himself. Can't he say a few comforting words to you? He deserves to be invalidated by you. 2. So, you're bringing up this issue now because you want us to analyze this mindset for you. This mindset is called extremism. In other words, either fully affirm him or completely deny him. You can't find balance in your heart to accept both his good and bad qualities. 3. So how can you avoid extremism? That would be not taking yourself too seriously, but also not neglecting yourself either. Love yourself 70% and love others 30%. Take good care of yourself professionally and be kind to others in your free time. Love others with the same compassion you have for yourself. This will help you cultivate a balanced heart. Thank you for your question, and may all the beauty in the world come to you as expected.

Hahaha, you're not a girlfriend, you're a female boss. Besides you, he has many roles in society and family in this world. Similarly, you do too. If you want him to explain something, right? Maybe it's because you love him too deeply or something, you can tell him about your feelings, he will understand. I wish you well and hope that you will hold onto that rope and walk together with him, but not hang it around his neck, right? Best wishes to you.

question: Afraid to go out, feeling nervous and under great pressure every time I have to leave, is this considered social anxiety?
description: I have not been sleeping well for the past few nights, I don't know if it can be considered social anxiety disorder.

answers.answer_text: Thank you for trusting me to answer your questions. From your simple explanation that you are afraid to go out and feel anxious and stressed when you do, and also have trouble sleeping, it is a premature and subjective conclusion to label yourself as having social anxiety. It is also irresponsible towards yourself. Let's first refrain from labeling ourselves. Let's try to explore the following: 1. How did the symptom of being afraid to go out or feeling anxious when going out develop? Were there any specific events that caused you to suddenly become like this? How long has this been going on? We need to find out the cause. 2. You have provided limited information, and I do not know your age, gender, or what happened to make you feel this way. If you are a minor, you should inform your parents about any discomfort you are experiencing and let them take you to see a doctor. 3. If you are an adult, how much does this symptom affect you? What are your physical reactions like? You need to observe and assess this. If it has only been a short period and you occasionally feel afraid to go out, you can try to find reasons to go out, such as for a meal, and see what feelings arise. Try to understand where your anxiety is coming from. 4. If this symptom has been persistent for a long time and has already caused severe physical discomfort, it is important to go to the hospital for a check-up to find out what is happening. 5. Trouble sleeping can also affect your mood and mental state. If it's not chronic insomnia, you can try meditation to relax your body and alleviate the anxious emotions. If it is long-term insomnia, you should see a doctor. 6. Typical symptoms of social anxiety disorder include excessive worry and fear in social situations, crowded places, or when interacting with others. The individual may be afraid of embarrassing or awkward situations, which can lead to feelings of anxiety and fear. I suggest not jumping to conclusions. If you are really not doing well, it would be better to seek help from a doctor. Wishing you health and happiness!

Hugs. Actually, it's not as simple as saying whether it's social anxiety or not. You can try some relaxation exercises and calmly ask yourself, what's really going on? Why can't I sleep? Is it nervousness? What is the underlying emotion? What are you thinking about when you can't sleep? What are you afraid of? What's outside the door? What situation are you most afraid of encountering when you open the door? Have you experienced this kind of emotion before? Take the time to become aware of yourself, there's no right or wrong, any answer that comes to your mind is a factor that affects you. You can write it down on paper and analyze it further, considering the feasibility, pros, and cons. Then, analyze and find some measures that can help you relieve the situation. For example, is there a piece of clothing or an item that can give you courage? Is there someone who can accompany you, or can you practice socializing at night (while ensuring safety)? You can also look back at your most successful experiences and the best things you've done in social situations, give yourself some confidence, encouragement, and rewards. Keep going! Believe that you can do it.

question: Should I let my parents know if my boyfriend is coming to visit me?
description: My boyfriend and I are from the same small town and our families live very close to each other. My parents are well-known teachers in the town, and I have graduated from college, while my boyfriend only finished junior high school. My parents strongly oppose us being together. My boyfriend and his parents run a spicy hotpot fast food restaurant. Since I am working in another city, my boyfriend wants to come and visit me. I don't want to have a long-distance relationship! Should I tell my parents or not? I want to tell them, but I am also afraid. The two families live very close to each other, so they will find out sooner or later. I am living with my older sister in another city, and I don't want her to lie for me as it has nothing to do with her. I'm really conflicted and I hope to get some help and advice.

answers.answer_text: I see your dilemma and distress. Your parents are well-known teachers in the town, and they may think that your boyfriend's parents' income from running a spicy fast food restaurant is unstable, and they feel that he cannot bring you a happy and stable life in the future. Moreover, you are a college graduate and he only graduated from junior high school, there is a large difference between the two of you. From your parents' perspective, they want their daughter to have a good match, and in their eyes, your boyfriend is not a suitable match for you in many aspects. Now your boyfriend wants to end the long-distance relationship and come to find you to be together. Because your families live very close to each other, even if you don't say it, his parents may know and it may reach your parents' ears. So, you are deeply torn. And you feel pressured to keep the secret from your sister as well. All these considerations have made you very conflicted. Have you asked yourself how you truly feel about your boyfriend's personal qualities? Can you pass this test within yourself? Perhaps the surface problem you have is the fear of your parents not agreeing, but the deeper issue is the uncertainty about yourself and your boyfriend's future. If your boyfriend had the same educational background as you, had a decent job or stable income, then you wouldn't hesitate and be so torn like now, and you would be very willing to tell your parents. But now the reason you are torn is because you also know that there is a significant gap between you and your boyfriend, and you have uncertainties in your heart about your relationship. Or perhaps you are not aware, but deep down, you do have some rejection towards your boyfriend. So this is the real reason causing your dilemma. Instead of asking whether you should tell your parents or not, perhaps you should ask yourself if you want to continue with your boyfriend, how to proceed, whether you have common ideals and goals for the future, and whether your understanding and communication on things can be smooth, these might be what you need to think about and face.

Poster, hello. After seeing your previous confession, it seems that you are still quite in love with your boyfriend, but at the same time, you are afraid of your parents' strong opposition, and you don't know what to do. The key here is to address your parents' concerns because parents' hearts are full of compassion. If your parents oppose it, it means they hope you can find someone reliable and live a worry-free life. If you sincerely want to be with your boyfriend and move towards marriage, you should try to let your partner achieve the results that satisfy your parents. Being good to you is just one aspect, but the most important thing is that your parents hope that he can fully guarantee your future life together. In my opinion, the best approach is for your boyfriend to achieve some accomplishments, and then you two can meet your parents together. This way, the chances of success will be higher. If you directly tell your parents about meeting, they will most likely have a higher chance of opposition, and it will be difficult for you to handle. I hope this can help you.

Hello, I can understand your feelings very well. Your parents, being teachers, probably value education more. Your boyfriend's educational background might make your parents think that he is not as outstanding, hence their opposition to your relationship. Now your boyfriend wants to come and visit you, and we can imagine your parents' reaction. However, even so, I still recommend that you inform your parents. Temporary concealment has no tangible benefits and will only increase your parents' dislike towards your boyfriend. Lack of education can be compensated for by good character. Your parents value education because they value character, as a higher education represents higher quality. If you hide it and your parents find out later, they will think his character is not good. So I suggest that you directly talk to your parents. You can change their perception by showing them the things he does for you and make your parents believe that he genuinely cares for you. Your parents' wish is for you to be well. You can also seek help, such as through your boyfriend's family, to improve the relationship between the two families. Finally, I wish you the best!

Hug the questioner~ I suggest that you tell your parents, as when it comes to marriage, it's not just about family circumstances but also about the character of your partner. You must really like your partner, which is why you don't care about their education background. But due to your parents' jobs, I think they probably have a stronger desire for you to find a partner who is at least equal in education and social status. This is why you feel conflicted between love and familial obligations. I think you may have already imagined in your mind how to tell your parents, how they will react, and how you should handle it. This is actually about mentally preparing yourself. However, we also have to consider your parents. They have raised you into an adult daughter who is getting married, so of course they want you to marry someone who can take care of you. No one wants their precious daughter, who they have cherished for over 20 years, to end up with nothing. Since both families live nearby, your parents will eventually find out, so it's better to tell them sooner. Leave more time for your parents to understand and accept your boyfriend. I believe if your parents discover that your boyfriend has good character, ambition, and truly cares about you, they will respect your thoughts and let go of their insistence on education. Summon up the courage to tell them. It's not a bad idea to listen to the advice of the older generation. Besides, your parents are teachers who have seen many, many students and have life experiences that allow them to see people clearly. After all, outsiders often have a clearer view than those immersed in love. Wishing you the best~

question: We are becoming more and more dependent on mobile phones. It feels uncomfortable without a phone by our side. What should we do?
description: Although everyone needs to use their phones every day, I feel like I can't go a moment without my phone. Most of my roommates charge their phones on the table before going to bed, but I have to bring mine to bed and keep it by my pillow to feel comfortable (even though I know it emits a lot of radiation); even when I shower, I bring my phone inside with me, even if I don't listen to music. In class, I can't help but occasionally check my phone for new messages. Whenever I don't have my phone with me, I feel restless and unenergetic... This has been going on for a very long time now, and I feel like it's getting worse. Do I have some kind of psychological problem?

answers.answer_text: Hello friend, first of all, I'm glad to see your question on this platform, which I assume you downloaded an app on your phone to access. (Just making a little joke.) To help ease your anxiety, I want to let you know that you're not alone in this situation. In this era of information overload, we all have become inadvertently attached to our phones, myself included. So, let's analyze the situation: 1. Firstly, I have experienced all of the situations you mentioned (keeping the phone near the pillow, listening to music with the phone while showering, and unable to resist checking the phone during class), and I have also felt the same anxiety as you. However, once you analyze the reasons behind it, you will be able to reduce this anxiety. In this era of information explosion, information is constantly bombarding us. Every time we see updates from friends or celebrities, or trending topics, it stimulates our brains to release dopamine, making it difficult for us to stop refreshing the screen. We crave the next explosive surprise, slowly succumbing to this desire. 2. After reading my description above, you will realize that this is not just a psychological factor but also a physiological one, which might help alleviate some of the guilt you feel. Don't be too hard on yourself. If this lifestyle is negatively affecting your studies or other aspects of your life, set small goals for yourself, such as limiting your phone usage to a certain number of hours per day. Personally, I started with six hours, then gradually reduced it to five, and now I'm down to four hours. Alternatively, challenge yourself in other aspects, like reading books or participating in activities to divert your attention from the phone. It might take some time to get used to it, so choose a method that suits your personal habits. Lastly, I want to say that the person with the strongest self-control is not the one who competes against themselves but the one who learns how to accept conflicting aspects of themselves and integrate them into one. So, there's no need to blame yourself. Good luck to you!

question: Why can't I feel the love from the people around me anymore?
description: I am disappointed with my college entrance examination results. It seems like everyone cares about me, but I can't feel it. I feel like a puppet.
keywords: Growth, self-growth, self-acceptance, and the meaning of life.

answers.answer_text: Hello, how do you view the disappointment of the college entrance examination? What do you feel from this experience? You mentioned that you know people around you care about you, but you can't feel it. Sometimes, when a person is trapped in their own emotions, it's easy to lose the ability to perceive warmth. I have also experienced a long period of low point in my life, and people around me cared about me and did a lot for me. Although I knew in my heart that they cared about me, I couldn't feel it. It's okay, as long as you know that there are people around you who care about you, it's enough. You may not feel it now, but it doesn't mean you will never feel it. It's also possible that they express their care in a way that you don't expect, so you can't feel it. When you have sorted out your emotions and come out of this difficult period, look back.

question: Lately, I keep crying over small things.
description: A few days ago, I got angry because I didn't go to the supermarket, and just now I thought of a small thing and started crying again. I even hit my head, feeling that I'm too ugly, too fat, and cry too easily. Am I just a burden?
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, fragile and tearful

answers.answer_text: Hello, I hope my answer can help you. Have you been under a lot of stress lately? In this situation, it is easy to get angry over small things. If so, you can think about what is causing the stress, and then try to solve the problem. Secondly, crying can also help release stress. It is a normal physiological expression of emotion for humans, and scientifically it is believed that crying has protective effects on one's mental and physical well-being. So sometimes it is good to have a good cry. When you are feeling sad, it is easy to have negative thoughts. Actually, others may not think there is anything wrong with your appearance. Don't have too much psychological pressure in this regard, everyone has their own shining points. If you are too concerned about it, take action and engage in activities like running or exercising to improve yourself. You need to give yourself positive suggestions, believe in your abilities. If you don't accept yourself, how can you expect others to accept you? Remember to love yourself more! I also suggest that you 1) relax your mind and don't overthink, live in the present and enjoy your life; 2) pay attention to adjusting your emotional state, engage in activities that make you happy and cultivate hobbies; 3) when you are troubled by emotions, communicate more with others, don't keep it all to yourself, and you can also seek counseling from professionals who can provide you with professional advice. Finally, I wish you happiness and smooth life every day~

question: How can I change myself if I have trouble speaking clearly in front of the public?
description: I only laugh really happily and can have long conversations when I'm with very close and familiar friends. I don't feel much communication pressure. In front of many people, such as at large events, sometimes I get so nervous that I can't speak a word. Actually, I know that I have social anxiety, so I'm not very willing to participate in certain activities. However, I don't want to have too much pressure and worries in this aspect, and it's possible that my emotional intelligence is really low. So now, I get nervous when speaking in front of a lot of people. I feel like it's really difficult for me to change the current situation and I don't know what to do.

answers.answer_text: OP, hello! After reading your description, I have gained some understanding of the questions you want to ask. In this regard, I'm sending you a virtual hug. From your description, I can feel the contradiction you are facing. Deep down, you really want to change the current situation, but due to environmental pressure, you feel nervous and unable to speak in a public setting. Although you have probably told yourself countless times not to be nervous, the tension in your body is beyond your control. Therefore, when you find yourself in a specific situation, you still feel anxious. Actually, I'm also someone who is afraid of speaking in public settings. Every time I have to speak on stage, I get nervous, my face turns red, and once I step off the stage, I don't even remember what I said up there. Even though I always tell myself not to be nervous and that they're just classmates who won't laugh at me, I still get nervous when it's time to speak. However, I still believe that one day, I will be able to stand on stage and speak without feeling so nervous, but with more composure and confidence. At the same time, I believe that you will also have that day when you won't feel nervous in public settings, but rather speak freely. Therefore, I have also summarized some methods to help you alleviate your current situation. (1) Start by analyzing the reasons for your nervousness and inability to speak. Determine whether it is due to external factors or internal factors. Only by understanding the root cause can you better solve the problem you are facing. If it is because you feel unprepared with your speaking content, then make sure to prepare well before speaking. This will to some extent reduce your nervousness and increase your confidence while speaking. (2) Every time you speak in a public setting, encourage yourself and reward yourself accordingly. Don't panic, take it slowly, and control the pace. Keep trying to speak in public settings and gradually accumulate experience. Naturally, you will become less nervous. This may be a long process, but as long as you don't give up, there will come a day when you can speak confidently in public settings. (3) Work on improving your language expression skills by reading books and watching videos. The world loves you. Best wishes.

OP, hello. I think my situation is the same as yours. When speaking in front of a large crowd, I also speak unclearly and my speech is fragmented, unable to form a complete sentence. A few days ago, I participated in an election, and I felt extremely successful on stage. But when I got on stage, I stuttered and my mind went blank. Maybe it's because there are unfamiliar people around, and the occasion feels a bit formal, making you feel like everyone's eyes are on you. I feel like the burden of my image is too heavy and I can't relax. But once you experience this kind of situation more, you will get used to it. In large events and such, we can adjust our mindset, boldly go up and speak, and not everyone's gaze is on you. You can also think from a different perspective. Why are you speaking on stage? It's because you are excellent, and speaking in a confident and appropriate manner, not to show others that you are suitable for standing there and speaking. Nervousness and the inability to speak are limited to formal occasions and large events. I don't think it's social anxiety. It might just be pure nervousness. I think OP can analyze why you are so nervous, if it's because you value this matter a lot. Before speaking on stage, you can prepare fully and not improvise last minute like I did, which made me unable to organize my thoughts. During the speech, you can encourage yourself and give yourself pep talks in your mind. Imagine that everyone in front of you is familiar or treat it as if you're talking to yourself. Try more and practice more. I believe both of us can overcome this. The above are my personal opinions that OP can refer to.

Hello friend! Sending you a warm hug! It's easy and relaxed to chat with familiar friends, but when it comes to being in a large group or attending big events, it can be nerve-wracking and overwhelming. I think the reason why it's easy and relaxed to chat with friends is because you are more familiar with them and feel more free, without many concerns. However, in large gatherings or with a bunch of people who you may not know very well, you might be afraid of saying the wrong things or not knowing what to say, which can leave a bad impression on others and make you feel anxious and lost. Actually, it takes practice to improve this situation. Try speaking up in crowds without being afraid of making mistakes. If you make a mistake, it can be corrected. Through continuous improvement and learning from mistakes, I believe that in the next conversation, you can be as relaxed and free as you are in front of friends and colleagues. Additionally, speaking in front of a large group is similar to chatting with friends and colleagues; you are only expressing your opinions through words, just with a different number of people. There's no need to be nervous. The above is just my personal opinion, for reference only. I hope it can help you.

question: A new 9th grade female student can feel warmth at school, but doesn't have any friends.
description: As a new third-year middle school student, I can feel warmth at school but I don't have a best friend, the kind of one-on-one best friend. I am quite sensitive as an individual. I don't like being too close to friends and others, otherwise I feel ignored. I don't have anyone to open up to about my daily life. I feel quite lonely. What should I do? Should I continue enduring this for the final year? I have a friend in a formal one-on-one setting, but that friend is carefree and not the kind of one-on-one friend.

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP~※ You can feel warmth at school, but you don't have friends to listen to your descriptions. I believe that you must be a girl with a rich inner world and strong emotions, and you have principles. That's why you have such high standards for friends and don't easily break them. It's not easy for many people in today's society to have few friends and not indulge in superficial relationships. In order to become friends, two people need to go through some experiences together, understand each other's personalities, and be able to accompany each other when they are vulnerable. Such people are rare, but not nonexistent. It's like dating - when we haven't met them, all we can do is wait. This waiting is not about isolating ourselves, but about communicating with others, building on a "good interpersonal boundary". In this process, you need to stay true to yourself, while also giving others the opportunity to become your friends. In fact, many friends are not known to become friends at first sight; they need to go through many experiences together to gradually understand each other. So, give others a chance, and give yourself a chance. Though you may feel that you don't have close friends, you can still feel warmth. I believe that you must be a very kind girl, so the world you see is warm in color. I believe that someone as warm as you will definitely find intimate friends! Best wishes!

question: What should I do when I am forced to make empty promises?
description: A person asks you for help when they are in trouble, but you honestly tell them that you can't help because you also have your own problems and limited abilities. Then they become discontented and filled with resentment. Do I have to make empty promises to satisfy them? Isn't that deceiving them? What kind of mindset is this? It feels similar to one beggar asking another beggar for food, and when the other beggar doesn't have any, the first beggar gets angry and demands that the other beggar promise to treat them to a big chicken leg in the future.
keywords: Interpersonal relations, communication, conflicts, social adjustment.

answers.answer_text: Hello OP! After reading your question, it reminded me of the skit "Let's Talk If You Have Something" performed by Guo Donglin and Mai Hongmei during the Spring Festival Gala many years ago. Although the skit is full of jokes, it actually portrays the helplessness of being the good guy. When others are in trouble, you help if you can, but you don't make it difficult for yourself if you can't. This is because you have a clear understanding of yourself and avoid putting yourself and the other person in a more awkward situation if you can't fulfill your promise in the future. This is a very correct approach. The other person may have a strong emotional reaction to being rejected, which may be due to their own distorted perception of reality. When people ask for help, it is often because they trust the other person and believe that with their abilities, they can definitely help themselves, which is why they ask for assistance. When the request is denied, there is a feeling of disappointment due to being rejected and suspicion and resentment towards the person who can help but refuses to. OP can think about whether there are any actions that may have caused this misunderstanding. For example, after carefully considering the request and realizing that you really can't do it, sincerely explain the reason instead of simply saying you can't help. This may make it easier for the person to accept. If OP's way of communicating with the other person is not a problem, but the other person still harbors resentment, then isn't it a fortunate thing to realize through this incident whether the other person is a friend worth taking seriously and making an effort for? Maintaining appropriate boundaries between people is the best expression of goodwill and respect for each other.

Hello, it is difficult to comfort someone whose heart is filled with anger. I can sense your helplessness and uncertainty in dealing with this person. From your description, it seems that he carries a lot of negative energy and is not easily uplifted. If I were in your shoes, I might choose to keep my distance from this friend. If I were to encounter such a visitor, I would focus on my own psychological well-being before engaging with him. As a professional mental health consultant, helping him would require a lot of energy and effort. What more for you? I sense that you want to help him but feel powerless. In this situation, I think it is important for you to take care of your own emotional state. If you are forced to interact with him, it might be quite challenging. Your task is to prevent your emotions from being affected or dragged down by him. Pay attention to what you can do and avoid attempting things beyond your capabilities. Putting yourself under unnecessary stress will not only fail to help him but also lead to doubts about your own abilities. As for whether you should paint a rosy picture for him, I believe it depends on how you feel during your interactions with him. If painting a rosy picture can give him hope, make him more positive, and help him in some way, then it might be worth it. However, if doing so only brings complaints and doesn't actually benefit him, then it's better to prioritize your own well-being. That is the most important thing, after all. Wishing you well, the world and I are rooting for you!

Friend, hello! Seeing the issue you've expressed, I believe it's not that you're afraid of being abandoned, but rather lacking self-confidence. The feeling of constantly being abandoned suggests that you don't believe in and trust the people around you. It's possible that someone has hurt you in the past, and you haven't dealt with the hurt properly. You may have accepted the hurt, but subconsciously refused to acknowledge it. In the future, you can do things that boost your self-confidence, which will make you stronger. Once you become strong, your mindset, emotions, actions, and behaviors will follow suit! I believe in you! Keep it up!

question: One day, suddenly fantasizing about my classmate, and then there were reactions afterwards. What should I do?
description: One day in my first year of high school, I was listening attentively in my physics class. Suddenly, an image of my desk mate (a male) taking off his clothes popped into my head. I didn't really like him as a desk mate, so I felt extremely embarrassed and my face turned red. Then the physics teacher started talking about sexual topics, saying that as we grow up, we'll understand that it's not a big deal. I thought he knew what I was thinking (possibly because I felt guilty, but also because he often claimed to know what students were thinking just by looking at them).
