Why is it like this? 2. How should you express your needs? Regarding the first step, at least for you, it is unreasonable. You are already 18 years old and should have your own independent thinking ability, but your mother is still using controlling methods to educate you, clearly disregarding your desires. During adolescence, communication should be the main approach, respecting the child's wishes. As another respondent mentioned, the way your mother is approaching it is quite direct, which is clearly a lazy educational philosophy. It's similar to the students I've seen before, where some fathers use a system of rewarding points for positive behavior and deducting points for negative behavior (the points can be exchanged for money or gifts). This approach is also a lazy way of parenting, treating children like machines. The end result is that children start to focus on material exchanges rather than emotional reciprocation when interacting with their peers. Education should never be reduced to simple input-output behaviors. To change this situation, it may require a serious and heartfelt conversation or the involvement of an authoritative figure to educate your mother. Regarding how to express your needs: firstly, you want to have your own space, to confide in others at night; secondly, you don't want to be treated like a child, you want to have your own autonomy, and not have your food or phone privileges taken away at the slightest mistake. If possible, the best approach is for the two of you to sit down and talk it out. We can directly ask your mother: what is your goal? Are the methods you are using really effective? What have you gained and lost from this? If you want to achieve your goal without hurting my feelings, what should you do? Can you accept that? If communication is temporarily difficult, perhaps inviting a third party to intervene could help. Lastly, I want to ask, where is your father in all of this? You are 18 years old and need to learn to have a sense of empowerment, to search for solutions when faced with things you cannot accept. Keep going and good luck!

Hello, I saw your distress and I hope I can help you. I see that you have been punished by your mother by deducting your meal expenses, taking away your phone, and other things because you keep scratching your pimples, which has greatly affected your way of studying and living. You feel controlled and restricted, which makes you very uncomfortable. I truly understand your feelings and emotions. Perhaps we can try to look at this situation from a different perspective. First, let's switch positions and think about it. Just looking at the issue of scratching pimples, from your mother's point of view, it does affect your appearance as a daughter. If you were in your mother's position, facing a grown-up daughter who repeatedly ignores reminders, can you come up with a better solution? Do you tie your daughter's hands? Or install surveillance to catch her every time she touches her face? Try to seriously think from your mother's perspective, and you might have a deeper understanding of your mother's good intentions, which will make you less resistant. Second, self-discipline. Managing yourself well is the most convenient way to gain more freedom. From this perspective, the more self-disciplined you are, the more your parents will trust you and the less they will control you. Of course, there may still be cases of parents intervening excessively, but in your case, it is your actions that have forced your parents to take measures that remind you to take it seriously. Therefore, as you become an adult, learn to manage yourself well (including taking care of your skin), and let your actions show your maturity and growth to your parents, and you may gain more freedom. Third, positive interaction. In times of conflict, promptly communicate your feelings to your parents, let them understand your emotions and mood, and discuss better solutions together. This will not only improve your relationship but also help you grow happier. Wishing you new discoveries every day.

question: My mom says we don't have common topics to talk about, what should I do?
description: Mom is busy outside, and I am living with relatives. Once, after I washed my hair, mom called. I told her that I just finished washing my hair and will take a shower later. Mom said, "Why don't we shower together? You are dragging your feet." I replied, "Did you call just to scold me?" She got a bit angry and hung up the phone. I realized my mistake, but I couldn't bring myself to apologize. What should I do?
keywords: Family, family relationships, communication between parents.

answers.answer_text: Hello, dear OP. After hearing your story, I feel like giving you a hug! From your narration, it seems like I can see a loving hedgehog mother and daughter. They clearly love each other and want to embrace each other, but they unintentionally hurt each other due to some objective reasons! Parents and children are supposed to be the closest people in this world, but they seem to be lost in the distance of reality! It can be seen that the main issue between you and your mother currently lies in communication, which is critical and judgmental in nature, a form of communication that contains elements of cold violence. Therefore, I suggest you learn some communication skills and try a different attitude and approach when communicating with your mother. Mother and daughter are supposed to be the closest people, and the solution to the problem is not just about saying sorry; being playful can also be a cute and effective way of apologizing. The more formal the expression, the easier it is to create distance between each other, while being playful is sometimes the best way to establish an intimate relationship with our parents. Because behind being playful lies love and dependence, we only playfully interact with those we love and those who love us and those we rely on. In a sense, being playful is also a way to express trust. I don't know the reasons why your parents are not by your side, but I believe they are also helpless in their hearts. So, you need to understand your parents and try to think about the problem from their perspective. Secondly, actively talk to your parents about your troubles, have more conversations with them, give them an opportunity to understand you, and give yourself a chance to be loved and cared for. Many problems arise from poor communication, so it is important to learn effective communication. I recommend you read some books on effective communication, which may be helpful to you. Wishing you well!

Hello, thank you for inviting me~ When I saw your mom asking you why you don't wash your hair and take a bath together, and why you are so slow with these things, I thought of my mom. Maybe most of our moms are similar. Then, I saw your conversation with your mom, and it ended on a sour note. I can relate to that too, because sometimes when I talk on the phone with my parents, they hang up on me at the slightest disagreement, and that feeling is really unpleasant. I understand you. Mothers have carried us in their womb for nine months and given birth to us. They are the most direct and intimate people in our lives and our initial attachment objects. Parents are the most primal driving force for children, and mothers are the first soil for children's growth. If the attachment relationship between mother and child is harmonious, loving, and warm, then our growth will be filled with happiness. On the other hand, the relationship between mother and daughter may become "mutually harmful," even a lifelong burden. Before answering your question, I'd like to talk about a movie I recently watched online. It's called "Spring Tide," which was released last year. It's a movie about the "Chinese-style mother-daughter relationship," social and family ethics, starring Hao Lei and Jin Yanling. After watching it, maybe because I was able to identify with it strongly, or maybe because I had similar experiences, I felt a bit heavy-hearted and touched. In the eyes of the mother, Ji Minglan, no matter what her daughter does or says, she feels irritated and annoyed. She verbally abuses her daughter, even taking away her granddaughter from her daughter to take care of, depriving her daughter of her rights as a mother. In her mother's mind, her daughter getting pregnant out of wedlock and living a disorderly life is just like her hateful husband. She never shows her daughter kindness but instead constantly mocks, targets, and says hurtful words, challenging her daughter's limits. She feels that after painstakingly raising her daughter, she now has to provide for her food and shelter, as well as take care of her granddaughter, sacrificing everything for it. But her daughter doesn't understand gratitude, is not filial, obedient, or repay her. She feels like she's living in a sea of suffering, in unbearable pain. On the other hand, the daughter, Guo Jianbo, doesn't feel her mother's warmth, respect, understanding, and love at all. From a young age, she only receives her mother's accusations, humiliation, control, and resentment. In this already incomplete family, the fragile mother-daughter relationship turns the entire family into a battlefield. In this kind of original family environment, the daughter feels a contradiction towards her mother: I hate my mom, but I still love her in my heart, and I long for her love. Even when she is in her forties and already a mother herself, she still can't understand: why is it that the mother, who should be the child's first attachment, the person who loves me the most, hurts me the most. This decades-long conflict only stops when the mother falls ill and the cursing in the home finally stops. The pain in the daughter's heart, Guo Jianbo's pain: the mother's dominance, cruelty, and heartlessness not only destroy a family, but also the image of a mother in my heart. A family is not a battlefield, and even if there is victory, it is not real glory. The detestable flaws of a mother will, without exception, deeply imprint themselves onto the daughter. The mother-daughter relationship becomes a repetitive cycle, and the genes flowing in our blood will subtly integrate into the child's body and mind, becoming difficult to erase. In the book "Madness and Civilization," it is said that under various social constraints, most people have already abandoned physical violence. Instead, they choose a more civilized form of violence - verbal violence - to continue to harm others (including loved ones). Not all love needs to be proved through mutual torment. The release of negative emotions is the source of conflict in family relationships. Sometimes, we intentionally or unintentionally go against our parents and can't help but retort or resist. Under the influence of our parents, we also vent negative emotions in the same way. We become replicas of their words and actions. Over time, it forms a complicated and contradictory emotional relationship of love and hate. I think any relationship is mutual, and we should try to understand our parents and learn how to stand firm in our own views while effectively communicating and getting along with them. Parents can also try to understand their children, guide them positively with their life experiences, and lead by example instead of expressing their own emotions. Perhaps in this way, with mutual respect, understanding, and empathy, love can nourish each other. What do you think? Since you are aware of your problem and feel that you have hurt your mom, and it's making you uncomfortable, but you can't bring yourself to apologize. Is that right? Actually, your mom may also feel the same way, you know. So let's take the first step and adjust our emotions, apologize to your mom calmly and sincerely. If you can't say it, you can write it down and send it to her through your phone. Let her see what you want to say. This way, you won't feel awkward, and I believe that the feelings between a mother and daughter can be conveyed. Families should be filled with love, not supported by resentment. Parent-child relationships need more understanding and the courage to express love. Keep it up! You're actually great, believe in yourself!

Hug, I really understand your feelings, received! Actually, many family relationships are not good not only because of distance, but also because the inner child cannot get the feeling of satisfaction, constantly demanding and seeking attention. And this itself is not wrong. I guess the reason you can't apologize to your mom is not because you don't know it's not good to do so, but because you feel guilty. Whether it's the guilt of not understanding your mom's feelings even though she works hard outside, or the guilt of hurting her when she is just trying to do good for herself. And wanting love, wanting maternal love, and wanting companionship from mom is not wrong either. Craving love and expressing anger or temper is not a mistake, and apologizing is not about seeking something. It's about understanding, caring, and empathy. I used to be a person who hated apologizing, especially saying sorry. I felt like saying sorry was like being insulted, like admitting I was weaker than others. I felt like they were just venting their anger, blaming me, and saying sorry was just pretending. When I chatted with a classmate before, she felt that I, just like another classmate of ours, didn't like apologizing, didn't like saying sorry! She understood me very well and knew that I had a strong sense of self-esteem. I've been thinking about this for years, not because of what she said, but because I kept blaming myself! I know I'm such a terrible person, such a useless person, but so many people like me, want to be friends with me, want to help me. I've hurt so many people and I want to apologize to them all, but it seems like I haven't done that for the most part! My heart will deny her (my classmate), criticize what she said, thinking she is criticizing me. My heart has always been restless, thinking that those who curse me probably just want to make trouble for no reason, and I find myself ridiculous. I don't want to apologize, not because I don't want to apologize to others. It's because I don't want to apologize to this version of myself, this version that is so terrible but can be understood. I feel like even if others blame me and punish me, I deserve it. But later I realized that others also blame me, thinking that being sad and feeling guilty won't make them peaceful and happy, but will make them self-blame. I used to love criticizing others very much, and it's still the same now. Because I love criticizing myself very much, I'm willing to not forgive myself, not apologize to myself, and not forgive any behavior of others, even just a little bit. Because I feel guilty, very guilty, so I'd rather ignore it. Actually, most of the time, what we should do most is apologize to ourselves. Why don't we want to forgive ourselves when these emotions and feelings are so normal and heartfelt guilt? Why don't we want to forgive ourselves when we long so much for our mother's love? This is not weakness! It has never been a mistake!! It's not because we're not good enough! It's because you, we are daughters of mothers who have an uncontrollable love, so don't blame yourself, don't feel guilty. Your mom will surely understand you! If you can't apologize next time, just call your mom every day, and listen to her. I wish you can understand this self that loves your mom, that longs for your mom's company. Slowly get along well with your mom, understand each other. Understand yourself, understand your mom. I wish you peace, joy, gratitude, thankfulness!

question: Can't get used to a life without a boyfriend, how to get through these few months?
description: When my boyfriend joined the military, I couldn't get used to the life without him and felt really sad when I couldn't reach him. I had to move out of the school dormitory because I needed to do an internship for transferring to another university, so I was left alone while all my roommates went for internships. I couldn't focus on studying by myself and kept getting distracted. I know that transferring to another university is important, but I always find myself daydreaming and I don't know how to concentrate fully on studying for the next few months.
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, anxious emotions, fragile and tearful.

answers.answer_text: From the description provided by the topic owner, it seems that the topic owner is currently going through a lot of suffering. The boyfriend is not by their side, they also have to transfer, and the roommate is not there either, so they can only rely on themselves to get through this difficult time. It must be very painful, so here's a virtual hug for the topic owner. The topic owner mentioned that because the boyfriend joined the military and cannot be contacted, they have not been able to adapt. Even when faced with the important task of transferring, they still can't concentrate on studying. The topic owner may need to think about why they are so distressed by the temporary separation from their boyfriend and what their boyfriend means to them. Is it dependence on the boyfriend or fear of something? etc. Alternatively, the topic owner may need to ask themselves a few questions to become more aware of their inner feelings and needs. This will help the topic owner understand themselves better. Regarding the topic owner's current situation, here are a few suggestions that may help: 1. Facing the separation from the boyfriend, it is indeed difficult for us to adapt suddenly. Therefore, the topic owner needs to plan some activities for themselves to divert their attention from the boyfriend joining the military. For example, chatting with friends or going shopping, etc. 2. During this time, the topic owner may experience a lot of emotional exhaustion, so they should take care of themselves and consume a balanced diet. 3. Facing the transfer, if they can't concentrate on studying, the topic owner can set small goals for themselves every day. When they achieve those goals, they should give themselves small rewards or encouragement, whether it's emotional or material rewards. This will give them more motivation to study. 4. Transferring requires intense studying, but studying excessively can have a counterproductive effect. Therefore, it is suggested that the topic owner should schedule some leisure and entertainment time every day. This will enhance efficiency.

1. It is not good to be unable to get used to not having a boyfriend. No matter how much you rely on another person, there are many things you have to face on your own, such as having a child in the future. Your future husband cannot replace or help you with that. 
2. A successful person is first and foremost an independent person with self-awareness, their own personal space, and the ability to be alone. Based on your description, you lack the ability to be alone. Only when you love yourself will others love you. If you don't have these abilities, and others become more successful while you remain stagnant, you will be left behind. 
3. The reason you are not working is because you want to switch to a bachelor's degree. Since you are having trouble studying now, why not go back to work? Working can also alleviate your current suffering.

Hello, OP! First of all, I want to give you a warm hug. From your description, I understand that your boyfriend is unable to be with you at all times due to serving in the military, which makes you feel uncomfortable and uneasy in your daily life. I completely understand your current emotions, as long-distance relationships coupled with worries about each other can intensify these feelings. However, we also need to take care of ourselves so that we don't make our partners worry and can focus on their military training. We should believe that no matter the circumstances, we can find the most suitable way to communicate with each other and maintain our feelings. As for the issue of not being able to concentrate on studying, we can try changing our learning environment, such as going to the library or other places, as such an atmosphere can help us study better.

question: How do I deal with my mother draining all my love for her?
description: My mother has a terrible temper and is very demanding of the people around her. She despises my father for being weak and incompetent, and she often expresses dissatisfaction with me and my husband. She doesn't have any close friends in her social circle. Since I started attending university, I have gradually developed my own thoughts, understanding myself and discovering my own identity, leading me to want to gradually break free from her control. However, she often uses harsh words to criticize me, saying that I am disobedient and have made her life miserable for the past few years. She even mocks me for having an education and looking down on her. I want to see her, care for her, and help her live a good life, but at the same time, I'm also afraid of being with her. Her sense of entitlement is too strong, and she will use any kindness shown to her as ammunition, keeping accounts of how much she has sacrificed for me and my father to prove that we are ungrateful and heartless. No matter how hard I try, she can always find something to be dissatisfied with and will never be truly content or live a peaceful life. Now that I have my own family, I can provide some material support to my parents and even gave them a comfortable new home, but she is still endlessly dissatisfied. I have spent a lot of time trying to understand her issues and concerns, but it has had almost no effect. Moreover, she has become somewhat neurotic, feeling that her marriage is especially miserable and constantly considering divorcing my father. What should I do?
keywords: Family, family trauma, family relationships, family control.

answers.answer_text: For someone with a strong need for control, giving them a sense of control in form will make them feel more at ease. For someone who has a strong need to give, allowing them to give and then expressing gratitude will make them feel that their efforts are worth it. Your mother has both a strong need for control and a strong need to give. On the surface, or in her words, you can obey her, but privately, you should do what you need to do. When your mother gives, express gratitude immediately, and she will not feel resentful in her heart, using it to attack you. Your mother's temper, criticism, including disdain and dissatisfaction, are actually manifestations of her own need to be strong. A strong-willed person never has an easy life; she has too many standards and limits in her heart, for herself and for others. The control and criticism you experience, as well as your father's disdain, your mother experiences the same, because the voice she expresses often reflects her own feelings. From your words, I can see that you are not internally confused, which may be due to what you mentioned: "Since I went to college, I have gradually developed my own thinking, understood myself, and discovered myself, so I wanted to gradually break free from her control." This is something to be grateful and joyful for. You are a strong woman! When you have enough material and psychological strength, you may want to save your mother, but you find it useless. Yes, your mother has lived most of her life this way, and it is not easy for others to change her unless she wants to change herself. When she is unwilling to change, helping her change will not only be ineffective but also increase her dissatisfaction. It is better to use understanding to achieve better results. For example, thank her more, agree with her more, and accept her more. You may think that you are agreeing with and accepting even when she is wrong, won't that encourage her "arrogant demeanor"? No, you should believe that your mother has a basic ability to distinguish right from wrong, even if her words are still hurtful. If your mother feels unhappy in her marriage, you can express your views with a casual attitude. Marriage is a matter between parents. It is up to them to resolve it. If you think too much about interfering, it will have a counterproductive effect. You can break free from your mother's psychological control and give her a sense of power in form. At the same time, you also need to be aware of whether you are trying to control your parents in return. Are those so-called good intentions, just like their good intentions for you, a disguised need for control? You are so intelligent, I believe you will find the answer in my response! Best wishes for the happiness of your whole family!

Your mother is habitually critical of people around her, and growing up in such an environment must have been tough for you. In your relationship with your mother, both of you are actually in pain, whether it's your mother's habit of criticizing others or your acceptance of her criticism. There can be many reasons for criticizing others, such as inner dissatisfaction, anxiety, fear, high expectations, and more. On the other hand, those who are criticized may become timid, self-doubting, and develop many negative emotions and behaviors. When being nitpicked, it's important to understand that it's not your own problem, set boundaries for yourself, and minimize its impact on you. I think you have already done a great job at this. For example, when she accuses you of looking down on her or treating her poorly, you know in your heart that it's not true and that you have done what you were supposed to do. Your mother's personality and habits have been ingrained for decades, and changing them is not easy. No matter how much you do for her, even providing her with a comfortable new home, it may not change her habits. I understand that you want your mother to be less miserable and that you want both of your parents to be happier, but your mother's life is her own, and her personality has nothing to do with you. So don't make yourself too anxious or worried. Take care of your own mental well-being first and then try to meet some of your mother's demands as much as possible. Being filial to your parents and doing what you can is enough. You don't need to see your parents' happiness as your responsibility.

Hello! Facing a controlling and negative mother can be quite helpless. Even if you put in more patience, care, and filial piety, it's still not possible to fulfill your mother's inner sense of lack. It also greatly affects the relationship between your parents and your mother-daughter relationship. From your mother's perspective, while she is blaming and complaining, her own life experience is also very bad. She feels like she is surrounded by thorns, hurting others as well as herself. We don't know what your mother's childhood experiences were like, but her strong sense of control and the need to constantly emphasize her own worth is a manifestation of her inner insecurity and lack of a sense of safety. She wants to prove her usefulness and need for attention through exaggerated blame and accusations. Your mother is not aware that there is any problem with her behavior and thoughts, meaning she is not bothered by it and doesn't have a subjective desire to change. By spending so much time trying to analyze her psychological issues, you will only reinforce her thoughts and behavior. From another perspective, your approach is also a form of control, trying to make your mother change according to your own ideas. If your mother doesn't want to change her state of mind, those around her can't easily change it either. This is a personality trait that has been formed over decades, related to her original family and life experiences. Perhaps there are things that she has experienced that you cannot fully understand. What problem do you really want to solve? Do you want to change your mother's thoughts and behavior, or do you want to change your mother-daughter relationship? For the former, seeking help from a professional psychologist would be beneficial, while for the latter, you can try adjusting your own perspective on these events. Family problems are also problems between family members. Managing the psychological boundaries of each person is the key to solving these problems. For controlling parents, their problem lies in repeatedly crossing boundaries, whether or not they intend to do so. Regardless, they are still other people, even if they are our loved ones. We can only protect our own psychological boundaries. Understanding the inner pain of your mother, being willing to understand and be more tolerant, is the basis for improving your relationship with her. We can only do our best to contribute to our elders, whether or not they can accept it or in what way they can accept it is up to them. What we can do is manage our own thoughts and behavior. I hope my answer can be helpful to you!

Hello: Do you want to change your mother or yourself? This question is important. If it is the former, she needs to see it from the bottom of her heart. If it is the latter, then all you need to do is to work hard. However, there is also a possibility that your mother will change as you change yourself, but that only happens when you have extremely strong energy. Analyzing and understanding the problem: 1. Your mother has a really bad temper and is very demanding of people around her. She despises your father for being weak and incompetent, and she often expresses dissatisfaction with you and your husband. She doesn't have any close friends. (It seems that your mother's character is quite "unique," demanding strict standards from people around her. What about herself? Is she the same? Or does she have "double standards"? If she treats others and herself with the same strictness, she may have "obsessive" problems. If it's double standards, then the problem is simple.) 2. Since you went to college, you gradually developed your own thinking, understood yourself, and wanted to gradually break free from her control. But she often uses hurtful words to accuse you of not being obedient, making her suffer for several years, and ridiculing you for being educated and looking down on her. (Actually, if you think about it, what she said makes some sense. But what she doesn't know is, "Is her reasoning wrong? Doesn't she allow others to resist?" Maybe your mother still has a stronger ability to "control people," and people with this personality can change, at least after being constantly struck. But the problem is, she will be hurt, unless a professional counselor intervenes to help her understand.) 3. You want to see her, care for her, and give her a good life, but you are also afraid to be with her. Because she feels a strong sense of entitlement, turning all the good she does for others into a weapon, settling accounts for how much she has done for you and your father, and then proving that you and your father are ungrateful, heartless people. (Hmm, you love your mother very much and want to care for her and help her, just like all the good things she has done for you. But her paranoid personality not only offends others but also hurts you and your father. Her goodwill always turns into bad things, and she remains trapped in her own misconceptions. She is in pain, and so are you.) 4. No matter how hard you try, she can always find fault with the good things in life and is never satisfied. She can never live a peaceful life. (Hmm, she has a hollow space in her heart filled with dissatisfaction, grievances, sadness, and pain. So it's not that you are not doing well, it's that her hole is too deep. Your current efforts are just a "drop in the bucket" for her. She turns all the pain into "not good enough." Maybe she doesn't want to, but in her pain, you and your father become mourners (accompanying suffering). When you want to break free, she uses moral blackmail on you. But please don't worry, one day she will understand, you have to live your own life first before you can save her.) 5. Now that you have your own family, you can provide some material support to your parents, and even give them a comfortable new home, but she still has endless dissatisfaction. You have spent a lot of time trying to understand her problems, but it has had little effect. And she has become somewhat neurotic, feeling that her marriage is particularly miserable and always thinking about divorcing your father. What should you do? (Dear, maybe you don't really understand your mother? Perhaps she was dissatisfied with life because of material shortage in the past. But now that the material aspect has improved, she is still dissatisfied with your father. And her dissatisfaction with you is because you don't understand her? From a psychological perspective, if a person stays in a certain state for a long time, they can become neurotic. As time goes on, as long as there is a problem that touches on or is similar to the edge, it can easily trigger a burst of emotions, usually others will have no idea why. Actually, her saying she wants a divorce may not necessarily mean that she really wants one. Sometimes you can just go along with her words, of course, there are also skills in this. Look for an opportunity to communicate with her.) Conclusion: I wish your family happiness and joy! I hope your mother will get out of her pain soon! If you have any confusion, you can message me!

Hello, I understand your feelings very well. Every family has their own difficulties, and this problem is indeed distressing. Your main issue is that your mother has a strong desire to control and is dissatisfied with the people around her. Although you want to care for her, you are also afraid of interacting with her, which has left you conflicted and confused. Your mother has a bad temper and demands a lot from those around her, and this is a result of her personality. It is difficult to change a person's character, but adjustments and efforts can be made in other aspects. 1. Understand your mother and think about the reasons behind her actions from her perspective. Does she constantly blame others because of high expectations, past hardships that have formed strict demands, or excessively high expectations of the people around her? Your mother's behavior reflects her inner feelings. Try to understand the reasons behind her actions by considering her background and life experiences, and empathize with her emotions. Truly feel her thoughts and slowly understand what she wants. 2. Be more tolerant and communicate more. Our mothers are the people closest to us, from the nine months of pregnancy to raising us to adulthood, and every mother's journey is not easy. When there is a disagreement, communicate more. Some things require discussion, and the emotional bond between mother and child needs to be maintained. Besides material support, the most important thing is spiritual understanding. Our mothers lived in a different era, and we may not fully understand the hardships they experienced. Therefore, we need to be more understanding and accommodating. 3. Do what you can, and let the rest happen naturally. Your mother has always had a strong personality, so let it be. If you constantly try to change your mother, it will only bring both of you pain and lead to more intense arguments and conflicts. As you grow older, you have your own thinking and have started to escape your mother's control, which is indeed a helpless move. What you can do is to visit home frequently, provide material and emotional support to your mother, and tolerate her dissatisfaction and criticism. Fulfill your duties as a child, and let time resolve the rest. 4. Help your mother build a social circle and encourage her to go out. Your mother may not have close friends, so you can try to help her make some friends or encourage her to join activities such as square dancing. This will not only help her relax but also meet new companions. You can also assist her in finding her interests and engaging in activities she enjoys, allowing her to integrate into a community of peers. I wish you and your mother to overcome this distress and live a happy and fulfilling life.

Growth is about finding breakthroughs, changing paths, spiraling upwards, and becoming a better version of oneself. Mental Journey: The original poster primarily describes the relationship issues with their mother. The mother has a bad temper, is demanding of people around her, despises the father for being weak and incompetent, and frequently expresses dissatisfaction towards herself and the father. As the original poster gradually grows up, they gain a deeper understanding of the relentless criticism and desire to escape their mother's control. However, the mother does not want to let them escape and often mocks and ridicules them and the father. The original poster has always wanted to make an effort to improve this aspect of their mother, but despite their best efforts, they are unable to make any changes, and their mother remains the same. Living environment: The mother's controlling personality greatly affects the original poster's life and creates a conflict in their desire to break free from the mother's control. Although the original poster has grown up and has their own life, the mother's strong sense of control is a source of immense pain, as they long to break free but are bound by blood ties, and desire change but feel powerless, leaving them with a profound sense of helplessness. Changing trajectory: What does the mother want? The original poster has always wondered why their mother controls them and wants to change her. To be honest, it is very difficult to change one's mother at her age; she has been set in her ways for a long time. The original poster wonders if they have ever considered that their mother's deep complaints reflect a deeper desire. What does the mother really want? Or perhaps, what was she most afraid of as a child or in the past? Why does she constantly seek control and fear losing something? Understanding what the mother wants and fulfilling her desires is the key to truly changing her. Communicating with the mother: Once the original poster understands what the mother truly wants, they can communicate with her about how to obtain what she desires. Small goals can be set to allow the mother to achieve them, building her confidence. Complaints cannot solve problems or fulfill one's desires. Cementing the mother's transformation: After achieving the mother's goals, it is necessary to solidify her new ways. This can be done by continually setting and achieving a series of small goals that allow the mother to solidify her own mindset, live with confidence, and face life in a new way. Understanding what the mother truly wants - communicating with the mother - cementing the mother's changes - changing trajectory - spiraling upwards - becoming a better version of oneself.

Hello~ Reading your description, I can sense that you are facing your mother's intrusive love, aggressive words, and her seemingly endless demands that drain your energy and leave you feeling empty. It seems like you have endless dissatisfaction and it has left you mentally and physically exhausted. You don't know how to deal with such a mother and it has caused you a great deal of distress. From your description, it seems like you haven't clearly stated what you want. I can see that you have many frustrations and helplessness. The last sentence asks, "What should I do?" Is it about what you should do or what your mother should do? When you ask "What should I do," what aspect are you referring to? Do you not want your mother to divorce your father? Do you not want your mother to deplete all your love? Do you want to replenish your own love? Do you want to help your mother sort out her own issues? Do you want to know how to deal with such a mother? Do you want your mother to stop interfering in your marriage and personal life? I understand that facing such a mother can make you feel at a loss and agitated. Firstly, for yourself, you need a "moment" to express all kinds of emotions and release the various feelings bottled up inside you. (For your mother) After releasing your complex emotions, you can slowly figure out what you need to do for yourself. It seems like your mother's behaviors fill your heart, emotions, and even your life. You will need certain ways to release the long-suppressed emotions in your heart. You need to understand that many things and actions revolve around your mother actively. Or in other words, your mother uses various methods (verbal violence, moral coercion, and frequently mentioning divorce) to seek attention from those around her. Just like a spoiled child who gets whatever they want, always finding a way to get what they desire through tantrums. And it usually works, so they continue to use these tactics. In this situation, the main focus is on the mother, and you will lose your "sense of self". Many things revolve around your mother's affairs. (This is due to your mother's family environment and life experiences) For you, 1. Learn to observe your own feelings and thoughts, slowly finding yourself again. 2. Learn to face such a "domineering" mother. 3. Understand why you always get caught up in this situation and understand why your mother behaves this way. 4. Only then will you slowly realize what you can achieve and what you cannot. Lastly, when you ask what to do, I simply hope that you understand that you have control over your own life, and you can find happiness and fulfillment in your own way.

I can understand the difficulties you are facing because you have a narcissistic mother. You mentioned that since you started college, you gradually developed your own thinking, understanding yourself, and discovering yourself, and you wanted to gradually break free from her control. However, she often uses hurtful words to accuse me of not being obedient, which she claims has made her suffer a lot in recent years. She mocks that I look down on her because of my education. I want to see her, care for her, and let her live a good life, but I am also afraid to be with her. Her sense of sacrifice is too strong, she turns everyone else's kindness into her weapon, calculating how much she has done for me, how much she has done for my father, and then using it as evidence that we are ungrateful and heartless. No matter how hard I try, she can always find something to be dissatisfied with in good times, never being satisfied and never being able to have a peaceful life. It is understandable that your mother is "narcissistic." Narcissism, as the name suggests, is self-love. Narcissism is one of the basic characteristics of human nature, and almost everyone has some narcissistic traits. However, these traits have a degree: if there is only a little narcissism, it is normal; if there are a particularly large number of narcissistic traits, then it is pathological. It is the influence of your mother's pathological narcissism that has affected you. Because your mother is narcissistic, she only cares about herself and never considers your feelings. She is more concerned about herself and has no empathy for her own daughter. She has never appreciated your efforts. That's how narcissistic mothers are, always picking out flaws and criticizing others. She only sees the shortcomings in her daughter and constantly criticizes them. Even if her daughter makes the smallest mistake, she will point it out and criticize it. Because of her narcissism, she wants her daughter to live in a way she likes, so she controls everything about her daughter and leaves her with no sense of self. Because of her narcissism, the other members of the family have to revolve around her (the mother) and completely ignore the daughter, which makes the daughter unable to feel the love of the family. So what should you do? Faced with these injuries, there is no other way but to first, accept them. Accept the harm caused by a narcissistic mother. This may make you feel unwilling or find it difficult to accept. But there is no other way, you can only accept it yourself, accept that your mother is not like most mothers who have love and care for their children, but rather a narcissistic mother. Because you cannot change others, you can only change yourself. Give up the hope that your mother will change and set yourself free. After all, you have your own life and should not be bound by the previous generation. After accepting it, you can try to release your emotions, release all the unhappiness you have experienced with your mother, and then break free from her influence and be your true self. Finally, you can choose to seek help from a professional psychologist.

Your mother has chosen a life of complaints and suffering, and as an observer, you can see clearly and genuinely want to help her, but often feel powerless. This is the situation in many families. I have become increasingly pessimistic about people's ability to change; you can never wake up someone who pretends to be asleep. However, I also have my optimistic side. I believe that there are also many people who have a sudden awakening. You love your mother, and in material terms, you can repay her. But when it comes to her mental well-being, what can you do if she refuses to listen? My suggestion is that when she complains and talks about her sacrifices, you can try to comfort her and patiently listen the first few times, but later, you can change the topic. Is this a form of emotional abuse? I don't think so. Why should everyone let her dwell in a "victim mentality"? Maybe it would be better if there were no audience. I recently stayed at my grandmother's house for two months. She constantly complains and blames others for many trivial matters. I used to try to console her. However, I found that it was ineffective and only made things worse. Proximity breeds contempt, it's really like that. In the same space, everyone's flaws are magnified. When she claims she has always been giving, it proves that she has never truly loved you. I read this in a book. When I look at the older generation around me, those who truly have love in their hearts never talk about how much they have sacrificed for others. Of course, I can't do it either. But I know that those who have a heavy sense of sacrifice are not genuinely expressing love. Because true love is willing to give and is filled with joy. To understand your mother's issues, you can find the answers by looking at her own family background. Who is really making her constantly give and feel obligated to give?

question: I just did something really stupid and feel embarrassed. What should I do?
description: I thought the guests outside had left, so I started singing with my headphones on. I feel so embarrassed. What should I do, what should I do?

answers.answer_text: If I were a guest, I would think you are very adorable because that is your truest side. Sometimes, expressing your true self occasionally will not cause others to feel disgusted; instead, they will perceive you as genuine and it will be easier to establish trust. Also, don't think too highly of yourself. Sometimes, the embarrassment you feel may only exist in the moment for others, and they probably won't even remember it later. Your emotions are just a result of overthinking, and even the embarrassment is only in your own perception.

question: My mom insists on buying expensive things for me to apply on the scar, what should I do?
description: Because I have a scar on my face from an injury, my mom doesn't want me to disfigure myself. After hearing what others said, she wants to buy me expensive products to apply on it, but I feel like they might not be effective. So I'm really conflicted, what should I do?
keywords: Family, family relationships, parental communication, family control.

answers.answer_text: Hello, from your description, I can see that both you and your mother are people who prioritize others over themselves. At the same time, I guess that both of you have an attitude of wanting to solve problems as best as possible when faced with them. In your mother's eyes, the more expensive the medication, the better the effect, and it also reflects her willingness to contribute more for your sake. In her eyes, you are definitely more important and valuable than money, and I believe that you must have your own thoughts and feelings about this issue as well. Have a good conversation with your mother, express your gratitude for her concern and love for you, and also share your true thoughts. The above are just my personal opinions, for reference only. Take care of yourself.

You are a happy daughter, and mom loves you very much! Mom hopes to help you remove the scars on your face, no matter how much it costs. It shows that mom loves you very much. Mom's idea is not wrong either. You are worried that it might not work. You can learn about the effectiveness of this ointment. After all, you haven't tried it before. Wouldn't it be better if it works? If it doesn't work, you can think of other ways to fulfill mom's wish and make yourself more beautiful. Are you hesitant and conflicted because you're afraid of spending money without results? You are also a sensible daughter. Actually, if the economic conditions allow, it is possible to find a way to restore the scars on a girl's face.

question: Should the visitor be more paranoid, should the consultation continue?
description: I consulted with this visitor for about two months. From initially understanding the situation to gradually delving deeper, both parties now accept and trust each other to some extent. However, while the visitor acknowledges the need for action and improvement, they are unwilling to truly take practical steps. Recently, I noticed that they have become somewhat paranoid, and their emotions fluctuate greatly (crying one moment, sighing the next, and laughing afterwards). Should I continue this consultation? There are certain issues with self-esteem and cognitive patterns. The visitor had previously undergone several years of counseling with another therapist, which ended in disappointment (they may have misunderstood many interpretations from their parents and the therapist; they can comprehend the words but not process them).

answers.answer_text: Thank you very much for the invitation, OP! Sending you a hug! It seems that the issues this visitor is dealing with have caused some difficulties for you, causing you to lose your direction and not knowing what to do. In previous counseling cases, I have encountered a similar situation. The visitor had been to counseling with me many times before, but her emotional changes were still apparent. At that time, I suggested that she try accepting her fear, but she was unwilling to do so. Or perhaps, I didn't realize that she didn't have enough inner strength to accept and face her emotions. That's why she released those emotions to me; it was her inner need. Later, she told me that she really hoped I could tell her that I am here with her and love her. At that time, I didn't ask her why she said that; I just said those words to her as she requested. Her response was to thank me for understanding and accepting her. In other words, when she still had noticeable emotions, I didn't provide enough understanding, acceptance, and support. She needed more attention, understanding, acceptance, and love. The situation with this visitor is quite similar. His emotional fluctuations and low self-esteem can be seen as a rejection and lack of acceptance of himself. Or it can be said that he lacks enough inner strength to support accepting and understanding his shortcomings. This also indicates that the depth of your attention, understanding, acceptance, and recognition is insufficient. The fact that he has already had many counseling sessions with you shows that he trusts you a lot. This is rare. If you were to end the counseling relationship like this and ask him to find another counselor, it would be a setback and hurt his psyche, affecting the progress and effectiveness of future counseling. However, if you want to continue counseling, you need to first adjust your own psychological state, put yourself in the counselor's position, maintain a relatively neutral stance and attitude, and express some of your own feelings and thoughts to the visitor, such as your confusion about his fluctuating emotions. Listen to what he says. This can release his inner pressure and make him feel that he is being attentively understood, accepted, and recognized by the counselor, making him feel safe. This can gradually encourage his personal growth and inner strength, enabling him to slowly accept and face the issues he has. He often misunderstands the counselor's words, which, aside from his own lack of understanding, have a lot to do with how the counselor expresses themselves. Inner self-esteem and lack of security are like those of an underage child. Talking to him using adult reasoning naturally won't make him understand. We can use language that is clearer and easier to understand, like how we speak to a child, without requiring deep thinking, making it easier for him to understand. This way, the pressure on him will be smaller, and he will feel more relaxed and at ease. OP, you can think about which moments during the counseling process with this visitor were more appropriate, providing sufficient understanding, acceptance, and recognition, and which moments were not. Think about when the visitor's emotional fluctuations occurred. Then, make some adjustments, change your attitudes and approaches toward the visitor, and see how it goes.

The description of the visitor in this paragraph is filled with judgment, which feels inappropriate. The reason why the visitor is seeking counseling is because they have their own issues - they may be paranoid, experience significant mood swings, have problems with self-esteem and cognitive patterns, and misinterpretations, otherwise they wouldn't seek counseling. Additionally, "ending in disappointment," who is the subject of the disappointment? Is the visitor paying for counseling to satisfy the counselor's narcissistic needs, saying, "You need to change, otherwise I'll be disappointed"? This kind of counseling is misplaced, and may not even have therapeutic effects for the visitor; it may just be compulsive repetition. Counseling should be centered around the visitor, regardless of the approach. We can only go along with the visitor's current feelings and follow their stages. Even if there is no change for decades, it may still be beneficial for them, as they have someone to accompany them during this difficult time, which they may not be able to find in their reality. To provide good counseling, supervision and personal analysis are necessary, otherwise we may mislead others and ourselves. Good luck!

question: 32-year-old woman, particularly afraid of appearing in crowded places, how to build self-confidence?
description: 32, female. Always lacks self-confidence and is particularly afraid of being in crowded places. Also dislikes talking to strangers. Feels like she doesn't have any strengths. How can she build self-confidence?

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP, hugs to you. I can totally relate. Your situation is somewhat similar to how I used to be, and it's a common issue among many girls. Your concerns and situations are as follows: 1. Feeling extremely anxious about appearing in crowded places. Try to exercise more and desensitize yourself mentally. 2. Not liking to talk to strangers. That's okay, no need to change that. 3. Feeling like you don't have any strengths. Discover your talents, unearth your potential, and find your own value. Build a foundation of confidence for yourself. This may be related to your childhood experiences or to your parents' traditional methods and attitudes of education. For example, traditional education methods, based on traditional concepts of "modesty as a virtue" and "reserved and not showy" ways, often practice a punitive approach in educating children, frequently using the "stimulation method". Under the influence of these traditional virtues, when parents have high expectations for their children but the children fail to meet these expectations, parents may be inclined to criticize and strike rather than praise and encourage. Many children may have never heard a positive and affirming word or evaluation. And so, slowly, these children are unconsciously hypnotized, gradually accepting their statements, and becoming extremely self-deprecating, looking down on themselves. This is a mental issue. There are also behavioral issues like everything being overly arranged, being puppeteered, so they are unable to experience the sense of achievement of accomplishing things, and feel worthless. Here are some solutions I have summarized: Work on inner self-development, give yourself more positive encouragement, practice mindfulness meditation, rebuild your confidence, and strengthen your inner self. Cultivate the "courage to be disliked", not caring about others' opinions, not comparing or contrasting, only comparing yourself to your past self, feeling comfortable with yourself is enough. If you don't know how to do makeup, just take care of your body, having a good complexion without makeup is just as attractive. If you can't achieve it at the moment, makeup is the quickest way to enhance your appearance. Exercise, dance, improve your body posture, get in shape, and you'll be much more attractive than having a pretty face alone! If all else fails, work on your inner self, have a mind filled with poetry and books, and radiate an aura on your own.

question: In my eyes, family members always have flaws. How can I change my perfectionism?
description: It's probably influenced by my upbringing. I have a severe tendency towards perfectionism. In my eyes, my wife and son always have flaws and are not as excellent as others. I also have an avoidant personality and rarely have confidence in myself. I feel down and constantly find everything unsatisfactory: financially inferior to colleagues, not doing as well as classmates, and my son not being as outstanding as others. How can I change this mindset?
keywords: Growth, personality development, character traits, self-improvement.

answers.answer_text: Hello! I saw your question and I hope I can offer you some warmth. There are many reasons that may have caused the issues you mentioned, it could be due to your own original family or it could have developed later on. But it's really great that you dare to face your problems and try to change yourself! Here are some suggestions: 1. When facing such problems, it might be because you care too much about others' opinions and overlook your own thoughts and your family's. So, you can choose to shift your attention back to yourself and your family, and you may unexpectedly discover many things you hadn't noticed before, and gain joy and happiness. Often, we care too much about others' opinions and neglect what is truly important. So, you might want to try concentrating on your own family. Every family is different, no one is perfect, and when you can't do something, don't force it. This way, you can experience more happiness. 2. If the confusion stems from your original family, then you need to change yourself. Issues brought by the original family are often not easy to solve and difficult to truly change, as they can affect your daily habits, personality, etc. In this case, you can try to help yourself overcome this confusion within your current family. You can involve yourself more in your family, try to spend more time and care for them, while also being mindful not to push yourself or your children and family too hard. Have confidence and love for your own family, rather than focusing on the external world. Try to live like everyone else, and as much as possible, avoid falling into the mindset of perfectionism. Lastly, I hope you can overcome your confusion and wish you a happy family! Best wishes!

Give the OP a hug! I can feel the OP's inner repression, loneliness, anxiety, and fear, as well as the lack of self-confidence. It's difficult for the OP to understand and accept themselves fully and it's also challenging to develop enough trust in others outside of themselves. It's hard to understand and accept others, even their own family members, just like how the OP sees their wife and son, thinking they have many flaws and are not as good as others. These circumstances are usually closely related to the environment in which they grew up, especially the relationship with their parents. The OP mentioned having an avoidant attachment style, which indicates a lack of intimate interaction and emotional communication with their parents. Facing intimate relationships, they lack a sense of security, and as a result, instinctively avoid understanding and accepting intimate relationships. This is a subconscious way of protecting oneself. The OP can try to change their perfectionism by first accepting and acknowledging their desire for perfection. Then they can explore the underlying reasons behind these thoughts and what they are expressing. What do they long for and what do these thoughts bring to them? Accepting these thoughts doesn't mean they have to act on them. The existence of "perfection" is relative. Without comparison, there is no absolute perfection or a fixed definition of a perfect goal. In other words, while accepting their pursuit of perfectionism, the OP can also accept their own shortcomings and self-denial. They don't have to fight against these thoughts, but rather allow them to exist in an unseen form, not "driving them away," and give them some freedom. They can also feel the acceptance and recognition that comes with it. Accepting these thoughts doesn't mean they have to do everything exactly as these thoughts dictate. They can do the things they want and are able to do, but also consider whether it's appropriate and the potential impact of doing them at that moment. If they can do it, they can, and if they can't, they can do it at the right time. For example, if someone is in a meeting and suddenly remembers that they haven't finished a document, and feels anxious and eager to do it, they shouldn't act on that thought at that moment. Instead, they should delay doing it until after the meeting. This way, they can satisfy their own needs and reduce their own stress. The desire for perfectionism is a subconscious need of oneself and accepting these thoughts is equivalent to accepting the true self, making the "size" of oneself larger, and enhancing one's strength. By meeting the needs of the self, they can easily and naturally feel the power of the self and face family relationships and life without these current troubles.

Hello, OP: I have observed that OP's perfectionism is causing distress, but I also noticed OP's bravery in expressing their concerns and seeking help from others. This undoubtedly helps OP to see themselves at a deeper level and better understand their relationships. I have observed that OP has their own awareness of the reasons for their perfectionism, which undoubtedly helps them to see their needs at a deeper level. Now I will share my observations, which may help OP have a more enriched perspective on possible issues. 1. How we treat ourselves is how we treat others. I have observed that OP often focuses on the faults of their wife and son, and rarely has confidence in themselves. They constantly feel dissatisfied and feel inferior in various aspects, such as economically, compared to colleagues or classmates, or feeling that their son is not as outstanding as others. From this description, what can be observed is that OP seems to be more prone to see their own flaws and those of their family members. This is because how we treat ourselves is how we treat others. If we are more prone to seeing our own flaws, we are also more likely to see the flaws in others. If we cannot accept the part of ourselves that is not good enough, we cannot accept the part of others that is not good enough either. Therefore, if OP wants to make adjustments, they need to redirect their energy back to themselves, first deal with their own relationship with themselves, live their own life well, and then work on improving relationships. 2. Accepting the real self, acceptance is the beginning of change. Our suffering comes from wanting our ideal self and not wanting our real self. The more we resist and suppress our real selves, the more we suffer. So, learn to accept the real self, accept the complete self. Wholeness is better than perfection. How do we accept? Accept the part of ourselves that cannot be changed and focus more energy on the parts we can adjust. Instead of exhausting energy on the aspects that cannot be changed. Only by accepting our imperfect selves can we have the possibility to accept the imperfections of our family members. Imagine a person who cannot even accept their own flaws, how can they have the ability to accept the flaws of others? 3. Reinterpreting our original family OP, as a perfectionist, probably experienced conditional positive attention in their original family. They had to achieve something before their parents or caregivers would give them something. This conditional positive attention suppresses the part of ourselves that we believe is not accepted, and we express the part that is accepted in order to gain recognition. However, this slowly distances us from our true selves and makes it harder for us to accept the part of ourselves that is not good. So now, as we grow up and look back, we realize that such relationship patterns were just survival skills from our childhood. Now that we are grown up and have the ability and resources to reexamine and reinterpret our experiences, we can ask ourselves if they still serve us. By doing so, we can break free from our original family. There is no perfect original family, but we can have a better version of ourselves. Our original family has an influence on us, but when we become aware of its impact and make an effort to reinterpret it, we can be reborn.

Hello, the original poster! After reading your description, I have a certain understanding of the questions you want to ask, so here's a virtual hug in four-dimensional space. From your description, I can understand that you have been influenced to some extent by your family upbringing, which may be due to your parents' strict expectations for you to strive for perfection in everything. It is not wrong to pursue perfectionism in life and work, but excessive pursuit of perfectionism can cause you a lot of distress. For example, you may always focus on the shortcomings of the people around you and even magnify their flaws. Although they may also have many strengths, your excessive pursuit of perfectionism may lead you to overlook these strengths and feel that they are not enough to offset the weaknesses. As a result, you may become overly critical of the people around you, which is not conducive to a harmonious family atmosphere. Additionally, you mentioned that you have an avoidant personality and lack self-confidence. I think most of the problems you are currently facing stem from your family upbringing. Growing up in a less than ideal family environment naturally leads to a lot of adverse effects on oneself. However, these influences don't have the final say, only we do. If we can make efforts to change some of the negative effects, that would be great. For those influences that we can't change, we can allow them to coexist with us in order to reduce their impact on us. From the latter part of your description, I can see that you like to compare yourself with others, but you haven't mastered the proper extent. As a result, the outcome is predictable – you will increasingly look down on yourself and become more and more lacking in confidence. Comparing ourselves with others is actually quite normal, but we must control the degree of comparison. If it becomes excessive, it can have a significant impact on our mental and emotional well-being. Moreover, when we compare ourselves with others, we must face our own strengths and weaknesses and not compare our weaknesses to others' strengths. It must be a comparison within the same category, only then can it inspire us to have a positive mindset. In fact, those who appear to be doing better than us have also worked hard for a long time and faced countless hardships. As outsiders, we only see their success and rarely see their efforts. Finally, I have summarized some methods to help you ease your current situation. (1) Try to discover the strengths and shining points of your family members. For their weaknesses, learn to be tolerant, after all, there is no such thing as a perfect person in this world, only people who will get better and better. (2) If you cannot achieve perfection in your endeavors, then strive to improve them to the best of your ability. At the same time, don't put too much pressure on yourself and learn to accept everything as it is. (3) Comparisons can be used for good; however, comparison should be done in moderation and can drive us to develop in a better direction. (4) Learn to shift your focus and engage in activities that interest you or read books for healing. (5) When you are under significant stress, learn to release this pressure through aerobic exercise or engaging in a sports activity. (6) You can confide in the people around you, share the things that have been bothering you, and release your emotions. The world loves you, and I wish you all the best.

Hello, I understand your feelings. The root of your problem lies in extreme lack of self-confidence. "It might be influenced by your upbringing, as I have a serious tendency toward perfectionism." Your upbringing placed a high demand for perfection on you, and your parents constantly criticized and educated you for any slight imperfections. This upbringing that demanded perfection has shaped you and caused you to develop an extremely insecure mindset and personality. In order to avoid any imperfections, you have gradually developed an avoidant personality, fearing being looked down upon or ridiculed by others. "In my eyes, my wife and son always have flaws, they are not as outstanding as others," "I always feel dissatisfied with various things: my finances are worse than my colleagues, I haven't achieved as well as my classmates, my son is not as outstanding as others." In a sense, it is because of your lack of self-confidence that you have created this phenomenon of yearning for what others have. Many people have such a mindset, longing for happiness that they perceive from others, while neglecting to find their own "happiness". It is like what Mr. Money said in the novel "Fortress Besieged", "the people inside the fortress want to go out, while the people outside the fortress want to go in." Think about the wife and child you have walked with. It is precisely because they tolerate your flaws that you can be happily together. Why can't you focus more on their strengths and good qualities? Why can't you sincerely praise your wife and child? Instead of complaining and feeling melancholic, it is better to cultivate and strengthen your self-confidence, take care of your family, and strive for a better life. This is the most meaningful thing. When you have confidence and feel the joy of striving for life, you will discover that everything in the world is so beautiful!

Hello, due to the influence of my original family, I have a serious tendency towards perfectionism. Now, perhaps through learning or reading books, I have deepened my understanding of myself and realized that my personality has been influenced by my original family, and this personality also affects my wife and son. I want to break this cycle. The original family - myself - wife, son. I am the mediator who forms the influence, so how can I change myself? From your description, I noticed the words you used to describe yourself, such as "economically worse than colleagues, not doing as well as classmates, son not as outstanding as others." These words that came out through comparison are quite negative. But are they true? Economically worse than colleagues: Have you compared with the entire company? Or with which colleague? Not doing as well as classmates: What does it mean to do well? Higher income? A higher job title? Son not as outstanding as others: How do you define outstanding? Is it academic performance or character? Through these questions, I believe you will have some reflection. We often get stuck in dead ends because we only see one road ahead, but if we look up and look around, we will find that there is not just one road, but there are roads on the left, the right, and even behind us. I hope this answer is helpful to you! Karen.

Hello~ The perfectionist tendencies towards others are an unrealistic idealization and expectation that others should be perfect, that they should do things according to one's own desires. On the other hand, the perfectionist tendencies towards oneself are driven by a desire to experience the feeling of failure, so one sets higher and higher standards for oneself, or is extremely afraid of being seen as incompetent and feeling inferior. Perfectionism is always related to cognitive issues. So perfectionists think like this: If I perform well and have strong abilities, then I like myself; If I don't perform well, it means I lack abilities, so I feel terrible about myself - performance becomes a measure of your abilities and worth. It is important to deeply understand that abilities can be developed. Through hard work, we can become smarter and better over time. Effort allows us to excel in something. And we don't have to excel immediately because we need effort, practice, and time to broaden ourselves and become skilled in unfamiliar fields. Even though failure can bring a sense of frustration, it does not determine a person's worth. Instead, it is a reason to work even harder instead of making you retreat, procrastinate, or give up. The focus should not be on performance, but on what you have learned, what excites and motivates you, and what you have changed and improved. Results are just a backdrop, while change and improvement are the core. So once your thoughts start to spiral endlessly and imagine the terrifying consequences of failure, at this point, as soon as you become aware of this emotion, immediately stop and tell yourself that it is perfectionism playing tricks on you, that the consequences of failure are just exaggerated. Also, take a look at how you define failure, is it a failure just because your income is not as high as your coworkers? Let me share a quote - "In the midnight hour, memories flood in, both beautiful and painful: the suffering, mistakes, unfinished business, and various things that make you feel ashamed and sad. However, everything, good or bad, pain or joy, is painted into the rich tapestry of life, becoming the nourishment of my thoughts and the driving force of my progress." Best wishes~

Hello there. I can understand the feeling of being very tired and exhausted. Perfectionists strive to do everything smoothly from start to finish, and any setbacks or shortcomings in the process can make them feel frustrated and inadequate. The topic you mentioned, which has also been of interest to me for a long time, is: what should one do if they discover that they are a perfectionist? Here are some of my own thoughts and suggestions on this: Firstly, recognize the root cause of your perfectionism. You are right, perfectionism may indeed be related to one's upbringing and, essentially, a lack of security. If you had strict parents who did not allow you to make mistakes, it is likely that you will not allow yourself to make mistakes as you grow up. Manage your expectations well. As a perfectionist, you may have an ideal image in your mind that you want to become, but even a small mistake can shatter that illusion for yourself. You may believe that you have to achieve a score of 100 to be excellent, but someone who can achieve a score of 80 is already very outstanding. Perfectionists often, when achieving 80 points, will think, "Oh why am I not perfect? I am indeed a terrible person." I just want to say, allow yourself to make mistakes, accept yourself making mistakes, and always remember that there is still 20 points of room to deduct. Only compare yourself to your past self. Ernest Hemingway (maybe it was Hemingway) once said, "Excellence is not about comparing yourself to others. True excellence means being better than your past self." As long as you make a little more progress compared to your previous self, I think you are an amazing person. When you compare yourself to others, objectively speaking, you will find that you have strengths and weaknesses compared to others, but your focus is only on the areas where you fall short, so why not let go of the obsession to be superior in every aspect and accept your own imperfections?

Hello! I sense that you want to change your mood~ In your eyes, both yourself and your wife and son always have shortcomings and are not as outstanding as others, which makes you feel unhappy. In this lifetime, we will eventually accept our mediocrity. We are all unknown, born in this world. The majority of people try their best, but in the end, can only have an ordinary life. Ordinary people cannot be perfect. We need to learn not to be enemies with our own mediocrity. Sometimes, we are unable to live a good life not because there are millions of people blocking our way, but because we are constantly fighting against our own mediocrity. Zhou Guoping once said, "Everything extraordinary in this world will eventually return to being ordinary, and its value should be measured by living an ordinary life. Greatness, brilliance, and success mean nothing. Only by truly living an ordinary life can one have a fulfilling life." You should try to accept your own and your family's mediocrity, and enjoy the ordinary. Perhaps life is not as bad as you imagine. Best wishes!

It's just acceptance. The OP said it's influenced by the upbringing in the family. I have a serious tendency towards perfectionism. In my eyes, my wife and son always have shortcomings and are not as excellent as others. I also have an avoidant personality, and I rarely have confidence in myself. I am always melancholic and always feel dissatisfied with various things: I am economically worse off than my colleagues, not as successful as my classmates, and my son is not as excellent as others. How can I change this mindset? Loving someone means accepting their flaws. The OP should love his wife and son very much! Besides understanding how to love others, we also need to understand how to love ourselves. Only when one's heart is filled with love, can there be surplus love to give to others. Therefore, it is important for us to love ourselves, unconditionally accept ourselves, change our beliefs, and alleviate anxiety. Unconditional self-acceptance means we need to understand that the success or failure of our actions does not represent our personal success or failure. There is no connection between them.
