You said, "My grandfather cheated and abandoned my father and his three siblings when my father was young, so I am particularly sensitive." From this, it appears that your father also experienced "trauma"; he also lacked "fatherly love" from childhood to adulthood, and the "emotional box" deep within his heart has also been in a state of emptiness. He is also a person who needs to be "cared for"! His "special sensitivity" is also a long-term lack of love resulting in "irrational" behavior! So, on the surface, this seems like your personal problem, but if we trace it back, it is actually a problem within your entire "family system"! If you want to solve it, you need to undergo "family system therapy"! My personal suggestion is that now that you have economic resources, you can definitely find a good psychotherapist for one-on-one counseling! Start with "cognitive therapy," and try to change your "cognitive patterns" and the related "emotional" and "behavioral" patterns! Then, guide you to "shift your perspective" on your original family and try to "empathize" with your father and mother, experiencing their "struggles"! If possible, you can also involve your wife and parents in a "group counseling" program, combining individual counseling to undergo "family system therapy" and fundamentally solve your problem! Of course, these are purely personal suggestions. I hope they can help you. If there is anything incorrect, please feel free to criticize and correct me!

Hello! From your description, I can feel that you are a responsible husband who is able to be self-aware in a timely manner, which is highly commendable. But you are struggling with not being able to control your emotions, causing great distress to your family, colleagues, and yourself. I truly understand your feelings of losing control over things and emotions, which make you feel uneasy. You always want to be in control of something, but it seems like you are constantly in a state of losing control, manifested by irritability, anger, and frustration. This is a stress response to your inner unease, and you are truly going through a lot. Looking at your family background, we can find some underlying causes such as childhood experiences, feelings of abandonment, and tense parental relationships, which can create traumatic memories in our hearts, leading to a lack of security and fear of loss. Perhaps having a sense of control or a feeling of being in control is the best way for you to reduce this uneasiness. So, you have created many so-called "standards" in your mind, derived from your own feelings, time, space, and the reactions of others. In your subconscious, if you can control the development of everything and everyone around you, you will briefly experience relaxation. However, this is highly unrealistic. There will always be a child in your heart that refuses to grow up, that wounded child who was not well protected in childhood. It is reluctant to grow up, regardless of age. Trauma cannot be healed, but we can try to face it, accept ourselves, and seek professional psychological help when you are not yet "psychologically capable" of facing all of this. We can never rewrite past experiences or choose our biological families, but we can choose to change ourselves. You have tried, but with minimal results, believing that it is instinctual and out of your control. This is a beautiful "excuse" found in your subconscious for not wanting to change. Without letting go and accepting, there is no way to move forward lightly. Carrying the "trauma," you will continue to suffer. Every outburst of anger, every moment of frustration, is a form of harm to yourself and the people around you. Therefore, learning to love oneself and improving the ability to love oneself is the only way to love your family and your life. I hope my answer can be helpful to you. Take care!

Hello, OP: I understand your feelings very well. You have set standards for everything in your mind, and whenever these standards do not meet your expectations, you get angry. You feel that you cannot control your emotions, but you also deeply understand that every time you get angry, it not only damages your relationships but also hurts your loved ones. You want to change but cannot control yourself. So every time you get angry, you feel guilty towards your loved ones, and you also blame yourself more and more. This conflicting and regretful emotion must be very difficult for you. In fact, OP, you are very intelligent. You know that the current solution is to find the reason behind your anger and communicate your feelings with others. You need empathy and to think from other people's perspectives, while also trying to find this reason online. You try to overcome it, but there are still two problems that can't be solved. Don't worry, let's take a look at the issues you mentioned together. "As long as something similar happens, I get angry immediately, like instinct, I can't control it at all." (In fact, from the moment you feel your authority is challenged, subconsciously, you start to fear your own anger, so you are waiting for the appearance of this emotion. Your thoughts are focused on this, and as a result, even a tiny physiological reaction can cause your excessive attention. This creates a conditioned reflex of anger and becomes fixed.) "When I am treated unfairly, I usually have a big fight, but I don't want to talk." (OP, do you see the contradiction in your statement? This mainly reflects the fact that on one hand, you are deeply affected by emotional distress, but on the other hand, you believe that everything should be according to your standards. This cognitive contradiction causes you great pain when encountering problems. And only when you change your way of looking at problems can your inner emotional cognition achieve unity.) So, now that we have identified the causes of the problems, what should we do? 1. Change your cognition. In your text, OP, you mentioned the words "unfair treatment." You mentioned that you feel that you are not able to hold the things you take, and this feeling makes you experience unfairness. However, in your previous text, you mentioned that your wife walks ahead, and she also holds things, but it's easier for her. In fact, the other person is also holding things. It's easier because, in our daily cognition, we usually think that women have less strength. But is this really unfair? In thinking about problems, we often instinctively start from our own perspective. The fact that your wife has fewer things may be unfair, but when you demand others according to your own standards, is that another form of unfairness? Fairness is relative and there is no absolute fairness. Often, we feel that things are unfair because of our own perspective. When we demand others according to our own standards and we don't meet them, they may also feel that they are being treated unfairly. Putting yourself in others' shoes helps you see the truth of the problem. 2. Strengthen communication. Strengthening communication actually helps us to align our standards with others. Our own internal standard and the other person's internal standard are not the same. Just like some people think that thin girls are more attractive and some people think that curvy girls are more attractive. Your standard, OP, cannot represent the standard in the other person's heart. Strengthening communication does not mean you have to give up your dignity or compromise with others, but it means that through communication, we adjust the standards in our hearts towards a common direction. For example, in the matter of carrying things, you can tell your wife before picking up things that heavy things should be carried together so that no one will be so tired. I believe your wife loves you and will agree to your request. And many times, if you feel wronged but do not express it, how can the other person know? 3. Shift your attention and relax by doing things you are interested in: When you force yourself to think about your standards and feel that you are going to get angry, the most important thing is to find a way to shift your attention and quickly get out of the present symptoms, to get rid of the suffering. For example, when you are in an environment that easily provokes anger, start reading novels or listening to music that you are interested in. By focusing all your attention on the novel or music, you may forget about the things you often associate with. In addition, you can also improve your compulsive emotions through Morita therapy, etc. Building on the foundation of changing cognition, facing your emotions properly is the root solution. I hope this text can help you, OP. Take care.

Hi! Based on your description, I have two observations that I would like to share with you. The first is that you have a clear understanding of your own issues and your principles of right and wrong. You seem to have a clear cognition. The second is that you are trapped by your own personality, specifically your tendency to explode in anger as a way to solve certain problems. You are aware that this explosive behavior is not right, but you find it difficult to control. Is that correct? It is my personal judgment that you may have become addicted to these outbursts. Just like smoking or drinking, this addiction to explosive behavior allows you to address some issues, such as when your psychological needs are being ignored. Through these outbursts, the people around you become highly attentive to your needs, even though it may harm them. At the same time, your emotions find an outlet for release. The benefits of these outbursts may be the reason why it is difficult for you to let go of them. So even though you know you should change, you may experience withdrawal symptoms during the process of change and feel that your previous way of explosive behavior is more comfortable. The deeper reason behind these outbursts may be that your psychological needs often go unnoticed. This could be a result of your upbringing, where your psychological needs were often not supported by intimate relationships. Perhaps there were attempts at communication, but they were met with heartless rejection or suppression, leading you to unconsciously believe that reasonable expression of your feelings does not meet your expectations, while explosive behavior does. Over time, this has become a habit or an addiction. As it is evident that it is significantly impacting your family life, it becomes hard for you to quit. The key issue here is the fear of having your vulnerable needs suppressed or ignored. When you feel you are being treated unfairly, speaking out calmly may not seem impactful enough. You may worry about facing suppression or neglect from your surroundings, making you question if you are being overly sensitive and leading to self-doubt, almost as if exposing your wounds to others only to be hurt by their insensitivity. One possible solution is to seek understanding and support from your wife, who can provide comfort and support during key moments when you calmly voice your experiences of unfair treatment. This can help warm your fragile inner self and provide a sense of security. Feel free to message me for further consultation or clarification.

【Learning to truly grow up starts with self-satisfaction】【First of all】, as you mentioned, your current behavior is like that of a child. When a mother doesn't buy you a toy, you cry, stomp your feet, and insist on getting your own way. This is how children behave: "If you don't meet my needs, I'll make you suffer. I'll cause trouble, regardless of whether you like it or not. I will make you uncomfortable. When you're uncomfortable, you'll concede and buy me a toy." 【Secondly】 Why are you addicted to getting angry? Because it works. People generally fear others getting angry, especially since you are an adult man. Consequently, they give in and you achieve your goal. Through this experience, you will continue to respond in the same way in order to accomplish your objectives. Furthermore, because you haven't learned new, healthy ways to satisfy your needs, you will rely on old patterns. Unfortunately, everyone fears you and may have negative interactions with you. 【Thirdly】 "I can't manage without you." Your current behavior is actually a typical "dependent" pattern. People with this behavior pattern have a negative belief that "I can't manage without you." Your self-satisfaction comes from external sources, and self-love is lacking. Recognizing this, your current task is to learn to "self-satisfy." 【Fourthly】 Change your mindset: "I can also manage on my own." When you can't carry something in the supermarket and the other person doesn't understand you, you can find other tools to help, like a shopping cart or putting it on the ground, or ask someone else for help. If no one understands, you can understand yourself or find someone else to understand you. Maybe the characters in a TV drama will understand you. 【Fifthly】 Learn to separate boundaries and understand that others may or may not understand you; it's their business, and you can't interfere. Learn to understand yourself or find someone else to understand you, or find something that makes you feel understood. This is something you need to do on your own, and it has nothing to do with others. If someone understands you, that's good. If not, do your own thing. After all, you can manage on your own. Self-love is always accompanied by independence. Only a person who can love themselves can learn to love others. Best wishes to you, Namaste!

Hello: You made it very clear above, and we can work together to make an effort and hopefully help you. Everyone has their own personality, and theoretically, there is nothing wrong with that. But as you said, you are not alone now, you have a family, so you need to take care of their feelings. There is a clear compulsion here, you must feel the same way as yourself. I believe you are also very clear about this, but you can't handle it. This psychological state needs the involvement of professional psychological counseling. Analyzing and understanding the problem: 1. When your wife goes to the supermarket to buy things, you wait for her for longer than your psychological time, and you get angry because you have to hold uncomfortable things while she walks ahead (she also has things in her hands, but they are easier to hold). She doesn't put the things on the chair at the door and open it in advance for you to put the things down, and you explode instantly (so may I ask, did you tell your wife how long your psychological time is? If you didn't, how would she know that it exceeded your psychological time? Did she know that you were angry? Did she understand why you were angry? I want to confirm this: is it that she didn't put the things on the chair, but opened the door early and asked you to put them down, and then you exploded? If that's the case, I feel that in your mind, you think- since she wants to open the door, why does she still ask you to put the things down?), 2. You set standards for everything in your mind, and you get angry if it doesn't meet this standard or if what you expect doesn't happen, no matter who it is. You have looked it up online, and this is a sign of a younger psychological age (even though you are already 30 years old), being overly centered on oneself, and having a need for control and a lack of satisfaction. The solution is to find the root cause behind your anger and communicate your feelings to others. There must be empathy and considering things from others' perspectives (you searched this online, which is correct, but these are just the first steps, the next steps are: how to find the root cause, how to communicate with others, how to express empathy, and how to see things from others' perspectives, etc. These require professional guidance and learning), 3. You are willing to try some of these methods, but there are two things that you feel you cannot overcome: a. Every time you encounter a similar situation, you immediately get angry, as if it is instinctual, and you cannot control it at all (that "instinct" you mentioned is a kind of inertia, it is also a habit. Generally, it is a habitual thinking pattern, such as muscle mode, thinking mode, etc. This needs to start with very obvious events and practice them one by one. Breaking them one by one will gradually change the habitual anger. To be honest, this takes time, and it will not necessarily have good results just by cooperating with a counselor's efforts), b. When you are treated unfairly (like what I mentioned above, if you can't hold the things you are carrying, and you don't want to speak up, if you didn't notice or do anything, you get angry), you usually have a big fight and don't want to talk about it (yes, this is also a habitual behavior caused by habitual thinking. We need to unravel the knot and even find out why you have such a strong feeling of being treated unfairly. Is it not something that just happened recently? And the previous event has been a knot in your heart that needs to be untied. This requires professional counseling. It's not something that can be done alone), 4. Why do you want to change: a. You don't want your wife and children to suffer, b. It will affect all aspects of your interactions with others, c. Your inner emotions are always affected (yes, I think you are unwilling to act and behave like this. Through your desire to change, I can see your determination to change. Now you just need specific methods and professional help. I think you can do it), Conclusion: I wish you happiness and joy! I wish your family harmony! If you have any detailed confusion, please feel free to private message me!

Hello! It's great that you can notice and have the willingness to actively adjust your potential issues. For most people, facing their problems can often be harder than correcting them, so I must commend you for that! The statement "I looked it up online, and it says it's a case of having a younger psychological age (despite being 30 years old), being excessively self-centered, and having a need for control with unsatisfied feelings of control" is actually quite vague. It's like using "immaturity" to label any problem a person can't handle. Coming to a certain conclusion is not difficult, but what's hard is providing the reasons behind the formation of this issue and suggesting a solution. This can be done through the "three steps": what it is, why it happens, and what to do. This situation can be explained and adjusted from the perspectives of psychology and cognitive neuroscience, where the relationship between the two is somewhat like software and hardware. From a psychological standpoint, this "anger" is more like a "psychological defense mechanism." Underneath this anger lies a sense of unease and even fear, meaning that your real emotions are not anger but rather fear and worry. Where do these emotions come from? What gives rise to them? These are what we truly need to address and handle. Cognitive-behavioral therapy can be highly effective in addressing and correcting irrational beliefs. Cognitive neuroscience, also known as brain neuroscience, published an article on the official website of China's Ministry of Science and Technology in 2007 titled "The Neurological Roots of Aggression and Violence." The article pointed out that individuals with high aggression have stronger activity in the amygdala, which is associated with fear, and weaker and slower activity in the prefrontal cortex, which is related to reasoning and decision-making. Therefore, exercising the prefrontal cortex can also have a positive impact on emotional issues. Research has shown that engaging in meditation practice for more than 8 weeks brings about noticeable changes in the left and right prefrontal cortex of the brain. I won't go into great detail about meditation practice, as there is already a dedicated section on the platform called "Meditation Planet" that provides detailed explanations, including some "breath-pressure reduction techniques" which show significant results with consistent practice. Of course, there are also more "direct and effective" methods, but they may also have certain negative side effects, such as aversion therapy and flooding therapy. These treatment options must be undertaken under the guidance of professionals and are not highly recommended. If your current situation is causing significant distress and has even started to affect your work, family, and social interactions, it may be worth considering seeking psychological counseling. Wishing you a happy life!

Hello! Actually, seeing your question, I felt relieved for you. Because you described it very clearly, it means that you have already spent some time and effort to analyze and summarize your own problems and the underlying causes. The kind of situation you described can indeed cause significant interpersonal relationship difficulties and discomfort. With your understanding of yourself, let's see what else we can do~ 【Turning your excessive attention to details into a great advantage】 "When my wife goes to the supermarket to buy things and I wait for her for longer than my psychological time, I get angry. I'm holding something that is not easy to hold, and my wife is walking ahead of me (she is also holding things, but they are easier to hold). She doesn't put the things on the chair at the door and open it in advance for me to put them down, and I explode instantly." From this passage, I seem to see what you look like when you get angry. You are probably very detail-oriented and have mentally rehearsed the upcoming life situations, hoping that the other person can pay attention to details like you do and do what you want. In psychology, there is a term that corresponds to this, called the "Golden Rule." It means treating others the way you want to be treated. Since you can consider these detailed moments of life, you can also provide good quality service in life, changing from "I demand" to "I can." This not only makes your loved one happy and relieves your discomfort but also allows you to realize that what you originally thought was a problem can be turned into an advantage, like being a meticulous butler in a five-star hotel. This process may be long or short. Considering the reasons you mentioned, those three points expose your loving and willing-to-give excellent qualities. So you can give it a try and make an effort. It's still the same question, turning around may reveal your great advantages. 【Conditioned reflex, going against the grain】 "Whenever I encounter similar things, I immediately get angry, like instinct. I can't control it at all." Behavior and physiology can be linked. When you encounter similar things, your body reacts physiologically first, and this physiological reaction triggers an emotional stress response. So let's start by adjusting the intermediate link. When the physiological reaction occurs, can we replace it with a different response? For example, humming a tune, smiling, or saying a self-suggestion phrase. By forming a set behavioral performance when similar things happen, it's like setting an alarm clock to signal us. The purpose of doing this is not to suppress emotions, because emotions cannot be completely smoothed out just by suppression. It is to give us more buffer time to think and adjust our coping strategies. I heard a story once. A mom used to get angry and curse a lot, which was embarrassing and worried for her sunny boy. So whenever he heard his mom being impolite to someone, he started singing. Of course, the result was very good. Mom was reminded by polite and thoughtful behavior and slowly changed herself, and the grown-up boy also had good singing skills. Since you have the intention to change, give yourself some more time and effort, and try cultivating a kind "signature move." 【Pay more attention to your inner child】 "When I feel treated unfairly (like the example above, I am holding something that is not easy to hold and it's slipping from my hands, but I just don't want to say anything. If you don't notice it or do something, I get angry). I usually have a big argument; I just don't want to say it." It sounds a bit exaggerated, but I understand you very well. Friends who have had similar psychological experiences will understand. It's not that we must have fairness, but because we want everyone and everything around us to develop perfectly. We hope things or environments are organized and taken seriously, and that everyone is well taken care of. Since everyone should think this way, why do I have to say it out loud, right? So when things don't happen as we expect, we become anxious and irritated. This kind of emotion shows that our inner child indeed feels neglected. So we need to take care of our inner child. We need to tell them that we should give others some time, and everyone's perspective and focus are different. If they notice it, it will definitely be done with love, and it will be done perfectly. When our inner child is calm, we will naturally feel comfortable. Actually, here, I want to say that speaking out our dissatisfaction and discomfort, just like you are now asking the question, can be very helpful in healing and improving ourselves. Because asking the question itself is a way of externalizing. In other words, as a teacher once said, we should learn to tell our own story. Dare to tell it to others, "I was a little angry just now. You didn't put the things on the chair, which I didn't expect, and it made me uncomfortable..."... Believe in yourself! If you have the original intention of asking this question, you will definitely gain a lot. In the process of cultivating and improving ourselves, it is also the process of accumulating energy and expressing love to ourselves. I suggest you try running or doing meditation, they may help you. The sky is blue, you are here, and life can be beautiful! The world and I love you!

Hello OP! After reading your description, I feel that you have a strong self-awareness. Let's take a look at your concerns together: "I have set standards for everything in my mind, and I get angry whenever something doesn't meet these standards or when things don't go as I expected, no matter who it is." You are demanding the whole world to meet your standards and not considering others as independent individuals. Each person is unique, with different abilities, growth processes, life experiences, etc. Because people are different, even when faced with the same situation, the outcomes will be different. Similarly, you also have high expectations for yourself, right? If your actions don't meet your own standards, you also tend to blame yourself, don't you? "I have looked it up online, and it indicates that this is a sign of having a young psychological age (even though I am already 30 years old), excessive self-centeredness, and a desire for control, an unsatisfied sense of control." What lies behind the need for control? It is fear, fear of losing control. It can also be said that deep down inside, you feel unable to confront the uncertainties in life, so you try to control everything. "The solution is to find the underlying reasons behind the anger and communicate your feelings to others. It is important to have empathy and consider situations from other people's perspectives. I am willing to try these methods. However, there are two things that I feel I cannot overcome: 1. Whenever I come across similar situations, I immediately get angry, as if it is instinctual and I cannot control it. 2. When I feel I am being treated unfairly (like in the example before, if I'm unable to hold onto something or if it's difficult to get, and the other person doesn't notice or do something about it, I get angry), I usually end up having a big argument because I don't want to say it." It is evident that you prioritize personal growth and continuously seek solutions. However, some methods are difficult to apply, and you end up exploding with anger. Now, let's look at the two points you mentioned. When things don't meet your expectations, you immediately get frustrated. There is a need in your heart that you don't express, and you expect others to perceive it and guess your needs. If they guess correctly, then it's fine. If not, you end up having a big argument. When you read this, what image comes to mind? OP, I believe you already have a child, right? When a baby has a need, they use crying to communicate with adults. They are unable to specifically explain what their need is, and adults have to guess whether they are hungry or need a diaper change. If the adult doesn't meet their needs in a timely manner, the baby will cry even louder. In our eyes, they are crying, but in reality, the baby is expressing their anger. In psychology, there is a term called "regression," which means that when adults face setbacks and feel powerless, they may regress to a younger stage and use coping mechanisms from that time to deal with the setback. Of course, there is another reason for the anger, which is "narcissism," believing that you are omnipotent and the center of the universe. In the infant stage, infants exhibit narcissistic traits because whenever they cry, the bottle is handed to them, and their diaper is changed. In short, whenever they make a sound, they are immediately satisfied. Therefore, they assume they are the center of the universe and can do anything. Lastly, I will share some self-improvement methods: 1. Try to understand and accept the differences between yourself and others, instead of assuming the other person is wrong and blaming them when they don't meet your expectations. When someone behaves differently from your expectations, try to understand their thoughts at that moment (because thoughts determine behavior). Through practice, you will not only become more understanding and considerate of others but also gain new experiences in your world. When you realize that you are about to explode in anger, you can try saying to yourself, "I am very angry, I want to explode, and I am behaving like an infant." (This method has personally worked for me.) 2. Learn to express your emotions and needs. The intimacy in a relationship depends mainly on sharing and accepting emotional experiences. I recommend the book "Nonviolent Communication." 3. Self-acceptance. When a person is dissatisfied and blames others for many things, it also signifies their dissatisfaction with themselves. It's good to have expectations for oneself, but it's important to allow oneself to make mistakes and accept that others can also make mistakes. Best wishes, FF.

Give the OP a hug! One can feel the OP's internal suppression, anger, and conflicts. They have thoughts that they keep to themselves, and when things don't go as expected, they get angry. Others don't know what's going on, so not only do the people around the OP feel uncomfortable and confused, but the OP themselves also feel worse. As an adult, expressing oneself with the attitude and approach of a minor makes it difficult for others to understand, accept, and recognize. This can bring unnecessary trouble and impact on one's normal social and family life. In the mentioned incidents, when the wife's behavior doesn't align with the OP's expectations, the OP becomes angry. Just like the OP said, they have a "standard" in their heart for everything. The OP uses their own "standard" to measure others' words and actions, expecting others to do things according to their "standard". If others don't, the OP gets angry. On the other hand, if others do things in a certain way, the OP doesn't get angry. This can be seen as others understanding, accepting, and approving the OP's internal "standard", satisfying the OP's ego. However, for others, these "standards" are the OP's own and not their own. The OP's demand for others to do things according to their own "standard" can be seen as attempting to control others according to the OP's thoughts, which prevents others from doing things according to their own ideas. It also makes it difficult for others to feel their own existence and worth, while also having to bear the pressure of meeting the OP's expectations. They also cannot obtain others' understanding, acceptance, and support for the OP's "standards" and thoughts. The OP keeps these "standards" hidden in their heart, and others can't see or hear them. Therefore, others naturally don't know what the OP is thinking, why they are angry, or they just feel inexplicably depressed. The external events are just stimuli, but what they trigger is the deep emotions in the OP's heart. The OP's reaction to things clearly exceeds the stimulus brought by the events themselves, indicating that the OP's heart has accumulated a lot of emotional stimuli and suppressed a lot of emotional feelings. It is these emotional stimuli that have had a significant impact on the OP's psyche. The OP's desire to control others to think and act according to their own thoughts can also be seen as an emotional projection from their heart, a denial and non-acceptance of oneself. They yearn to feel the existence and worth of themselves by controlling others, in order to satisfy the needs within. To resolve this situation, the OP can consider making an appointment with a suitable counselor to release their internal emotions. While communicating and sharing with others can release some emotions, it cannot repair the internal wounds. Even if some emotions are released, the wounds still remain and will generate emotional stress. Only by releasing emotions and repairing the wounds can the problem that troubles the OP be truly solved. Once the problem is resolved, the OP no longer needs to project their internal expectations onto others, and they won't easily get angry and hurt their family.

question: Not too much dislike for studying, but fears school and teachers, cry every time going to school.
description: I have been to many schools, but the current one seems to make me hate it even more. I'm scared of teachers pushing me to do homework, afraid of going to class, and at home I absolutely don't want to do any assignments. I just want to avoid my classmates after school, but at school, I present myself as humorous and enjoy being with everyone. Because of studying, I even feel like dying, but I feel a little better when I go to the tutoring class that I voluntarily enrolled in. However, deep down, I still think I have depression. It might sound sudden, but that's how it is.

answers.answer_text: Seeing you express your true feelings so honestly, I applaud your courage. Changing schools multiple times and having to adapt to different class groups, different teachers, and different environments in a short period of time is a process that requires adaptability for a student. Building relationships with others requires mutual understanding and familiarity, but it takes time. Frequent school changes may disrupt the relationships you have just begun to establish with teachers, classmates, and the environment, as well as the teaching methods you have just become familiar with. Facing uncertainty, each of us feels worried and afraid when encountering a new environment and unfamiliar people. This feeling of not being in control puts you in an unstable state. On the other hand, you also have expectations. You want to present a positive image to others and care about how others perceive you. You are very humorous, and humor is extremely valuable in interpersonal interactions. Congratulations on possessing such a quality! This is a powerful resource within you, and I invite you to fully utilize its value, to experience the joy that humor brings to yourself and to your classmates, and it will also bring you positive interpersonal interactions. When you mentioned not wanting to do homework and not wanting to be pressured to do homework by teachers, I can truly understand you. The pressure on students nowadays is really huge. There is a lot of content to study, and every subject has homework, as well as many extracurricular assignments that are not required by the school, perhaps even from detestable cram schools. The most painful thing is that these cram schools are not voluntary. The pressure from school, the pressure from the new environment, the pressure from teachers, and the pressure from parents all feel like towering mountains overwhelming us, truly making it difficult for us to bear. I am glad that you have extracurricular classes that you enjoy and voluntarily enrolled in. There, you feel that learning is not so boring, and there, you have control over your own learning. This is something you genuinely desire! This is very important. Because there, you can find respite, and there, you can find enjoyment. Perhaps there are teachers you like, classmates you like, and subjects you like. I invite you to spend more time with the classmates, teachers, and subjects you like, trying to interact more with them, and communicate your frustrations to them. Another very important thing is to communicate with your parents and express your true feelings. I invite you to have your parents take you to a psychologist or counselor who can help you. Each of us may experience a dark period, and when we are moving forward in the darkness, we might feel lonely, and we might feel helpless. What we can do is to once again place our hope in something. Will a beam of light shine in? When the light shines in, the darkness will gradually fade. After the night is dawn, and in this world, many people silently support you, silently pay attention to you, and silently love you.

OP, hello~~~ First, give OP a hug. 1. Fear of being pressured by teachers to do homework and not wanting to do assigned schoolwork. 2. However, OP still enjoys being in school and with classmates. 3. OP feels better in tutoring classes and it helps alleviate some discomfort. [Analysis and Suggestions] 1. OP mentioned not wanting to be pressured to do homework and not wanting to do assigned work, but is not as averse to voluntarily attending tutoring classes. It can be seen that OP may not dislike studying itself, but rather dislikes being forced to do certain things or being urged to do certain things. Is it uncomfortable for OP when Mom at home rushes OP to do something? 2. From the later description, OP also knows that this is not good. As a student, being full of aversion towards school is not conducive to their own development. So, since OP feels comfortable voluntarily, take some time off and think about what OP wants. Reflect on what kind of work OP wants to do, what kind of preparation is needed, and change from "you must" given by others to "I need to for my future dreams." Perhaps OP's enthusiasm will improve.

question: Why is it that as I grow older, I become more and more repressed, irritable, and distrustful of people?
description: When I was 16 years old, I hated my parents, so I went to a big city to work and intern by myself. At that time, I didn't have any friends or relatives in the big city. I would sometimes cry in secret when I was bullied or had my achievements stolen at work. Sometimes, I couldn't hold back my tears and would cry openly on the busy streets. I actually talked to my colleagues about my feelings, but later I found out they were laughing about it behind my back and never spoke to me again. After that, I felt like there was no point in saying anything. Your troubles are just a joke to others, how could they possibly understand! The loneliness and helplessness of being alone, the office politics between colleagues, the pressure to perform well, the lack of understanding from others, the misunderstandings with my family - I felt like no one loved me. I slowly felt like an abandoned child. Every time I saw parents buying things and having fun with their children, I felt envious and sad. I just wanted to ask why I didn't have that. But I didn't know who to talk to! When I was diagnosed with depression, I had to tell myself that it was fake, that it wasn't real! Because I still had to live! In those two years, I would often have breakdowns until three or four in the morning. Gradually, I became sensitive, repressed, irritable, and stopped trusting people. Later on, I went back to school, thinking I was better, but I realized that I couldn't escape from it at all. That lack of trust, sensitivity, and irritability seemed to be ingrained in me! I tried so hard to overcome it! Why is it me?
keywords: Emotions, depressive emotions, anxious emotions, panic and helplessness.

answers.answer_text: Hello. I give you a hug. It feels like we are talking face to face. After listening to your description, I understand that you have many concerns. It is clear that you really want to change your current situation. However, dear friend, don't get too caught up in imagining your future self after making changes. Instead, accept and embrace your true self. Don't rush to change, take it slowly. You can gain a clear understanding of yourself, which indicates that you are a person with a kind heart. You just don't know how to give and accept love. 1. You haven't faced your depression and are avoiding your true self. 2. Deep down, you long for love, but you approach it with hatred. 3. You can't control your emotions and isolate yourself. 4. You want to change yourself but don't know how. The most fundamental belief in your heart is that you don't feel loved, and that's why everything seems bleak. The opposite of love is not hate, but rather, it is resentment. You desperately desire warmth, so you develop hatred towards everything you want to love. If you can understand this and change your mindset, I believe the warm fire in your heart can be reignited. I hope the following suggestions can help you break free from your self-imposed limitations: 1. Acknowledge your depression and seek medical treatment and psychological counseling. Having depression is nothing to be ashamed of. Trust your doctor and counselor, they will help you rediscover yourself and promote a healthy body and mind. 2. Shift your focus onto things you want to do. Try cooking a meal you enjoy, engage in gardening activities, and maintain a certain amount of physical exercise. I believe a fulfilled work and life will bring a sense of joy to you. 3. Love others to love yourself. Invest more love in people and things in your life. Do not hide or isolate yourself. Interact more with others and engage with life. I believe you can rediscover the feeling of love. Don't dwell on the past, look forward to the future! Lastly, remember to cooperate with your doctor and counselor. Believe that self-adjustment and external support will make you better and better. Do not give up on the beauty you desire. Keep going! The world and I love you! All the best.

Hello~ Based on your description, the OP did not leave home and find a job alone until they were not yet an adult. They were bullied and had to handle everything on their own. When they shared their inner pain with their colleagues, they were met with "laughter" and their colleagues did not sympathize or comfort them. Feeling hurt, they slowly closed themselves off. One of the purposes of having explosive emotions is that it allows one to hurt others before they can be hurt themselves, so that others will not get close to them. Emotions are like a dam, without an outlet for release or venting, when they accumulate to a certain point, they will collapse and the dam will be completely destroyed. Sometimes, talking to others, writing a diary, engaging in vigorous exercise, etc. are like small openings in the dam, slowly pouring out bit by bit, so that it doesn't reach the point of collapse. As for the "lack of trust" you mentioned, perhaps in your life experience, there has never been someone deserving of your trust, or perhaps you have never felt the care and love from your family. Living in an environment devoid of love, filled with blame, insults, violence, and suspicion, one learns to behave this way. Life experiences, over time, further reinforce and accumulate negative experiences and perceptions, projecting the negative aspects onto new people one meets, so others always see the worst side of oneself. Try organizing and resolving past experiences, placing them in their rightful place in your heart, and then start anew. I will also share something with you here: increasing irritability is the inner self telling you that you are currently doing very poorly and need help, it is a reminder to yourself. If the people you have known previously cannot be trusted or provide help, try reaching out to others, such as seeking psychological counseling, as it provides an opportunity for yourself.

Hello! @Hello, I read your experience, and I really want to give you a hug! It is understandable that you have become irritable and distrustful towards people. It's because you experienced a lot of darkness and setbacks at a young age, and you weren't prepared for it, and your parents, who should have been your guides and comforters, are no longer around. Your heart is dried up, drained by the external world, and you no longer have gentleness and passion for life. But you are not satisfied with who you are now, otherwise, you wouldn't seek help. This is not what you want. ○ It is important to mention that adolescence is a very important period (generally between 12-19 years old) for the individual's self-integration. Who am I? My abilities, worth, ideals, my position among others, and shaping my worldview, etc. Due to anger, you decided to go to a big city to work alone. I don't want to say this is a bad choice, because it also brought you new perspectives and allowed you to experience life firsthand. However, at the age of 16, you lacked experience in life, and you were also isolated. Work pressure and tasks squeezed your time, making it impossible for you to even think about issues related to self. The working environment, including various rules in the company, also made it difficult for you to adapt. When you can't even control your own life, you will have no time to consider interpersonal relationships. Please believe that not everyone is unworthy of your trust; it's probably just that you invested in the wrong people. Back then, you urgently needed an emotional outlet, and you didn't judge whether the other person was worthy of trust, thus causing you secondary harm. @I have to say that you really don't cherish yourself. Because you don't cherish your soul, depression came. If you continue to neglect, your mental health will collapse. You need rest now. You might as well take a break and sort out your emotions. The stage of self-identity transition didn't go well, so it's better to spend some time thinking about the lessons learned from these years of experience. Seek help from the people who are truly worth trusting, such as your parents, without worrying about losing face and staying silent; take the initiative to seek reliable external help. Your emotions need an outlet, perhaps you need someone to listen. Believe in your resilience. When your pain is understood and soothed, you will gain the courage to start again and realize that you are also worthy! You mentioned being afraid of becoming distrustful towards others. So don't choose to doubt others! Security comes from within yourself. The harm caused by others' deception and betrayal is not because it disappoints you, but because it makes you feel abandoned. When you are confident enough, the betrayal of others is just sending a message that you made a mistake, and then remember to cut your losses in time. Without this worry, trusting others will not be something to fear. @The time you spent in the workplace struggling will not only have negative effects but also teach you things that can help you when your spirits are exhausted. Through these experiences, you won't be too delicate, and you will become more experienced in dealing with things like participating in clubs. Return to school and fill the gaps in knowledge. Only with knowledge and abilities can you have choices. I hope my answer can help you!

Hello, dear. After reading your description, I really want to give you a hug. I know you must feel very lonely, helpless, anxious, and have a lot of emotions. You said when you were 16, you went to a big city to work alone because you hated your parents. Can I assume that you didn't get along well with your parents at home and went to another place to escape their influence? I believe you made that decision because you were very unhappy with your parents. However, in the big city, you had no friends or family, you were always by yourself. Occasionally, you considered your colleagues as close friends, but they didn't see us the same way. We and them are not in the same circle, and this loneliness remains deep in our hearts. At the same time, you start to doubt if there are any real friends, if anyone truly understands your feelings. As you grow older, when you see other people's family situations, you always feel like the abandoned one, the one with such a big difference in circumstances despite being around the same age. Your emotions continue to be suppressed, but you can't find anyone to talk to. You become depressed, irritable and stop trusting people. I think you must have gone through a lot of struggle, confusion, and still can't make sense of these relationships. You want to break free, but those feelings continue to hold you back. Overall, it seems like the current situation is that we have no friends, no love from our family, no one to accompany us, and we feel very lonely. The emotions become oppressive, and there is no one to confide in, no matter how hard we try, it seems to have no effect. Why me? Why am I the one suffering? Why am I the one facing this kind of situation? Can it be changed? I feel hopeless, I can't feel hope. Can someone tell me if it can be changed? This is perhaps the fundamental reason for you asking this question. I believe there is hope in what I see of you, because you haven't given in to the current situation. You are still seeking help, seeking direction, and finding ways to change. Firstly, if those feelings of distrust, sensitivity, irritability, and oppression seem to be engraved in our bones, let's start by changing what is deep-rooted. We and our environment are part of the same system. We know our hands can pick up things through our intentions. When we can't see light around us, we can fill our inner selves with light through our imagination. We can imagine the light inside our bodies, warming ourselves, gradually driving away the cold darkness from within. We can use our intentions to experience the changes in our bodies. Secondly, after we have experienced the changes in our bodies through our intentions, we start to believe that we have value. When we believe in our own worth, we can hold our heads up and confidently interact with others. Through confident interactions, we gradually attract attention, no longer being insignificant. Thirdly, once we have attracted the attention of others through interaction, what we need to do is to make them trust us. Why is it about making them trust us instead of finding someone we can trust? Because finding someone is difficult. Through my survey, we will find that almost half of the people are not in good situations. Therefore, in the process of seeking someone, it is certainly challenging. However, when we ourselves are trustworthy, we can attract many people who can trust us. Fourthly, when we have attracted trustworthy people, we know that life can gradually improve. We know that besides power struggles, there are real friends. These true friends may be able to empathize because they may have had similar experiences. They may belong to that half of people who are not in a good situation. When we find these people, we will know that we are not alone and helpless anymore. Of course, when we encounter them, we should pay attention to mutual assistance and listening to each other. Sometimes, we don't need to give too much advice. Fifthly, we want to meet similar people, but we also need to know that similar people may absorb our light and drag us into darkness. We need to strive to maintain our own light and give light to others, caring for ourselves and others. Sixthly, I know you are tired, but I still want to tell you that you are probably around 20 years old now. You are no longer the 16-year-old you. Perhaps the 16-year-old you was more helpless and naive, but the 20-year-old you has grown up a bit. Your shoulders may be broader, and your arms may be stronger. Do you feel that your actual strength now should be much greater than when you were 16? I want to tell you that now you can slowly change your situation. Your strength is growing day by day, as long as you don't let it defeat you, you will always have the ability to overcome it. Dear, if you are tired, you can find a counselor for guidance. If you are tired, you can temporarily put down all responsibilities and worries, and empty your mind, allowing your heart to relax. Don't let yourself be silent in that dark space all the time. Trying to go out and see different lives, different scenes, and see how others do it. Don't always stay in your own loop, only by breaking the cycle can there be a possibility of change.

Not believing in people is because you lack a sense of security, and being irritable is due to some unmet needs in your inner self. This situation is closely related to the protagonist's upbringing. The protagonist said that when they were 16 years old, they resented their parents and went to a big city to work as an intern alone. At that time, they had no relatives or friends in the city. They would sometimes cry in secret when being bullied or having their achievements stolen at work, and sometimes they would cannot help but cry on the street. They actually confided in their colleagues, but later found out that they were being laughed at behind their back and never spoke about it again. Afterward, they felt like there was nothing worth saying, and that their distress was just a joke. Understandably, being mocked by others gives them a sense of superiority, so there is no need to care about them. In this world, only oneself understands oneself. In fact, during our childhood, we had full trust in this society, but in the process of growing up, we encounter problems beyond our understanding, which may make us feel helpless or traumatized, resulting in a sense of insecurity. For example, if the protagonist is in a bad mood and confides in a colleague who mocks them, they may not dare to express their emotions in front of others, believing that displaying emotions is wrong or bad, and thus becoming increasingly emotionally detached and depressed. Therefore, a sense of insecurity is actually a common phenomenon in the process of growing up, and what we need to pay attention to is that a sense of insecurity is a distortion of our perception of reality. If left unaddressed, a sense of insecurity will gradually deepen in our hearts, becoming a part of our personality and affecting our thinking and cognitive habits, thus impacting our lives. Each of us encounters new setbacks and difficulties in life, but driven by a sense of insecurity, we are more likely to compare our current problems with those we were unable to cope with in the past, especially during childhood, thus generating negative psychological feelings and affecting our judgment of reality. Therefore, if the protagonist wants to solve this problem, they may need to try to reconcile with their parents, such as contacting them regularly. Additionally, they also need to release their anger. It is recommended that the protagonist learns boxing. If they do not find a way to resolve their fear and anger towards their parents, they will transfer it to their spouse and children. To avoid blaming others, what we can do is to release our anger and sadness. When you learn to vent your anger and sadness, your mind will no longer be depressed due to the accumulation of too many negative emotions. The negative effects brought by your parents will also decrease, and the harm you have suffered in the past can be repaired, allowing you to achieve true emotional and inner peace.

Hello, I saw your troubles and I hope I can help you. I see your independence and resilience, as well as your grievances and sadness. I feel sorry for your lonely wandering, but I admire your bravery in facing it. Life teaches us many things, things we are willing to bear and things we are not. No matter what has happened, the power to choose has always been in your hands. You need to learn to make choices for yourself. We can try to make adjustments in a few ways: First, say goodbye to the past. Let everything that happened in the past stay in the past. You can try writing a letter to your past self, reflecting on those feelings and putting an end to the past experiences and hurts. Tell yourself that both the good and the bad are already gone, and now is the starting point of everything. Second, set firm goals. Recognize your lack of trust, sensitivity, and irritability, as well as the underlying causes of these negative emotions. If you want to change, you need to firmly know what kind of person you want to become and take action towards it. Labels like being engraved in your bones or just being temporary can change as you approach your goals. Third, have reasonable expectations. I can tell that you have endless expectations for family relationships. Understand that misunderstandings and lack of understanding may not have formed overnight, so don't expect them to be resolved immediately. You can try taking the initiative to resolve conflicts. If you are not sure why you resent your parents, as you mature and grow older, try looking at your parents from a different perspective. They have their own difficulties. Even if complete reconciliation is not possible, make an effort to be understanding. Try a different way of interacting, and maybe you will have a different experience. Injuries are like ditches encountered on our journey. Falling into them is called setbacks, but climbing out is called growth. Your refusal to give up is your greatest strength. Keep going! Wishing you new gains every day.

Hello, dear reader. I can understand how you are feeling right now and I sincerely hope that my words can offer you some help. You mentioned that at the age of 16, you left home to work in the city. You had to commute alone, and sometimes you were bullied or had your accomplishments stolen at work. When you confided in your colleagues, they would make fun of you. Sometimes you would cry secretly, or even cry right then and there on the street. You feel more and more that others can't understand your feelings, and you envy seeing others and their families getting along happily, while you feel lonely and helpless. The issues at work and problems in your family make you feel like an abandoned child. Later on, you returned to school, but the previous hurts have made you distrustful of others, sensitive, and irritable. First of all, I admire your independence and courage, and I want to say that you have worked hard all these years. Hugs to you. Why is it that as you grow up, you feel more and more suppressed and distrustful of others? This might be a stage in your growth. Since you have entered society and experienced its realities firsthand, both the good and the bad, it's not all negative because there are both indifferent and selfish people as well as warm and sincere ones. In fact, as you accumulate work experience or even just through reading books, you will find that you can have better relationships with your colleagues. I once read a sentence in a book that went something like "Maturity is when a person doesn't reveal everything about themselves to others," which is similar to how one should interact with colleagues. There is inevitably competition in the workplace, and the best way to build relationships with colleagues is to focus on work matters, occasionally have meals together, and discuss personal matters with friends outside of work. Learning to communicate and choosing the right person to share your feelings with is important. For example, now, you can record your thoughts and share your troubles on various platforms. Is returning to school what you desired? Many people who enter the workforce after graduating from school often regret not putting in enough effort during their time on campus, realizing how precious it was. I'm not sure how you feel, but regardless, your previous solitary life has come to an end. Now, you are no longer fighting alone. You can find support here, and you can try to find yourself again and discover a state of comfort with the help of your classmates and teachers. Befriending your teachers and seeking their assistance in school is effective, and I believe you will gradually overcome the unhappiness of the past. I recommend the books "Be a Emotionally Stable Adult Every Day" and "Ten Letters to Young Poets." Wishing you a happy life!

Hello, dear questioner. Give you a hug and a thumbs up! You are currently facing some problems and feeling confused and upset, and that's normal! I have seen many young girls who bravely overcome the lack of attention, negative judgment, and even discrimination from their parents. They believed that they were not the kind of person their parents said they were, and they went on to achieve great things. Some became company bosses, and others opened successful businesses, employing many people and making contributions to society! You also want to grow, but is the path to growth any easier for them? They also had no support, and they also faced the same challenges as you. Sometimes you just have to fight for it and refuse to be looked down upon. This simple mindset gave them the courage to keep going, accepting the ups and downs of the process, allowing themselves to be imperfect, allowing themselves to cry, allowing themselves to laugh, as long as they continue to strive and have goals! From this, you can see that the key is the goal that drives you to persist. As long as that goal is still there, you can find ways to overcome everything. So what if no one helps you? So what if you are beaten down, manipulated by others? You are different! Because you have already chosen a different path, right? Isn't that why I gave you a thumbs up? The road ahead is not smooth, yes! Sometimes you will get tired and stop, and that's normal! But never believe that you are mediocre! Isn't that right? Keep working hard! Good luck!

question: Should I go back to school for the upcoming September to repeat a grade?
description: I had to take a leave of absence due to severe depression and had a history of self-harming tendencies. With the added pressure of school, I couldn't continue and decided to take a break in the first semester of sophomore year. Initially, I thought that taking six months off would help me adjust my state of mind. As the new school year was approaching, my mom took me to get a certificate for resuming school, and the test results showed significant improvement, changing to mild depression. The doctor responsible for the test asked me to make a decision based on my condition in the past week. During that period, I had been in a good mood, so I thought it might have influenced the test results. Yesterday, when I thought about going back to school soon, my emotions collapsed. My heart raced, and my hands and legs trembled. I felt that life had no meaning. My condition hasn't improved noticeably. If I take another year off, I might have to delay graduation by two years, and I may struggle even more to adapt at that time. So, what should I do?
keywords: Growth, stress management, work, and study.

answers.answer_text: Hello! It would be a good idea to consult with your treating doctor before deciding whether to return to school or not. Since you have been receiving professional treatment, you can discuss your situation with your doctor. You mentioned that the test was based on your condition in the past week and showed improvements. It's great that you can already feel some improvement, as the main difference between depression and depressive mood is the long-term feeling of low mood. It is normal to have emotional breakdowns from time to time, even for people without depression, let alone for us who have depression. From your question, it seems that you are currently feeling anxious and afraid of both returning to school and not being able to keep up. However, there is no need to worry too much. Even if you go back to school, don't put too much pressure on yourself, because depression can affect your ability to learn. Just do your best. If the situation doesn't improve, you can choose to continue taking a break at home without too many concerns. If you find it difficult to adapt to school life in the end, you can also try self-study and exams. There are many paths to success. Your health is the most important thing, so take care of yourself first before considering other things. Remember, you are the most important. I had been advised to take a break from school multiple times due to my depression, but maybe I was a bit stubborn and insisted on carrying on. During that time, I also had doubts and talked to a trusted teacher about it. She didn't directly tell me what to choose, but she helped me weigh the pros and cons and assured me that she would support me no matter what decision I made. In the end, my condition did not improve, and I did not perform as well as I could have on exams, but I never regretted my decision because I had tried my best. You can also discuss this matter with someone who understands your situation and whom you trust. However, the final decision always lies with you.

question: 25-year-old female, my mom insists that I take the civil service exam, but I prefer to have freedom. What should I do?
description: I have been graduated for two years and have been working in the court for two years (as a contract worker). I can see the strict hierarchy within the court, the hardships of the judges, and the clear hierarchical structure of government officials. I feel that working in the court is very stressful. My mother is not in the legal profession, but both she and my sister believe that being a government official has less stress, stability, and it is not as hard for a girl. I told her that the legal profession is free and flexible, with the ability to manage one's own time. The atmosphere in a law firm is relaxed and there is no serious hierarchical relationship. Plus, you can earn more money. My mother said that you need to put in a lot of efforts to become an outstanding lawyer and it's too hard. I said that I can be an average earning lawyer, at least I can meet many people and broaden my horizons. The circle of government officials is small. I want to find a partner, but my mother said that the epidemic is severe now, there are many viruses, so it's better to work for the country. I'm very puzzled. On one hand, I want to follow my heart and have some adventures, but on the other hand, I am also worried that I don't have a secure job and solid experience, and I'm afraid that I won't have enough to eat if something unexpected happens in the future. What should I do... My parents' opinions have some merit, but I don't want to live a monotonous life every day.
keywords: Career, career management, job search skills.

answers.answer_text: Hello, questioner. As someone who once listened to their mother and took the civil service exam, but then quit after three years following their own advice, my suggestion to you is simple: do what you love and listen to yourself. Based on your description of the problem, I have outlined the following points for your reference: 1. "Mother says" vs "I say" – What does "Mother says, Mother thinks" mean to you? Parents' opinions have some merit, and we should respect them. From your mother's perspective, she believes she is not wrong. She doesn't want you, as a girl, to work too hard. She wants you to have a stable job and a worry-free life without setbacks. However, that is her expectation, her idea of what is good. What are your expectations? If your expectations are the same as your mother's, then there is no need to struggle. But if you expect a life that is free and not monotonous, that's different. 2. What can I do? What do I want to do? You were able to work at the court for two years, and you also mentioned wanting to be a lawyer. This shows that at least for the profession of a lawyer, you have confidence and ability. So at least you can do jobs related to that. What do you want to do? If you genuinely want to become a lawyer, then you will willingly put in a lot of effort and be willing to endure hardships for what you want to do. In this regard, everyone is the same. Everyone will put in a lot of effort for something they love and will persevere. We need to differentiate between work, occupation, and career. About work, occupation, and career, there is a fantastic interpretation by Professor Li Mengchao that I would like to share with you. "Work is what you are currently doing, it brings you income, perhaps it is the work you have always wanted to do, or maybe just temporary part-time work; occupation is a career direction that includes many jobs, it may be something you want to do for a long time, or at least five to ten years; career is something you want to do in the long run, something you are prepared to devote your life to. You are willing to spend money, labor, and even sacrifice your life for this career. It's a lifelong commitment. When occupation, career, and work are combined, that is certainly happiness. However, not everyone has a combination of the three, some may need to work first before achieving their career." So you can examine yourself and have certain expectations for work, occupation, and career before planning. 3. Iron rice bowl and "no food after unexpected events" Due to the pandemic, those who are not employed by the government may indeed experience more anxiety because their income is not guaranteed. They may even worry about their livelihoods. However, if you were to visit Wuhan this June, you would find that people's lives are still going on. You cannot see the marks of disaster on their faces. Wuhan's hot dry noodles are still delicious, Wuhan people are still vibrant, and Wuhan's crayfish still have a lingering fragrance. Donghu Lake is still beautiful as ever. Life goes on. If there are difficulties, they can be overcome. In my opinion, this is the most beautiful aspect of being human. Iron rice bowls have their benefits, but they also have limitations. Everything has two sides. If you want an iron rice bowl, you have to sacrifice a certain degree of freedom. And if you want freedom, you have to sacrifice a certain degree of security. However, if a person has enough confidence and security within them, they will not be limited by any job. They should have the ability to support themselves in any situation and make their lives increasingly better. So, believe in your ability to do this as well. These are my answers. Good luck!

Hello, I can understand your conflicts and dilemmas. This problem may seem like a career choice on the surface, but fundamentally, it's about you not growing up. You still seek help from your parents and they still see you as a child who hasn't grown up, intervening in your decision-making. If you don't listen, your parents may become sad, nag, have a gloomy expression, get angry, and threaten you in various ways. Although you are 25 years old, psychologically breaking away from your parents, neither you nor your parents can live without each other. In the process of creating one's own world, separation is an eternal subject. There are three separations in a person's growth. The first separation is at birth, completing the physical separation from the mother. The second is around 6 months to 3 years old, when the baby gradually realizes that she and her mother are two separate individuals and wants to break free from the dependency on the mother. This period is also referred to as the "separation-individuation" stage by psychologist Margaret Mahler. The third separation is from the original family, from 3 years old to 18 years old or even longer. After completing this separation, a person can have a sense of self as a subject who can say, "This is my world, and I have the final say," and better build their own world. If the separation from the original family is not completed, it is difficult to live with this sense of subjectivity. If the third separation is not completed, you will continue to encounter more similar difficulties in the future, such as choosing a partner, having children, and raising children. "I think my parents' opinions have some validity" shows that subconsciously you still rely on your parents and are using them as a shield because you want to separate but are afraid of hurting your parents. However, if you really want to make a decision about whether to become a civil servant or a lawyer, there are many authoritative and professional resources available. For example, you can ask on Zhihu, search for answers on the Deto app, or get to know more friends who are civil servants or lawyers, join lawyer groups, and their answers and advice will be much more authoritative than your parents'. "But I don't want to live a monotonous life day after day" shows that you still want to have a world where you have the final say. This is an instinct of human beings and a necessary way to live out your true self. My advice to you: If you still live with your parents, I suggest moving out or developing yourself elsewhere, making yourself stronger, and seeking solutions from more professional and authoritative sources. Make it clear or imply to your parents that you have grown up and have your own life. Parents can offer suggestions, but whether to adopt them is up to you. These suggestions may be difficult for you and your parents at first, but over time, your parents will have their own richer lives, and you will have a world where you have the final say.

I understand your current mood very well. You feel conflicted as you had planned for your future life, but reality shattered those plans. The feeling of helplessness comes from within, and that stubbornness in your heart has been worn down by your mother and sister. Based on the text, you should be from the 90s generation. You don't want to listen to their opinions, but you have a slight hesitation about your current state and future life. Indeed, society imposes various roles on women. For example, you are currently your mother's daughter, a court employee, someone's classmate, and in the future, you will be a mother, a wife, a daughter-in-law, and so on. Each additional role comes with responsibilities that require your time and energy. These roles will influence our life choices. I believe whether you choose to be a civil servant or a lawyer, you will excel. You can use strengths and weaknesses to consider what suits you best. For example, write down the strengths and weaknesses of being a civil servant and a lawyer on a piece of paper, then evaluate your own strengths and weaknesses, and consider which ones you can overcome and which ones you cannot. Whether you become a civil servant or a lawyer, you will continue to work in the public security, prosecution, judiciary, or law enforcement systems in the future. You have already spent two years in this system, so you should have some understanding. When making a choice, you should be clear. This is also a plan for your future life, and this profession may be lifelong. I believe that after careful consideration, you will have a new understanding and appreciation for your career development, and then you can boldly make your choice. I'm here, waiting for you!

Seeing the term "contract worker," it should mean that you are not a regular employee, right? If you are outside of the regular employment system, I suggest trying to become a regular employee because the benefits will be much better. Although you are doing the same work as regular employees, your income will not be as high. If you want to stay in this job position for a long time, you need to pass an exam in order to achieve your desired income. Additionally, you mentioned that you enjoy freedom, but this depends on personal choice. People still need to work and earn money to support themselves, which is the main theme of life. No one can enjoy complete freedom every day. Any job, even freelance jobs like being a writer, has various unknown aspects to life. Therefore, you should understand the significance of work and life. It is impossible to desire complete freedom without working. Actually, you can choose a career that you enjoy, a job that you can control. In your spare time, you will have plenty of time to yourself. You can go traveling or engage in other activities. Achieving a balance between work and life, just like many people nowadays pursuing freelance work and side jobs, is what they aim for. When you can achieve a balance and face yourself, you will not feel miserable.

Hello! From your description, it can be seen that you are torn between being a relaxed and independent lawyer and a less stressful government official job. From your description, it seems that you are well aware of the advantages and disadvantages of both. Your mother's perspective is that she hopes you can have a more stable job. Although she is not engaged in government work, being a government official is indeed considered a good job in the public eye. Furthermore, your mother mentioned that the current pandemic is severe and there are many viruses, so being a government employee is better. This point is not without basis, after all, the pandemic is spreading and many places are laying off employees, including lawyers. Being a government official is relatively more stable, and what your mother said about needing to put in a lot of effort to excel in a law firm is also not unreasonable. However, from your perspective, you want more freedom, to meet more people, and not to live a monotonous life every day. You don't want to be restricted. Indeed, this is your inner thoughts and also the thoughts of young people today. So now, in choosing between stability and freedom, I think if you really want to be a lawyer and have thought about the pros and cons but still truly want to be a lawyer, you can communicate more with your mother and express your thoughts regarding her concerns. I believe that in the end, your mother will support your ideas. If you are still uncertain, it may be because deep down you feel that what your mother said makes sense and your desire to be a lawyer isn't firmly established yet. In that case, I suggest you not rush to change jobs and wait until you have made up your mind. Actually, when you ask for advice on making a choice, your inner self already has an answer, you just want others to validate your choice. Follow your own heart. The above is solely my personal opinion, for reference only, and I hope it can help you.

Hello, cutie. I want to discuss this matter with you from a different perspective. In summary, what kind of conflict did you have with your mother?
