Who is in charge at home and who loves themselves more? Who loves the other more? 46. How do your parents solve family problems or difficulties? 47. Has your marriage or relationship received blessings from people around you, especially your family? 48. Evaluate your mother. What makes you comfortable and uncomfortable about her? 49. Evaluate your father. What makes you comfortable and uncomfortable about him? 50. Did you see your parents having sexual intercourse when you were a child? How did you feel at that time? Did you have any negative emotions towards your mother? 51. How is your relationship with your father? Are you now close to your father, such as hugging or leaning on him? How does your father evaluate your partner? What is his attitude? 52. What are your parents' expectations for your marriage? 53. What have you learned from your parents' marriage, and what are you afraid of? 54. Describe the way your grandparents get along. Who is in charge at home and who loves themselves more? Who loves the other more? How do they solve problems when they arise? If the four elderly people have passed away, ask your parents about them. 55. Do you think your father loves your mother? How does he express his love? Have you ever felt jealous? 56. Describe the way your grandparents get along. Who is in charge at home and who loves themselves more? Who loves the other more? How do they solve problems when they arise? If the four elderly people have passed away, ask your parents about them. 57. How do you view your parents' marriage and your current love or marriage? 58. Evaluate the influence your father has on your choice of partner. 59. Who is more popular with the opposite sex, your father or mother? What is your attitude towards it? 60. Which is more important, romantic love or familial love? Which one would you choose and why? Your emotions and their sources. 61. What is the biggest physical and mental injury you have suffered from childhood to now? How did you overcome this pain? 62. What do you fear the most? What makes you feel uneasy when you think about it, whether it's a person or a thing? 63. Do you have any obsessive-compulsive disorder? In what aspect? When did it develop? What is the reason? 64. What is your attitude towards death? Are you afraid or accepting? What makes you associate with death and fear it? 65. Do you watch horror or thriller movies? How do you feel if there are scenes that hurt or demean women, or scenes of self-harm? 66. What kind of people do you look down upon? Why? Do you think others look down on you? 67. In your experience of dating and relationships from your first to your current one, do you tend to be the giver or the receiver in the relationship? 79. Do you experience sexual climax? 80. What kind of sexual patterns do you enjoy? Do you have a tendency to enjoy being abused? 81. Do you have the habit of masturbation? Do you like or dislike your own body? Do you feel guilty about masturbation? Do you have any fantasies? 82. How do you feel about temptations or manipulative relationships, especially sexual relationships? Do you enjoy them or fear them? Are you more active or passive in such relationships? 83. What do you enjoy most in your current marriage and what do you fear? What touched you, and what makes you uneasy? Are you afraid of yourself, of uncontrollable relationships, or of losing the feeling of being loved? 84. Are you afraid of how people around you will evaluate your personality and marriage? 85. What actions from the opposite sex make you feel comfortable or safe, such as patting your head, hugging, or patting your shoulder? What do you do to make yourself more attractive to the opposite sex? 86. What are your requirements for a partner in terms of limits? What limits can you set for a partner? What things have you done for each other at the limit? Your life perspective. 87. Is there anyone around you who you particularly envy? Why? What do you envy about them? 88. What kind of marriage relationship do you expect? 89. Can you accept a relationship where each individual pays for themselves? 90. How do long-distance relationships or living apart make you feel? What makes you feel pleasant or unpleasant? What causes anxiety? 91. Would you sacrifice your own life goals and career for your partner? 92. Are you afraid of your husband or yourself cheating? What would you do if you or your partner cheated? Is emotional infidelity or physical infidelity acceptable? 93. What is your ideal partner like? Among the partners you have had, who is closest to this ideal? 94. What are your expectations for children? 95. How do you interact with and raise your children? What is the order of priority between you, your partner, and your children? 96. What do you think you will be doing at the age of 40-50? What is your vision for your old age? 97. Which stage, adolescence, middle age, or old age, do you fear the least? Which one do you fear the most? Why? What are the reasons? 98. Evaluate your current occupation. Are you satisfied? What are you dissatisfied with? What kind of occupation can you continue to do until old age? 99. What is your attitude towards money? How is your relationship with money currently? 100. What are the current challenges in your life? What would be your desired outcome after resolving them?

question: Should I tell my parents about my self-harm? I don't want to upset them.
description: I am currently in the hospital. The self-inflicted cuts are too deep and need stitches. The doctor said it's better to inform my family about my condition. So, I tried mentioning it to my mom on the phone. Her first response was, "Are you crazy?" It made me even more upset, and I don't want to communicate with her anymore. Besides, my mom has a heart condition, and I really don't want to upset her. She sounded like she was crying. I really don't want this. But they don't know the situation, and they won't allow me to go to a mental hospital. What should I do?
keywords: Family, family relationships, and parental communication.

answers.answer_text: Hello, the latest update is that I received a call from the hospital today and my mom has been hospitalized due to a heart problem. I am very worried about her condition and I feel guilty for causing her so much stress. I want to talk to her and let her know everything, but at the same time, I'm afraid of how she will react. She has a history of heart disease and I don't want to worsen her condition by telling her about my mental health issues. I care about her a lot and I don't want to burden her with my problems. I'm not sure what to do, but I know that I need to take care of myself and try to heal. Thank you for your support.

question: "Why are many friendships built on relationships where they need my help?"
description: Since the beginning of my junior year in high school, I always thought that life was normal, and my interpersonal relationships and interactions with classmates were also normal. But why is it that since I moved from an eight-person dormitory to a four-person dormitory (which is half more expensive but with better treatment), those roommates who used to be together with me started ignoring me? One friend who used to always be with me felt that I was no longer useful to her and cut off ties with me. Many friends seemed to think that I was useless and cut off ties too. Why is it like this? Why are so many friendships built on the basis of needing my help? Now I find myself on the verge of having to do everything by myself. Is it my fault?

answers.answer_text: Hello, I understand your feelings very well. After reading your description, it reminded me of my relationship with a classmate in junior high school. In the first and second year of junior high, our homes were in the same direction, so we went to school and went home together every day. We were like best friends who could talk about anything, at least that's how I saw it. In the third year of junior high, I moved up to an advanced class, while she stayed in the regular class. Because of the advanced class, the teachers suggested living in the dormitory, so I chose to live there. In order to go to her classroom, I had to pass by my own classroom. But when we met, she wouldn't talk to me anymore. Sometimes I would say hello to her, and she would just give me a brief smile. At first, I couldn't understand why we, who used to be inseparable, had become like this. Did I do something wrong? I was sad and upset about it for many days. Later, I realized that she wasn't someone who valued friendship. We used to be close because we went to and from school together. The deterioration of our relationship wasn't my fault. Even till today, none of my classmates have any contact with her. You mentioned that your friends who used to always be with you think you are useless now, so they cut off contact. Isn't that too absolute? They didn't explicitly say they wanted to end the relationship. It's just that you are in different environments now, and there are no more common topics. Our lives are like a train, people come and go, most of them are short-term passengers. Those who can stay with us for a longer time are few and far between. So for those people who come and go, don't get too caught up in whether they are still on the train or not. In our lifetime, we will meet many friends, but most of them are shallow relationships. To have two or three close friends is already very lucky. Even if you are now alone, those who genuinely want to be friends with you won't distance themselves just because you moved dorms frequently. As for your previous roommate, if you meet, you should still say hello, but whether the friendship is deep or not, let it be up to fate. They say love can't be forced, and the same goes for friendship. The most important thing for you now should be to shift your focus to your studies, become better and better, and believe that you can do it! May we fearlessly move forward together on the road of growth. - Wen Xi.

Hello there~ The essence of interpersonal relationships is cooperation, not utilitarianism. For example, if two people get along very well, their relationship may be good, and in this process, they actually benefit each other - we can obtain joy from each other, so I am willing to hang out with him. The usefulness or uselessness between people is often unclear, unlike in business transactions where people may think that cooperation is useful and no cooperation is useless. The so-called usefulness or uselessness is actually unquantifiable. And few people really get to know someone because they are useful or stop communicating with someone because they are useless. So you need to look at them and understand the reasons for not continuing to communicate and maintain contact with you. It is very likely that it is not because you are useless. For example, it may be because after changing dormitories, there will be fewer intersections between you, and you will no longer live together and share life as closely as before, so it is normal for your communication to decrease. Or maybe it's because you have different opinions on certain issues, so they may deliberately or unintentionally isolate you. And that friend who thought you were useless and then broke off contact with you, how did he explain why he wanted to end the friendship? I don't think he said it was because you were useless. If he did say that, then he is indeed wrong. If two people have a mutually beneficial relationship, then they cannot be called friends. So the most important thing is to see what changes have happened in your life, and why your relationship has changed like this. I don't think it's as simple as whether it's useful or not. If possible, you can have a good chat with those people whose relationship with you is not as good as before, and let them talk about their thoughts and opinions.

Subject: Hello, I think there are a few things to consider regarding this issue. First, think back on how you and your friends became friends. Did you come together because of shared interests, or was it due to being assigned to the same living arrangements? If it's because of living arrangements, there might be a lot of passivity involved. Your close contact and interaction could be mainly because you live in the same dormitory, and without this premise, naturally the relationship would become more distant. Secondly, think about whether it's just one friend who has distanced themselves from you or if many friends are doing the same. If your friendships were normal before 12th grade, it's strange that many friends have changed since then. Is it possible that your judgment of others has been influenced by one person? In short, a true friend wouldn't leave you just because you're no longer useful. Perhaps your attribution has deviated, or maybe these people are just your dormmates.

question: I can't control the urge to find him, my heart is so conflicted. Should I give up or follow my heart?
description: I accidentally clicked on the "People Nearby" feature in WeChat and saw a very unique profile picture. I was curious, so I said hello. I found that he was very polite and didn't seem like a bad person, so we decided to meet the next day. That night, we had dinner together and chatted. When I first saw him, I didn't feel any sparks, but I thought he looked handsome and tall. After dinner, I planned to take a taxi home, but he insisted on riding his motorcycle to escort me home, and I agreed. He drove quite fast, and I placed my hand on his shoulder as we chatted and rode home. As we talked, I felt that he was really warm and gentle, and he had good manners. Then I hugged him, just a simple hug, because he was driving so fast. I joked that he did it on purpose, but he said no. Out of courtesy, I asked if it was uncomfortable to hug like that, as I respect people's boundaries. He said it wasn't and told me to keep hugging him, so I wouldn't be thrown off. After that, we spent a few days together as friends. On the fourth night, I passed by his place a couple of times, and he invited me to come up. I jokingly agreed. After finishing my dance class at night, I texted him and asked him to escort me home.

answers.answer_text: Hello, there are many ways for two people to meet and being nearby is just one of them. It's natural to have doubts, especially with recent events. I believe you have been following the news as well. As the saying goes, time reveals a person's true character. When it comes to a relationship, especially with a stranger, it's important to take things slowly and always remind yourself to protect yourself. May everything be well.

question: A good friend's husband is irresponsible, loves playing games, and even meets up with female online friends?
description: I have a good friend around me who has been married for a year. The husband comes from a well-off family, and the mother-in-law opened a shop for them, so their life is not difficult. However, her husband often loves playing games and going to internet cafes. One time, she got so angry that she went back to her parents' house and stayed there for a month. During this time, her husband had an emotional affair and went to see a female online friend in another city. Later on, they reconciled, and she felt that in order to move forward, she needed to digest these things and keep an open mind. But not long after, she discovered that her husband was still chatting with that woman. Recently, they've been having marital problems, and she reached out to me several times to confide in me. However, I can't give her advice, and I don't know how to comfort her and solve these issues. I don't want to see her so unhappy. She wants to resolve the situation and live a good life. Does anyone have any good ideas? Is there a way for her to escape from this suffering?

answers.answer_text: It is really difficult for outsiders to help with household chores. It's understandable that women would be frustrated in such situations and vent to their friends. But after venting, they realize that life remains the same without any change. We say that the life we talk about is the life we live. When we constantly complain, we tend to put ourselves in the position of a victim and feel sorry for ourselves. Look, how unfortunate I am, how unjust it is, how incompetent he is... You will find that because of such thoughts, our physical energy becomes lower and lower, making it difficult for us to activate creativity in our marriage. In other words, besides complaining and avoiding, we can't seem to come up with any solutions. Let's turn back and talk about the man. What happened after just one year of marriage that made it so boring? Is there only one person in a boring marriage? When faced with unsolvable issues in a marriage, running back to one's parents' home for a month is not a wife's behavior, it's a child's behavior. Similarly, when things go wrong in a marriage, this man didn't try to do anything, but chose to escape through emotional infidelity. In an intimate relationship, the wife is not a wife, the husband is not a husband, they are just two children competing with each other. So, in order to solve these problems, both individuals need to have this awareness and be willing to grow for the sake of a better marriage.

question: Feeling useless and irrelevant, I don't know how to continue living.
description: I always assume that unrelated people dislike me and feel like everyone in the world hates me. If someone compliments me, I panic and think they are mocking me. I struggle to form close relationships, even with my family. Being around my family feels awkward and uncomfortable, and I crave friendships but fear social interactions. Sometimes, I will initiate interactions with people but then distance myself when they try to get closer to me. I have become weak and sensitive, constantly magnifying the difficulties in everything and feeling like I can't succeed. I constantly doubt and suspect the people around me, thinking they are isolating me or talking badly about me. I have no sense of security and don't know what to do. I also have trouble focusing on my studies. I am not sure if this is related to the constant criticism and belittlement I received from my family and teachers when I was younger, always being told that I couldn't do anything right. Now, I feel worthless and that my life is a mess. I feel really uncomfortable and don't know how to move forward.

answers.answer_text: You said, "I'm not sure if it's related to the constant criticism I received from family and teachers when I was a child. I was always being scolded and told that I couldn't do anything right. Now I also feel useless and my life is a mess, I feel so uncomfortable and I don't know how to go on." I think when you associate with the criticism from your family and teachers in your childhood, it becomes an important and influential experience for you. As children, we internalize the judgments of our family as "this is who I am," and we see the criticism from teachers as "I am really terrible." It's hard for us to separate ourselves and say, "This is how others see me, it's not who I really am!" Although it's difficult, I want to tell you that as we grow older, we can try to see that "only I can define myself," okay?

question: Everyday life is routine, how can we make every day meaningful?
description: What can I do if I feel that my daily life is too routine and lacks meaning?
keywords: Growth, self-growth, work and study, the meaning of life.

answers.answer_text: Poster, hello! After reading your description, I have a certain understanding of the question you want to ask, so I'm sending you a virtual hug. The problem you mentioned in your description is actually something that most people encounter, so it can be considered normal. Because most of us live this way, doing routine things every day, especially for those who have a family, their focus is stability, so they tend to stick to their careers and rarely seek change. However, everyone has their own attitude towards life. Some people enjoy a structured life, while others don't. They prefer new things and excitement. In their eyes, freshness is important because these people believe that their lives should have as many possibilities as possible, rather than being confined to a framework. I have summarized some methods to help you alleviate your current situation. (1) If you have time, take a good look at everything around you. I believe you will discover many meaningful things because having an eye for beauty is important. (2) Create some small surprises for yourself in your spare time to add some excitement to your life. (3) Spend time reading books to enhance your cultural literacy. (4) Try to discover things that interest you and work hard towards them. (5) However, the person who can make the change is you. If you want to change, then take action. The world and I love you. Best wishes.

Hello, I saw that you feel a lack of meaning in your life due to the current routine lifestyle, and you are experiencing inner distress. The fact that you find the urbanized life meaningless shows that you are someone who lives positively, which is great. Because you provided limited information, I don't know what your routine life looks like right now. From my understanding, it may mean that your life is stable, and you do the same things every day. Currently, I have a similar lifestyle. I attend classes in the morning, offer counseling in the afternoon, and study in the evening. I rarely leave this building because I live here and work here, so I don't go out much. However, I don't feel that this kind of life has no meaning; on the contrary, I quite enjoy it because I am doing things I love. So what I would like to say to you is, first, you need to understand your personality. Do you prefer a more stable lifestyle or one that is full of change? Only by knowing your preferences can you make better choices. Second, a routine life doesn't necessarily mean it has no meaning. You can find meaningful aspects within this kind of life. You can add a sense of ceremony to your life, such as dressing up nicely every day or having afternoon tea. This can make your life more meaningful. Third, you can enrich your leisure time by cultivating more interests and hobbies. For example, reading books, practicing yoga or doing some exercise can make your seemingly boring life more interesting. These are my personal suggestions, and I hope they will be helpful to you.

question: Dad always favors my younger brother, regardless of right or wrong, and always says that my brother is a bit better-behaved.
description: Today, I had an argument with my younger brother. The reason was that he shouted my name, and I asked him what he wanted. Then we started fighting, and she scratched my hand, leaving wounds. My dad didn't say anything and just held my brother's hand, saying let's go buy some apples for him. I cried, I cried my heart out, but my family acted as if nothing happened, playing with their phones and watching TV beside me. I really don't know if I am truly their biological child. My sisters always joke that I was switched at birth, and I have seriously considered this. I dare not think about it, I dare not believe it, but their actions have made me have to believe it. I really want to die! Since middle school, I have felt that there is no meaning in my life. I hate this family, I hate my sister's temper tantrums, I hate my mom's loud voice, I hate my brother's mischievousness, and I hate my dad's excessive focus on academics! I hate myself for being so pathetic! There is no one I can rely on, and the person I like doesn't like me back. I really don't know what to do anymore!
keywords: Family, family relationships, parent communication, and the process of growing up.

answers.answer_text: Don't be angry, talk about us. How old is your younger brother? He is not sensible. Let children tolerate him and play with him more. In the future, you can even ask him to help you run errands at the supermarket. Your parents have mental health issues, but since you are a normal person, you should be understanding. Let me share a personal experience. I used to have a younger brother who passed away. When he was alive, I really disliked him and would often hit him and say, "Why don't you go die?" But when he actually died, I cried my heart out, wishing I could take his place and die instead. I changed my signature to: "Only after losing do we realize the value. Being aggressive and unrestrained ultimately leads to self-destruction." - "The Art of War" by Sun Tzu.

question: I'm only in middle school, but I feel like I have depression. What should I do?
description: I was born in the 2000s and I will start 8th grade in September. During the middle school entrance exam, my dad got blamed by his "friends" and was sentenced to one and a half years in prison. I saw the police take him away with my own eyes. In my hometown, they value boys more than girls, and since I got accepted into a private prestigious school, the tuition is expensive. My grandmother has been wanting me to go back home and become a "child bride" for another family. My mom suddenly had to start working since she used to be a full-time housewife. She often gets angry out of nowhere and scolds and beats me. My older brother also dislikes me and never really talks to me. Nobody has cared about my feelings because I always smile and make jokes to show that I don't care. Most of my classmates have a good relationship with me, mainly because I'm easygoing and any sad things never stay overnight, and I'm very considerate. Even the teachers make comments like this. But as long as there's no one around, I can't smile no matter what. I feel very uncomfortable inside, don't want to move, and have trouble sleeping at night. Sometimes I even think about committing suicide. I'm too afraid to talk to anyone, maybe because I want to save face, I always show the good side to others. I always tolerate what others do and afraid of ruining the good relationships I have with them. It feels like tolerance and smiling have become my way of life. I always feel inferior for no reason when interacting with others. Do I have depression?
keywords: Family, family trauma, family relationships, and the process of growth.

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP. Giving you warm hugs (づ′▽`)づ Based on your description, I understand that: (1) You always show the good side to everyone, but deep down, you feel upset. (2) You want to know if you have depression. Here are my analysis and suggestions, hoping to help you: (1) I admire your strength and smile despite facing gender bias, abuse, and ridicule. It seems like you interpret this as saving face, but I have a different view. From the ashes, we rise; strength is forged through adversity. These words wouldn't exist without smiles and resilience; you're simply in the process of strengthening yourself. (2) I'm not certain if you have depression, but I suggest talking to a counselor at your school. They might be able to genuinely help you, keep your secret, and provide you with some techniques. Believe in your own strength. Finally, here's a quote for you: "The darkness you see may just be the night before the dawn. With hope, keep going, and you will get better. The world and I love you. Best wishes~"

question: I feel extremely annoyed by my colleague asking for information about my family. How can I reconcile with myself?
description: I am extremely disgusted when my colleague asks me about my family information, as if she has touched a hidden corner of my heart. When I am emotionally stable at that time, I would give vague answers to brush it off. But if my emotions were unstable, I would feel a rush of blood and a sense of irritability. My father has a simple mind, while my mother is irritable and solves problems by raising her voice. As a result, I have always had a strong desire to prove myself, being someone else's child since I was young, even though I have a master's degree. I know that I shouldn't isolate myself, and that I should open up and embrace life. But how can I reconcile and resolve this emotional trauma?

answers.answer_text: Hello: People have things in their hearts, the more they accumulate, the longer it lasts. Since it is a mental knot, it needs to be untied. It may be painful, just like a tumor in one's heart. If it is not removed, it will stay there, always present. Often things are not as serious as we imagine, but we feel that they are. Don't worry, since it is a knot, it can be undone. Analyzing and understanding the problem: 1. You are extremely disgusted when colleagues ask you about your family, as if they are touching the hidden corner of your heart. When you are in a stable mood, you may give vague information to brush it off, but if you are emotionally unstable, you may feel a surge of anger and a restless feeling. (It is normal for colleagues to communicate with each other, but information about family is a sensitive spot in your heart. We cannot prevent colleagues or other friends from asking about family matters, so we can only deal with this part of sensitivity. I guess your childhood and family have brought you a lot of shadows, becoming the "pain" in your heart. Like a hedgehog with trauma, you instinctively hurt whoever touches it. And you also know that this anger is not directed at your colleagues, but at the helplessness and pain caused by your unchangeable family situation.) 2. Your father has a simple mind, your mother is irritable, and problems are solved by raising one's voice. You are extremely strong. From childhood to adulthood, you have always been the child from other families and have a master's degree. (In a family where the woman is strong and the man is weak, you unconsciously become strong. There is a sense of strength in your heart: you dislike that your father lacks the responsibility of a man, and you dislike your mother's irritable upbringing. Your strength comes from an invisible resistance to them. What can you do about it? You can only make yourself stronger, so you keep striving, continuously striving. But deep down, you are not happy. Therefore, when colleagues ask about family matters, it easily touches the pain in your heart.) 3. You know clearly that you should not isolate yourself, but rather open up and embrace life. But how can you reconcile and untie this mental knot? (People often say, "It is easier to change mountains and rivers than one's nature," but they didn't say it's impossible. After so many years, you have been using the same thinking pattern to understand things, and the same family perspective to look at them. It has become a strong "mental knot" in your heart. If you want to untie it, you need to understand yourself more, and then let yourself understand yourself more, see yourself, and slowly some ice will melt, some mental knots will slowly open. First, reconcile with yourself, then you can see them differently, then you can reconcile with them. Don't worry, it is possible.) Conclusion: I wish you happiness and joy! I wish you success in whatever you desire! Feel free to private message me if you have any confusion!

Hello, I see your concerns and I hope I can help you. From your description, I can tell that you are extremely disgusted when colleagues ask about your family information. You feel like your innermost secrets are being touched, and you even become irritable when your emotions are unstable. I can understand your mood and feelings. You don't want to isolate yourself and want to open up and embrace life. We can try to make adjustments in the following aspects: Firstly, accept your true self. It is normal to not want others to inquire about your family information. Everyone has corners in their hearts that they don't want others to touch. Don't blame yourself for this. You can explain to your colleagues that you don't like this topic or change the subject. Generally, colleagues won't have different views of you because of this, so there's no need to be overly nervous. At the same time, the exaggeration of this matter reflects your importance and entanglement with family relationships. You can try to sort it out on your own. What did the "child from someone else's family" experience in childhood? What shaped your current personality and interpersonal communication patterns? What positive and negative influences did your parents have on you? Look at the past from a third-party perspective, see the most authentic self, and bravely accept yourself. Allow yourself to be imperfect. This is the first step to unlocking the knot. Secondly, accept your parents. From your description, I see that your father is mentally simple and your mother is irritable, using a loud voice to solve problems. I guess they may be controlling parents, keeping you in a suppressed state of being controlled since childhood, and also shaping your drive for perfection. The reason you don't want to talk about them now is probably because you have repeatedly tried to meet their expectations, but your expectations of them have never been realized. Starting from now, try to look at your parents from an adult's perspective, see their hardships, whether it's the simplicity that you thought, their irritability, or solving problems with a loud voice, they might be the coping strategies they could choose in life. Imagine putting yourself in their shoes, given their background and conditions at the time, could you do better than them? Maybe they are not the way you expected them to be, and their way of loving you is not the way you like, but as parents, they have indeed done their best. Accept their imperfections and try to understand them from a different perspective. Let go of your perfect expectations of them from your heart, and you may no longer feel so entangled. Thirdly, establish your own social circle. Every personality has its own advantages. From your words and lines, I can see your self-discipline, drive, kindness, and sensitivity. These are all your strengths. Don't doubt yourself because of others' opinions or feel that you have to get along with everyone to be open. On the contrary, having boundaries in relationships can help you meet more like-minded friends. Reconcile with yourself first, and the world will naturally reconcile with you. I wish you new discoveries every day.

Hi there! First, let me give you a warm virtual hug, and I hope my answer can help you. First, I want to commend you for being an amazing child in other people's eyes throughout your life. That's quite impressive! Although the personalities of my parents and Sisi's parents are quite similar, Sisi hasn't been able to portray herself as the "ideal child" like you have. I must admit I'm a bit envious of you. Sisi also mentioned that her family situation is somewhat similar to yours, so I believe your reluctance to share your family circumstances with others is a way to protect yourself. Personally, I don't usually like discussing my family situation either. Perhaps it's because my father has a simple mind and has never expressed his love to me, whereas my mother tends to solve problems by raising her voice and scolding me, making it difficult for me to feel loved. I feel like I lack affection, but I don't want to share this miserable side of myself with others, so it's really hard for me to talk about my family situation. So, considering your deep-rooted feelings, are they similar to mine? Therefore, instead of saying that it's your personal issue, it might be more accurate to say it's an issue between you and your parents. Now, as an adult, I can get along with my parents harmoniously, so let me share how I managed to resolve the issues between them and me. Growing up, I've come to realize that my parents are also pitiful in a way. They belong to an older generation that didn't have the opportunity to receive much education, and their living conditions were not the best, so they had to endure a lot. For example, my mother didn't receive gentle treatment in the past, so she doesn't know how to treat others gently. As for my father, he didn't receive much education, so he doesn't know how to educate his children. Additionally, his lack of confidence resulted from his childhood experiences, making him introverted and unsure how to express love to his children. Therefore, for both my parents, I use the same approach: I treat them well and show them kindness. Through my words and actions, I let my father know that I love him, and gradually, he has started to change and make me feel his love. As for my mother, I tell her that yelling at others is not good, and I teach her to be more gentle. Although she still occasionally raises her voice, I can feel that she has become more tender than before. This is my approach, and I encourage you to give it a try as well. Hopefully, you can reconcile with your parents. As for sharing information about your family, I agree that you don't have to say too much, but it shouldn't lead to being angry with others. I hope this can help you with your dilemma. Take care!

Our entire lives are greatly influenced by our families of origin, and by the way our parents treated us when we were children. There are certain aspects that we dare not touch, and we can only release them in an environment that we consider safe. The person asking the question said, "I understand that I shouldn't isolate myself, and that I should open up and embrace life, but how do I reconcile with this unresolved issue?" We need to understand that our families of origin are not perfect, and that our parents' treatment of us was not right. We cannot make them change for us, but we can try to love ourselves. So how do we love ourselves? First, we need to put ourselves in our parents' shoes and try to understand them. The reason they treated us in that way, appearing unloving, is because they were accustomed to it. Their parents treated them the same way. They thought that was love, so they treated us the same way. We need to learn to understand our parents, understand that they were also people who "were not loved" because they did not have love themselves, so they were unable to give love to us. Understanding our parents actually means letting them go, and letting ourselves go as well. Now, what we can do is to give up seeking love from them, to give up immersing ourselves in the time when they did not love us, and instead, look forward and start loving ourselves. We need to treat ourselves as the child we once were, be our own parents, accompany ourselves, understand ourselves, and love ourselves. After we love ourselves, our mind and body will be healthier, and we will know how to love ourselves, so we will no longer need to seek love externally. Then, we can break free from external expectations and bravely live the life we want.

There are two ways you can regulate yourself. On one hand, take care of yourself and don't be too hard on yourself. Do things that make you happy and comfortable. If this question is indeed sensitive to you and you don't want to address it, you have every reason to refuse the person's inquiry. Just tell your colleague directly, "I'm sorry, this question is sensitive to me and I find it difficult to answer." Sometimes, when people ask me about my salary or if I'm married, I feel it's crossing a line. Why should I tell you? Are we that close? Should I make myself uncomfortable just to satisfy your curiosity? In such situations, it doesn't matter if you open up, just brush it off casually or say it's not convenient to disclose that information. If it's something you truly mind, we usually only want to share with close friends. We don't have to bare all just because someone asks us, it makes us seem a bit too cheap, right? Trust has to be earned. As you said, it's enough to give some vague information, like saying they have retired or what occupation they have, and then don't say much more or change the subject. The other person should understand that. If they keep pressing, it means they lack emotional intelligence, and you don't have to pay attention to them. On the other hand, remind yourself that your colleagues don't mean to intentionally upset you; try to maintain a tolerant mindset. They have no idea about your concerns and perhaps just want to find a casual topic. If you can think this way, your emotions won't be so agitated because the other person is clearly unaware. Your family and your colleagues are not related, and they won't keep on dwelling on this matter. Usually, it's just a passing mention, so tell yourself not to take it too seriously. Your parents' situation is not your responsibility, nor is it your fault. Don't burden yourself with something that doesn't belong to you. Think more about how outstanding you are and how high your education is. You have many commendable qualities, and your dysfunctional family doesn't define you. You are the one in control of your own life. Yes, we have been hurt in the past, but we should try our best not to let those hurts continue to affect us. Even if we spend most of the time embracing life, it's still good. Be more tolerant and understanding towards yourself, and it might help you let go of the burden.

question: My partner is being controlling, and my parents also forbid me from marrying someone from another city. How should I make a decision?
description:
1. What should I do if my boyfriend is too controlling? I know he means well, but I have my own thoughts. It feels like he wants to put me in his pocket and take me everywhere. Since I've been with him, my ability to live independently has almost completely diminished. 

2. There's another issue. My parents have made it clear that even if I get married, I must marry someone local and not move too far away from them (in their eyes, even leaving the city is considered going to a different place). But I want to explore the outside world. I genuinely love my boyfriend and I'm also planning for the future, but I already feel resistance now. Should I tell my boyfriend about this matter? Doesn't he have the right to choose his own future? He's preparing for a graduate entrance exam, will it distract him? There are so many complicated problems in life, and I'm asking all the teachers here to provide an answer.

answers.answer_text: Give the poster a warm hug~ Reading through the whole paragraph, it feels like the poster hasn't been true to themselves, they always seem to be suppressed, always putting others first, where did their own true feelings go? They want to make choices for their own life, but it seems like there are obstacles everywhere and their own strength is insufficient. First of all, the boyfriend is controlling too much, who gave him the right to do so, allowing him to have a say in every little thing, making him think that you can't do anything well, not independent enough, hence he tries to control you too much. The parents have also made it clear that they don't want you to be too far away, isn't this also a form of control? Think about it, have you ever lived an independent life from childhood to now? If not, then let yourself become independent, make others feel at ease, give yourself a certain degree of freedom, that's the task at hand for the poster. Be aware of your own inner self, clear about what you truly want, have the courage to make choices and the willingness to make decisions without regrets. Brave enough to be yourself, we all need to grow up step by step.

OP, hello~~~ First, let me give you a virtual hug. From your description, I can understand that: 1. Your boyfriend is controlling and it makes you uncomfortable. 2. Your parents oppose you living in another city. 3. You don't know whether or not to discuss it with your boyfriend because you're afraid of disturbing his exam preparation.【A little bit of analysis and advice】1. You mentioned that you still have feelings for your boyfriend and hope to continue the relationship, so the issues in the relationship need to be resolved. You can talk to your boyfriend and let him know that you feel he is being too controlling. If you can't say it face-to-face, you can write him a letter expressing your thoughts. 2. Your parents' opposition is also a sign of their care and protection. However, whether to go to another city or stay is ultimately about your own future. Only you will bear the consequences of this decision, so it should be based on your own hopes and desires. You can have a conversation with your parents, expressing your genuine desire to experience life outside and consider their advice in weighing the pros and cons before making a final decision. 3. Finally, decide whether or not to inform your boyfriend about these issues based on his personality. If he is easily influenced by external factors and tends to be emotional, it's best to wait until after his exam to bring it up. If not, and he is the type to mediate emotions well, you can actually discuss it together. I hope this helps you.

question: A 10-year-old girl behaves differently towards her parents and other people, but what exactly is she like?
description: My precious child behaves differently in front of me and others. In my eyes, they appear very well-behaved, but they do not let others bully them in front of their classmates. They don't treat their grandma well because they have only been living together since they were seven years old. Older people tend to nag, which has caused deep conflicts between the two. I can't see clearly what kind of child my child is. I am very curious!

answers.answer_text: In fact, not only children can have multiple facets, even ourselves, we may behave differently in front of different people. Children behave very obediently in front of us, which should have something to do with our parenting style. We can think back to how we educated our children and see if there are any discrepancies between their behavior and our expectations. When with friends, children will not easily let others bully them, indicating that they already have a sense of self-protection, which is a good thing. There may be some conflicts when they are with their grandmother, which is related to the nagging and routines of older people. Because there are already certain preconceptions, we need to communicate with our daughter in a timely manner and try to eliminate unnecessary misunderstandings. It is natural for children to have multiple facets because human nature tends to seek benefits and avoid harm, so they will make adjustments according to different situations and find the most suitable methods for themselves. We can have a heart-to-heart talk with our child as an observer, listen to her opinions on these matters, give her some advice, and hear her ways of dealing with them. Actually, it's not that we can't see what kind of person our child is, it's that we only see a part of them, so we become curious and want to know about their other aspects. However, in this process, we need to pay attention to our child's privacy. For example, we should keep their little secrets confidential or not easily touch upon them. The world loves you and so do I.

question: Is it credible for a 99-year-old girl to claim that she has been married and has children?
description: I like her. But she told me that she was married and has a child. I feel like she is lying to me. People who were born in 1999 shouldn't be able to get married back then, right?

answers.answer_text: In rural areas, having a banquet signifies getting married, which is more deeply ingrained in people's hearts than a marriage certificate. Because both sets of parents and relatives know about it and have given their blessings. Similarly, it is not surprising to get married at the age of 16 in rural areas. My classmate got married after graduating from junior high school and became a grandmother in her thirties. It's not about whether one should get married at a certain age, but rather it is related to one's living environment, family background, personal needs, and so on. Many people who get married early either listen to whatever their parents say, or sacrifice themselves for the sake of their parents and siblings, feeling helpless. Whether she is actually married or not, by telling you this, she doesn't want to harm you, cause you distress, and she also doesn't want to cause trouble for herself.

question: Do the feelings between sisters become less genuine as they grow older?
description: There are 5 children in my family (one older sister, two younger sisters, one younger brother). I am the second child. When we were young, my older sister always treated our third sister poorly because she liked me better than my third sister. (My third sister ran away from home 10 years ago, and sometimes I really miss her...) Nowadays, the relationship between my older sister and my fourth sister is good, and I don't feel jealous. But I can feel that my older sister always uses her body language to show off how good her relationship with my fourth sister is in front of me. I didn't think much of it before, but now I notice these things. For example, sometimes when I talk to my fourth sister, my older sister interrupts and my fourth sister can't continue the conversation with me and ends up talking with my older sister instead. For example, sometimes when I ask my fourth sister a question, my older sister always answers it before my fourth sister can. I feel that her behavior of being impolite and craving attention is becoming increasingly repulsive to me. I understand that my older sister is seeking attention. (One reason I can think of at the moment is that my older sister lived at my grandparents' house until she was 9 years old and lacked parental love. When she returned at the age of 9, my father was strict and demanding towards her, while he doted on me, so I think my older sister is competing for love and care in front of me, trying to find her sense of existence. I don't know if my analysis is accurate.) I would really like to hear the analysis from a professional. Thank you. Seeking the truth.

answers.answer_text: Hello! From your description, it seems that there have been some changes in the relationship with your once very close sister. In your eyes, her relationship with your younger sister is closer and she seems to show off their intimacy. It seems that you are a sensitive person and have deep feelings for both your sister and your younger sister. You are probably looking for some reasonable explanations for these changes or subconsciously hoping to return to the relationship pattern from childhood. From your sister's perspective, she did not grow up with your parents and lacked their care, which may have caused her to feel abandoned and lacking in security. Even after returning to her own family at the age of 9, she may have still faced strict treatment from your father. During her growth process, she continuously looked for a relationship that she considered safe to comfort herself. For example, when she was younger, she formed an alliance with you and treated your younger sister in a certain way. As she got older, she formed an alliance with your younger sister and treated you in a similar way. Regardless of the stage, she needs someone by her side to control this kind of relationship to prove that she is not alone and abandoned. However, this process does not necessarily mean that she has hostility towards you or deliberately isolates you. It is just a defense mechanism, not targeting anyone specifically, but you happen to be one of the roles in this relationship. From your perspective, you also want to return to the relationship state of your childhood. We can only say that the relationship between sisters also needs to be maintained with effort. Before getting married, the relationship was pure, but after getting married and starting their own independent families with children, they became busy with their own lives, and it is inevitable to drift apart from each other. However, this kind of relationship will still return to its original pure state after the children grow up because family love is eternal. The reason you analyze the current relationship so thoroughly is actually a kind of nostalgia for your past sister. This feeling of "loss" makes you tend to overinterpret your sister's behaviors. In other words, often it is just your subjective perception, and the reality may not be as complicated as you imagine. While maintaining a distant relationship with your sister, we can also check whether we have lost the respect, attachment, and care we had for her in childhood. I believe you love your sister, and if your love is reciprocated, you hope that her response to you is better than her relationship with your younger sister. This is a more objective perspective, and if it makes you unhappy, please disregard it. Deep sisterly love means that more care and love is always better. In the future, everyone should take care of each other without distinguishing between who is closer or not, and should be less calculating and more tolerant. You will have more love. I hope you are happy!

From the picture you have described, your sister does indeed show some tendencies to express herself and seek attention. However, it must also be said that there are reasons for such behavior. Previously, she left home and lived with the elders, and then returned, which must have made her feel out of place. In a situation where she feels out of place, it is understandable that she wants to assert herself and make an effort to fit into the family. Your expression seems to suggest that your sister has stolen your limelight (if you feel uncomfortable with this statement, well, please forgive me, I am just objectively analyzing, and if there are discrepancies, it is just my subjective interpretation of your words). So, with such actions from your sister, you may feel a sense of insecurity in your position. This kind of thinking is like there can only be one leader, and if your sister is doing well, it means she has taken your place, and you feel like a failure or have been eliminated. But I think you can also think in a different direction. You are a family, although your sister, you, and your younger sister now have your own families, you still have a family blood relationship after all. So, I hope you can love and care for each other more, and deepen your relationship. As for how to become more like a family or become more like competitors, I think this is something you need to consider carefully, and of course, your feelings also need to be understood by yourself. Your sister did not grow up in the family when she was little, which provides you with a certain psychological foundation. You also feel that she should stay outside or not be too close to you, rather than make an effort to integrate into the family. Just like your father's attitude towards her, treating her badly is also because your father also has a premise in his mind, that is, she did not grow up living with him, and there were fewer interactions between your father and you and your sister, making the relationship between you not as close. So when your sister suddenly becomes so proactive and aggressive in joining your family, it makes you uncomfortable in terms of distance, and you can't help but push her away. You need to understand your own emotions. You've also mentioned that you really like your sister, but compared to the deep bond you have with your siblings, your relationship with her is more complicated. This is appropriate because we often think that what we feel in our hearts is the truth, but we overlook the period of time when you didn't live together and the period of adjustment when your sister first returned. So, the direction of your relationship development needs to be towards intimacy and how to resolve conflicts or this kind of underlying turmoil between you. Talking about reasoning and knowing a lot doesn't necessarily mean we can navigate through life smoothly. What we need to do is to solve each conflict and emotional fluctuation in your real interactions. Good luck to you, and know that I and the world love you.

Sister, hello. After reading your experience, my understanding is that you want to confirm if your thoughts are correct. You think that your older sister and fourth sister are good to each other in order to establish their sense of presence in the family. I am very curious about the mindset you had when you wrote this whole paragraph, which is very rational in describing and analyzing without adding emotional color. I am not very clear about what the truth is. If you want to understand your sister, based on the limited information you provided, I have some understanding of her. 1. Your older sister lived at your grandmother's house until she was 9 years old, lacking the love from parents. With five children in the family, everyone lives with their parents, except for her alone at your grandmother's house. Imagine, for such a young child, what does it mean? Will she think she is not obedient or cute, consider herself as redundant, or feel burdensome? 2. After your older sister returned home at the age of 9, your father was very strict with her. Usually, little girls want to be close to their fathers and receive their love. However, your father was very strict with your older sister. What does this mean to her? It is possible that she wants to receive her father's love but also thinks she cannot obtain it. How can she get it? Perhaps by being like a little mother in the family, taking care of her younger siblings? 3. Your third sister left home ten years ago. How old was she at the time? How old was your older sister? What was the reason for her leaving home? Did she leave voluntarily or were there hidden circumstances? How would this incident affect your older sister? Would she think that there are too many people in the family, and if she is not well-behaved, she will be sent away or even "leave home"? 4. You did not mention your younger brother. I imagine that in the family, your younger brother doesn't need to do anything special and naturally receives unconditional love from your parents, is that correct? Or do you mean that your mother loves your younger brother the most? And you also mentioned that your father loves you the most. In that case, it seems like neither your older sister nor your fourth sister receives any love. Maybe no matter what they do, they cannot receive love from their parents, so they take care of each other. When you open up your feelings to understand your older sister, maybe the truth doesn't matter. Best wishes.

Hello, OP: I have observed some of your questions about sisterly relationships, and I also noticed that you have actively expressed your concerns and sought help from others. This undoubtedly helps you better understand yourself and understand relationships. The relationship between people is a dynamic process that changes over time and personal experiences. Different interpretations and experiences of life will change the attitude towards relationships. Now, I would like to share my observations in the post, which may help you have a more comprehensive perspective on relationships. 1. People who lack love, if they don't make up for it themselves, will always seek validation. I noticed your description of your sister when she was younger, how she was primarily raised by your grandmother until age 9. For her, and for you, it seems like there were two separate circles - you and your parents were in one circle, while she was in another. When you are together, it is easy to feel a sense of not belonging. You might feel that she is trying to take away love, snacks, toys, etc. And your father is stricter with her. So, how did she fit into your family? By being obedient and taking care of her younger sisters, which is a good way to be accepted and acknowledged by your parents and you. This way, she can also receive love. On the other hand, the desire for validation is often accompanied by a fear of not being validated. This can manifest in behaviors and emotions that might lead her to bully her younger sister. Now that you have grown up, it seems like your relationship dynamic has changed, but there are still some similarities. Consider this - now your relationship is like you being the "third sister" and your parents have become the "fourth sister." She still needs the validation of the "parents," so she has to perform well in front of them. This can lead to seeking attention and proving herself to the "parents" through criticism. And as you have become the "third sister" because your older sister desires validation, her other side is a fear of not being validated, which she projects onto you through occasional criticism. 2. Recognize your older sister's limitations and learn to balance the relationship. What is the best and most enviable kind of relationship? It's one that can withstand attacks - the kind where you trust that even if I criticize you, you won't leave me. She feels safe in your presence, which allows her to be her true self. From your post and comments, I can see that you are doing certain things very well. Firstly, you have a keen perception and have recognized your older sister's limitations. Praising her meets her narcissistic and validation needs. This is also a form of respect for her. However, it's understandable that you feel uneasy when your older sister speaks negatively about herself in front of your younger siblings. In this case, we should also learn to respect ourselves. You can directly describe your sister's behavior and express your feelings, or you can try to get her to think from a different perspective. You can also use humor to lighten the mood, for example: "I may not be perfect, but I'm always trying my best to treat you all well!" Learn to balance your relationship, respect your older sister, and respect yourself. Your older sister has limitations, and so do you. As for you, the "third sister," if you feel guilty in your heart, it would be good to apologize to her for not treating her well and bullying her when you were younger. This might bring you some inner peace.

Title: Hello! Thank you for your question and invitation. I can tell that you had a close bond with your older sister and treasured this family relationship. In your interactions with your older sister and your younger sister, you tried to understand and empathize with your older sister, feeling sorry for the difficulties she faced in her childhood. However, the words and actions of your older sister towards both you and your younger sister are perplexing and uncomfortable. As an older sister myself, I can somewhat understand the frustration that arises when there are tensions with an older sibling, but it can be difficult to express these feelings. Many people cannot comprehend what it's like to grow up with numerous siblings. For a child who could only play alone, having an older brother or sister was a desire, even if it meant arguing and fighting, it was still better than being lonely and bored. As the saying goes, "A mother gives birth to nine children, and each child is different." As we grow older, the temperament and ways of interacting with others among siblings will inevitably differ, leading to conflicts and discord. From a different perspective, it is precisely because of the deep sibling bond, a bond that others cannot experience, that some troubles arise. Just as the natural cycle of the seasons and changing climates continue to provide us with sunshine and air, the only thing that changes is our state of mind, not the deep bond of blood. When you feel that there is a rift between sisters, consider it as an opportunity to reassess the relationship and strengthen the bond. You mentioned that in your childhood, you had a better relationship with your older sister, but she always treated your younger sister poorly, and sometimes you truly miss her. You must have discussed your younger sister leaving home with your older sister, what kind of girl is she? What happened back then that led her to make such a decision at such a young age? How has she been doing all these years? Do you keep in touch with her? What are your older sister's thoughts on this? From your post, it is evident that all of you love your younger sister. As an older sister, perhaps you feel that taking care of and accommodating younger siblings is natural. However, the way you and your older sister treated your younger sister during your childhood might have made her feel excluded and unwelcome, and that could be why she left home, making it difficult for anyone to feel at ease. Perhaps your older sister, like you, feels some guilt in her heart. If you could turn back time, both of you would surely treat your younger sister with more friendliness and harmony. Now, only your younger sister is by your side, and perhaps, like you, your older sister hopes to give her more care and help to make up for the guilt she harbors towards your younger sister, unintentionally disregarding your feelings. If possible, find an opportunity for all the sisters to have a calm and honest conversation, where you can reflect each other's feelings like a mirror and see the love between each other. These are just my personal thoughts for your reference. Best wishes to you and your sisters~.

OP, good evening! I understand your distress, and it must be an unhappy situation. It seems like you have a deep emotional bond with your older sister, and her behavior may have made you sad, upset, or even a little angry. Let's try to make sense of the whole situation. [Sibling Rivalry] Your older sister grew up with your grandparents, and even when she came back to her own home, she didn't receive much love from your parents. There are possibly two explanations for your sister's thoughts and actions. One possibility is that she wants to receive more love from your parents. More love means more attention, and more attention means being more successful. After all, she is the only child who was sent away by your parents, which may have made her feel like she is unwanted. To prove that she is not unwanted, she needs more attention and love from your parents. The other possibility is jealousy. She may be jealous that her siblings get to live with your parents and receive their love, while she doesn't. She wants what she can't have. Regardless of which possibility it is, the ultimate goal might be to compete for your parents' attention and love. [Blood is Thicker than Water] Your sister was sent to live with your grandparents, and as a young child, we don't know what she has been through. Since it was a boarding situation, maybe she experienced more hardships. Perhaps the past difficulties have influenced her behavior today because of her need for parental love, or maybe she also feels jealous of her siblings, causing her to temporarily lose sight of what's important. She is being driven by her inner needs, but may not necessarily see the reasons behind her actions. If she could understand this, she would naturally understand the importance of loving her siblings and parents, and she would receive love in return. Ultimately, family bonds are strong, and no matter how much internal arguing there may be, in the end, siblings are still the closest. My suggestion for you, OP, is to not dwell too much on your sister's behavior. Her behavior is her own lesson in life, and all you need to remember is that she is your sister. Focus on doing what you should do, and eventually, your sister will come to her own realizations. Lastly, I wish you happiness and joy, OP!

Hello, the relationship between sisters actually remains true as we grow up, it's just that our feelings are different from before. As we grow up, we all have our own busy lives and spend less time together compared to when we were younger, but the love between sisters is the same as when we were little. From your description, it seems that you care a lot about having a close relationship with your sisters. When you were little, you were close with your older sister, and now you want to become closer to your younger sister. And when you feel distant from your younger sister, you think about your middle sister. Are you looking for a sense of belonging or is your older sister seeking validation? You have always said that your older sister is looking for validation, competing for love and attention, and you define this behavior as impolite. But why does it bother you? Maybe because you also desire care and love from other family members. You mentioned that your father loves you and your sister likes you as well, so when you are so concerned about your sister competing for love, is it possible that you are also competing for love, afraid of losing their love? When your heart is filled with love, you will naturally care for others, feel sad for your youngest sister who ran away from home, understand that your sister lacks love and show her care, instead of feeling resentful. If your heart is filled with love, your younger sister will naturally be closer to you. We all want to be close to love, like flowers attracting butterflies. So, try to fill your heart with love first, instead of seeking love from those around you, and then go and care for others. I believe you will harvest a harmonious relationship with your sisters. Keep going, and best wishes to you!

I want to say that after growing up, we all become adults, and the world of adults should be different from when we were children. Influenced by various factors, our innocent thoughts from childhood become more complex as we age. Sometimes, we may even struggle to control ourselves. For example, when we were young, we might always want to go everywhere with our older sister and be inseparable companions. But as we grow up and develop independence, there may be times when we can't go together due to different priorities or obligations, and we gradually get used to the feeling of being apart. This just means that the form of intimacy has changed, but it still represents our growth and our own pursuits and lives, which naturally leads to some distance. However, blood is thicker than water, and that kind of intimacy will still be there. As long as you haven't had any major conflicts or unresolved issues with your sister, trust in this relationship. You can also talk to your sister about your concerns and confusion, as communication is the best bridge. In addition, when you mentioned your sister competing with you for attention (I'm not sure if I misunderstood), it may not be directed at you personally, but rather a result of her own growth experiences, such as seeking validation and feeling heard. From a psychological perspective, these behaviors can be defense mechanisms or survival strategies. Maybe you can talk to her about the things that make you uncomfortable and make her aware of her own behavior, and then discuss together whether such behaviors are appropriate. I believe that if your sister cares about your feelings, she will make some adjustments. Seeing that you have come for help with this sister relationship issue, I believe you value this relationship a lot and it has been causing you distress, right? So try communicating with your sister, it might be helpful. But if she is unwilling to communicate or denies your claims, you can choose not to argue with her for now and give each other some time to cool off. During this time, I believe both of you will reflect and think, and this process of reflection will be helpful to both of you, as it might bring to light some aspects that you previously overlooked, such as whether you are overly fixated on this relationship and getting caught up in minor issues. Of course, if you firmly believe that your thoughts are not misguided and the problem lies with your sister, and you still have affection for her, then give her time to realize and change on her own. All you can do is be understanding and forgiving, as long as it doesn't cross any personal boundaries, right? I hope your relationship with your sister improves over time.

question: Is it really difficult to practice empathy? Does true empathy exist in the world?
description: We often talk about putting ourselves in others' shoes, but I find it difficult to truly do so in reality. Even when I try to see things from others' perspectives, my own thoughts often mix in. To be honest, I find it challenging to understand what others are thinking, let alone trying to understand what they have gone through.

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP. You raised a good question that shows you have been making efforts to try to empathize with others, but you haven't found the right way yet. When we talk about empathy, it's actually about thinking, not feeling. No one can completely detach themselves from their own feelings and pretend to be someone else. However, effective empathy can help us understand others' feelings and perspectives. The purpose of empathy is not to guess others' feelings or prioritize them over our own. Empathy is a step in the information-gathering process before making decisions. By gathering information through various channels, we can understand what others are going through, and their emotions are part of that information. It's like playing chess, where you first need to understand the situation and know what is happening, how each move affects each piece. Only then can you think about how to move your own troops while considering how the opponent will move theirs. We often practice empathy to improve our relationships with others, so after understanding the situation, we still need empathy. Empathy may sound like you are forcing yourself to pretend to be the other person and imagine their emotions, but in reality, human emotions are universal. You just may not be aware of their connections and lack training in making such associations. For example, an elderly person who has lost their partner would be very sad, but as a young person with no experience of romantic relationships, you cannot fully empathize. You can only deduce the situation logically, that this elderly person has lost something important and is likely very sad. Though you can't fully understand their sadness, you can consider that they are feeling much worse than when you lost your beloved bicycle as a child. So, when you speak to the elderly person, you can offer sincere words of comfort, which is within the scope of your ability to empathize. The ability to empathize is positively correlated with our ability to recognize and manage our own emotions. That's why children with little life experience cannot empathize well and people who cannot manage their own emotions also find it difficult to empathize. One useful method is to practice naming our own emotions or describing the events when we experience emotions. This can help us gain deeper insights into our emotions. The application of empathy also depends on our attitude towards others. If you believe that humans are a shared destiny community, then you would be willing to empathize with the stories of people all over the world. But if you think you only care about your parents and family, then perhaps you wouldn't be willing to invest effort into empathizing with others. In short, whether it's empathy or simply putting oneself in another's shoes, it's all about making life better. If you have motivation, you will naturally gradually develop these skills through practice.

question: How to deal with spending money recklessly, lack of motivation, retaliating against parents' lack of understanding, and being disobedient?
description: Spending money recklessly, retaliating against my parents' lack of understanding, being disobedient, but my parents do not know that I am spending money recklessly, not making progress, or understand why I am unable to repay or make progress. What is wrong with me? Does this have any meaning?
keywords: Family, family relationships, parent communication, growing up process.

answers.answer_text: Hello! From your description, it can be seen that you have high expectations for yourself and your parents. You desire understanding from your parents for your inner thoughts, as well as wanting to enjoy the obedience and care from them like when you were younger. From the perspective of developmental psychology, the process of human mental activity is continuous from birth to death, and the same event has different meanings for children and adults. Therefore, the valence of psychological effects is also different. For example, when you were little, crying would lead your parents to guess the reasons behind it, such as hunger, thirst, tiredness, etc., and they would always provide you with psychological satisfaction. However, as we grow up, we can express our inner thoughts to our parents through language, but at this moment, parents may not be able to accurately understand our thoughts, or they may treat us in ways they believe are good for us, leading us to feel misunderstood and disobedient. In such situations, you want to get your parents' attention, so you engage in impulsive spending and a non-progressive lifestyle to draw their attention. But after implementing these methods, you find that your parents still haven't understood your inner thoughts, which to some extent makes you feel that they don't value you enough. However, you believe that your parents have noticed your impulsive spending and non-progressive behavior, thereby paying attention to your longing for understanding and love. Based on this analysis, I suggest that you have a good and open communication with your parents, specifying the aspects in which you feel they have not understood you and expressing your reasonable expectations of them. By opening your heart and conveying your inner thoughts to your parents, I believe this approach will gradually make you feel understood and loved by your parents, and hopefully provide solace for your inner grievances.

Hello! From the words between the lines, I can sense your troubles. I hope my answer can be helpful to you. Your current problem is that you spend money recklessly and lack motivation, as a way to retaliate against your parents' lack of understanding and compliance with you. From your question, I can sense that you don't want to behave like this. You are also dissatisfied with your current life and want to change it. This proves that you want to develop in a positive direction and improve your relationship with your parents. You don't know how to deal with your parents' lack of understanding and compliance, so you chose unwise methods such as reckless spending and lack of motivation, as a way to retaliate against them. At the time, this method may have satisfied a small desire in your heart, but afterwards, you mostly feel empty. However, your parents have no understanding of the reasons behind your actions, so this method is useless and meaningless. By doing this, your parents may also be dissatisfied with your behavior, further deteriorating your relationship. It must be said that parents generally have good intentions. Their starting point is always for our own good. In their eyes, we are always their children, so they cannot easily let go and give us autonomy. We may feel that we have grown up, thus resulting in conflicts with them. How can we make our parents understand us?
