description: During the meeting, I happened to overhear something that wasn't of much use to me. I glanced at my phone, and at that moment, my aunt didn't purposely lower her voice and said, "Playing with your phone is better than not attending the class at all." I felt extremely embarrassed internally and had a particularly awkward feeling, but I couldn't express it. I remembered that whether there were many or few people, I found it difficult to not care about other people's "negative comments" about me. Even if it was advice, I felt very upset about this hurdle. After hearing it before, I felt like I was in an "ice cellar," and it lasted for a long time. Do I have a psychological problem?
keywords: Growing up, improving one's character, personal qualities, and self-development.

answers.answer_text: We can start by understanding what negative evaluation means. Negative evaluation, in most cases, refers to others evaluating the methods of others from their own perspective, without considering the feelings of the individuals involved or trying to see the problem from the other person's point of view. Sometimes, their own perspective is also unfounded. Therefore, negative evaluations that we receive may not necessarily be true or useful. For example, when the questioner attends a meeting, we all know that people can get distracted. If we happen to look at our phones when the content doesn't concern us, the person might say that we should not come to class if we're just going to play with our phones. But where is the person's attention focused then? If the person is truly paying attention or if we are genuinely disrupting them, it's reasonable for them to remind us. However, if the person reacts so strongly simply because we glanced at them, it indirectly shows that they are not paying attention themselves. Moreover, they fail to take into account the emotions and reactions of the questioner and those around them. They don't make any effort to lower their voice. Wouldn't their behavior affect those around them? If the questioner were to tell the person to be more considerate and mindful of their impact, the person might respond with even more aggressive words and actions. In their worldview, everything they do is right, and any actions we take must meet their expectations to be considered correct. Therefore, we don't need to argue with them too much, and it's okay to selectively ignore some things they say. It's normal to care about others' evaluations of us. For example, when we go out, people may comment on our clothing and appearance. Some may say we look cool, others may say we look unconventional, some may even ask us for fashion advice, while others may gossip on the side. With so many evaluations, which one is correct? In fact, many things are not strictly right or wrong, but rather vary depending on people's perspectives. Therefore, the way we perceive things will also differ, making it difficult to determine who is right. We need to have a certain ability to discern, to know what truly benefits us and to differentiate between others' thoughtless comments. We need to find what is truly useful for ourselves. When faced with evaluations, we can consider the basis for why the other person said what they did, whether they truly considered our perspective, or if they genuinely have our best interests at heart. If the person is making baseless evaluations, regardless of whether they are positive or negative, we can simply ignore them. However, if the person is genuinely considering us and our feelings, we can humbly accept their input because these are the people who truly understand and love us. The world and I love you.

The title holder is not alone. Most of us are unwilling to hear others say bad things about us, and we instinctively argue back. So even if someone really says something bad about us, we may not necessarily change or do as they say. Each person should be responsible for their own life, and that is enough. Why would we interfere in other people's lives unless it is just about the issue at hand and does not involve personal attacks? For example, if a teacher tells you that you did a math problem wrong and need to correct it, then you just need to accept the correction. Let's say I am overweight and someone tells me, "Wow, you're really fat. You should lose weight instead of eating so much." Although what they say is right, would I feel happy? Definitely not. I would feel that they are being intrusive and hurtful, and I would feel upset. Whether I am fat or what I eat is none of their business. In the case of the title holder, when someone says to you, "You should listen in class instead of playing on your phone," my first impression is that it's disrespectful. Whether you listen in class or play on your phone is your own business, what does it have to do with her? Even if you end up not doing well in class because you were playing on your phone, it is your own responsibility, not hers. So it's purely unnecessary and it only annoys others. Does that mean you will start listening in class and admire her after hearing this comment? No, you just feel awkward and annoyed. Not expressing your opposition and being able to let it go is a display of knowledge and emotional intelligence. After all, if you start arguing, it will never end. So in many cases, pointing out someone's shortcomings directly and giving a negative evaluation is not a good way to communicate. Some of the high-emotional intelligence people around us would never directly make negative judgments about others. On the contrary, they would inspire others and let them recognize their own problems so that they are more willing to improve. They give the initiative to change back to the person involved instead of trying to force others to change. In regards to playing on the phone, a different approach could be asking, "Do you think you might miss some content in class while playing on your phone? Do you think your efficiency would be higher if you listen in class first and then look at your phone during free time?" This way, the choice is given to you, and the other person is actively guiding you to think in a direction that is beneficial to your own development, so you willingly change. The title holder needs to distinguish whether the negative evaluation from the other person is constructive or if they genuinely have your best interests in mind, or if they are just imposing their own values on you and making you feel uncomfortable. I think the people who truly love us will not make us feel awkward or upset. They will silently support us or kindly remind and inspire us. Usually, the people who make us feel upset are simply considering things from their own perspective and imposing their thoughts and beliefs onto us.

Hello! After reading your description, I'll share my feelings. I feel that you are a person with strong self-esteem and a clear mind. You are sensitive to negative emotions, which is a trait that you are not satisfied with at the moment. I don't think you have any psychological problems, but if you feel very uncomfortable, you can try to make changes. Firstly, for anyone, it is very common and necessary to feel negative emotions towards the attitudes and behaviors of others around them. On one hand, receiving negative emotions can improve our objective understanding of things, and on the other hand, it may make individuals realize that they are being judged negatively by others or by a group and need to improve. Just like depressive emotions, this is a signal. Maybe you feel that these negative signals are too strong and are disturbing your normal life or psychological balance. In that case, it would be worth exploring the reasons behind it. During the process of growing up, experiencing too much criticism and advice that is more aimed at people than at the matter itself may cause you to feel frustrated, resulting in being very sensitive to other people's criticism and advice. Or perhaps, lacking a family or school environment that can objectively recognize your strengths and weaknesses, or not cooperating with others to do things, can easily lead to an idealized self that is detached from the evaluations of others. When faced with suggestions or criticisms from others, you may have a bigger reaction. Regardless of the reasons, although the waves may be turbulent within you, your interpersonal relationships and actual life will not be significantly affected. This indicates that this psychological pattern is normal, but you may need to care more about yourself. As for how to change this state, my opinion is to observe more, communicate more, and engage in more cooperative activities. Observe the various character traits of people in life, how they handle criticism and advice they receive. Even if a person is often criticized, no one can take away their right to self-confidence. With so many people in life, praise, encouragement, ridicule, objective advice, expectations or indifference are all normal. Learn to differentiate between them and gradually explore ways that make you comfortable. When encountering something, share your thoughts with others and interact more. Through this, you will have a more realistic understanding of yourself, interpersonal relationships, and objective matters. With the premise of loving yourself, the closer things are to reality, the stronger the power they give you and the greater psychological energy they provide. During the process of cooperation, feedback is more frequent and mainly focused on the matter at hand, so experiencing this more can also greatly benefit your future life. The process of transforming from a cocoon to a butterfly is never comfortable. It's great that you recognize that something feels off and are willing to face it. Your mindset is one of balance, and you don't have any psychological problems. It's also great that you are willing to adjust. Just like the balance of weights, it is impossible to reach another balance in one go. You need to constantly try and actively seek positive feedback from the outside. I believe in you and I love you!

Hello! When I hear the words "negative evaluation," I feel like I am not being recognized or accepted. I hate myself for not being good enough and I feel unjustly treated. If I try to express my feelings, I worry that others will think I'm just making excuses and I also feel embarrassed and ashamed. But this kind of emotion follows me everywhere, affecting my daily life, work, and interpersonal relationships. It feels like when we were children, always studying or doing things cautiously. It was normal if we did well and our parents didn't say anything, but if we made a mistake or got distracted, they would scold us loudly or criticize us in front of others. Because we were not good at expressing ourselves, we could only silently endure the grievance. Actually, our parents love us very much, but their upbringing has made it difficult for them to express their love. They only want to teach us how to do things out of a sense of love and to prepare us for the future. However, they don't know that their way of expressing love can also hurt their children, even though it is not their original intention. When faced with such situations, stop and gently tell yourself, what does he/she want me to do by saying that? For example, when Auntie said that sentence, she wanted me to pay attention in class because she thinks it's good for me. This is her perspective, her intention is good, and I understand her. But whether or not to listen is up to me, it has nothing to do with her. This way, you can let go of your anxiety, allow yourself to use your phone, and also appreciate her good intentions without minding her words. Every time a similar situation happens, pause, first acknowledge and accept yourself, and ask yourself, what do I want to do? Wish you all the best!

Hello, questioner. Upon seeing your question, you must have your own reasons for these behaviors that others have pointed out about you. These are things that others cannot understand. When faced with advice from others, it's normal to feel uncomfortable, which is perfectly reasonable. Having these emotions does not determine whether you are good or bad. So, first of all, you need to accept and allow yourself to have these emotions. Then, assess whether the advice from others is suitable for your situation. Embrace yourself, understand yourself, and you will have the strength to face the advice from others and your own emotions. These are some personal thoughts, hoping to give you some ideas.

You can try to imagine the scene when your aunt says to you, "Playing on your phone is worse than not coming to class," and you respond, "It's none of your business!" Imagine that your heart no longer feels blocked, but rather feels smooth and pleasant. It seems that your aunt said the "right thing" at the "right time." Obviously, for you, you cannot refuse this "rightness." The result is that your boundaries are violated. So the reason you feel so upset, the reason you can't move on, is because you have been violated and don't know how to defend yourself. Because you are trapped in the discourse of "rightness". You have also said that you think it's useless to pay attention in class when you feel the meeting is not relevant. You have a clear judgment and understanding of yourself, and you don't need others to teach or judge you. Only in this way can you "grow out" the ability to control yourself. Good luck to you!

question: Lovesickness, feeling like there is no escape, how should I face it with what kind of mindset?
description: I don't want to like her, but I can't do it alone. I have gone far away, leaving my hometown and cutting off contact with the people around me. I thought that a new place and new things could alleviate this condition, but in the past two years, I have gained nothing. I have returned to my hometown again, and it has changed. The county where I lived for 10 years no longer has the taste I remember. It has become bigger and more prosperous, but it feels unfamiliar to me. I haven't grown up, and I am still tormented by lovesickness. I feel like I can't escape it anymore. I know that I love her but can't have her. Many years ago, I tried to avoid my liking for her, but I was tormented by longing. We were desk mates back then, and after being separated into different classes, I continuously tried to reconnect with her. I confessed my feelings, but I was still tormented by longing. When facing her, contacting her, or embracing her, my purpose was to find her flaws. Every time I found something wrong with her, I would experience a momentary relief. But then another thought appeared: all of these actions were driven by my own efforts, they were not genuine and not real. It was just something I wanted to believe. The image of her in my heart remains unchanged. Once again, I discovered her flaws, and the cycle repeats. Some people may ask why I don't pursue her. Well, I also want to, because if I were to obtain her, then I would no longer be tormented by lovesickness. But then, how should I face the situation next time? It's tormenting.

answers.answer_text: Got it, you will no longer long for it. It seems to be saying: Longing, to some extent, brings you some wonderful experiences. This makes you afraid of not longing anymore. So, what are the "benefits" that longing brings you? This is worth thinking about. After exploring, maybe you can see if there are other ways to replace the "longing sickness". After all, the "longing sickness" has tormented you for many, many years.

question: Feeling scared and useless when comparing oneself to others, what should I do?
description: At first, my friends were not as good as me, but later they all developed better than me while I remained unsuccessful. The neighbors always bring it up, and I feel very sad. I feel so useless.

answers.answer_text: Hello. It seems that your neighbors are not doing so well either. In this era, successful people encourage and inspire others to progress, while unsuccessful people talk behind others' backs, hoping that others don't do better than themselves. Therefore, there is actually no need to care about the idle talk of these people. On the contrary, nobody is perfect, so you should analyze your own strengths and learn more skills. Get along well with yourself. As the saying goes, "After thirty years on the east bank of the river, after thirty years on the west bank." You need to find your own path in life, work hard, and stick to it. Life is a marathon, not a sprint, and effort is likely to be proportional to reward. Anyway, keep working hard day after day!

question: The workload is enormous, I am on the verge of a breakdown, and there are risks in both resigning or not resigning, what should I choose?
description: The workload is extremely heavy and there are still unfinished old tasks when new ones come in. The clients are constantly chasing after me as if it's a matter of life and death. I feel like I owe a loan shark with the long-term pressure causing extreme anxiety and even breakdown. There are some minor physical issues, such as headaches, stuffy ears, and chest pain, which I believe are all influenced by emotions. However, none of the following three solutions seem feasible, so I am in a dilemma. 1. Not quitting the job - my current emotional state is particularly bad and I'm worried it will affect my pregnancy. I'm already over 30 and don't want to wait for a few more years to have a child. 2. Quitting the job - as a married woman who hasn't had children yet, I am not well-regarded in the workplace. What if I get pregnant within a few months? Will everyone think I'm the kind of person who specifically joins a new company to get pregnant and deceive for maternity leave? People generally wouldn't say much if I were pregnant in my familiar old company, but it might not be the case in a new company. 3. Quitting the job, getting pregnant and giving birth, and then finding a new job - I would lose at least a year or more of income and would have to bear a large sum for insurance on my own. It doesn't seem worthwhile, and I feel like I'm trapped... If there were good methods to reduce work overload, improve work efficiency, or release stress, I would prefer to have a child in my current job. Thank you for your response.

answers.answer_text: Hi! The main concerns mentioned in the text are: 1. High work pressure, 2. The pressure of being pregnant at the same time, and 3. The importance given to how the company views pregnancy. Based on the psychological knowledge mentioned in your description, it seems to be related to the issue of perception. We tend to automatically filter out important things and ignore unimportant ones, which happens unconsciously. In the description, it can be felt that the person prioritizes work responsibilities, followed by how the company views them, and finally the pressure of being pregnant. Is that correct? Of course, pregnancy is more important to you, but from the description, it seems that work responsibilities and colleagues' opinions are given more importance than the pregnancy itself, to the extent that they influence your decision to become pregnant. Personally, I suggest adjusting the priorities. Your psychological issues might be better resolved if you prioritize your own pregnancy first, work responsibilities second, and colleagues' opinions third. This way, you can focus on preparing for pregnancy, manage your workload during busy times, and the company might consider your actual situation instead of being too demanding. Regarding work responsibilities, do your best and strive to be at peace with yourself, as not everything can go perfectly. We need to clarify our own coping strategies, act boldly, and that is being at peace with ourselves, don't you think? As for the outcome, no one can give a definite answer, but if we choose the best way and it doesn't work out, other options might not work either, right? Feel free to message me for any questions or uncertainties.

Hello~ Thank you for inviting me to see your confusion. I feel that it also belongs to the difficulties faced by modern professional women, namely the problems of employment and childbirth. It can be seen that you are able to objectively, clearly, and thoroughly analyze the facts of your current situation, as well as a series of potential problems you may face in the future. Perhaps it is because of the "dilemma" you are currently facing, combined with the pressure from your job, that has led to extreme anxiety and even breakdown! Your body is also experiencing some minor ailments, such as headaches, ear fullness, and chest pains. When our emotions fluctuate, it can have an impact on both our physical and mental states, and our physical condition will also react accordingly, resulting in a psychosomatic disorder, also known as a psychophysiological reaction. I recommend that you relax and adjust your mindset in order to approach your problems more rationally. What do you think? From the three points you listed, it may seem like a question of how to choose, but upon deeper understanding, another layer of issues can be seen. The key issue may be related to your anxiety. Usually, when we face difficulties and decisions, we often think that as long as we make a choice, we can avoid anxiety and solve the problem easily. However, the reality is that no matter what choice we make, whether it is to resign or not, or to have a child or not, we cannot escape anxiety, and new problems will always arise, making it difficult to have a foolproof plan. After all, we know deep down that everything, including people, is constantly changing. Anxiety is a fundamental human emotion that develops in the process of struggling with and adapting to the environment for survival. In recent years, some newly married couples have faced the dilemma of survival and childbirth. Due to various limitations in their lives, they have experienced practical concerns about parenting. As for your own situation, only you know best how to weigh the pros and cons. I think our answer can only serve as a reference. In the face of reality, it is often impossible to achieve a perfect result of having the best of both worlds. There must be sacrifices in order to obtain something. It may be worthwhile to quiet your mind, listen to your true thoughts, and consult with your spouse and family. After all, if there are family members to share the burden, there may be more suitable solutions. Regardless of the choice you make, as long as you have no regrets and take responsibility for your choices, bravely face the consequences of your decisions, you can strive to live a good life, and your family will support you. Keep going! Wishing you happiness~.

Hello. It's a pleasure to give you some advice. From your description, I can sense that you have a certain level of self-awareness and have started to plan for your future. At the beginning, you mentioned that there are a lot of things to handle and they often give you a headache, increasing your stress level. Based on your current feelings, there are a few points that need to be addressed:

- The constant workload is indeed overwhelming, and it makes me wonder about your position in the company. It is important to consider whether the workload is inherently this heavy for your position. From a rational and objective perspective, what are the responsibilities associated with your position? How does it differ from your current situation?
- I can tell that you are a capable person, but perhaps you tend to help with tasks that are not originally your responsibility out of kindness, which in turn exhausts you. 
- Each person's career choice and company selection requires objective evaluation. For you, this job didn't come easily, and while we should cherish it, we should also pay attention to other impacts it may have on us, such as the physical symptoms and emotional instability you mentioned.
- When it comes to the intersection of health and work, of course we hope to have a balance between the two. But currently, work is outweighing health and threatening it.
- If we want to achieve a balance between the two, we need to make decisions in our work from a perspective that considers both, instead of thinking, "This job is urgent, but I'm not feeling well today. However, the client is in a hurry, so work should take priority. I can't afford to lose my job..."
- I don't know if you have ever experienced what I mentioned earlier, but many times people worry about being fired, so they compromise on certain things. However, when this way of thinking becomes a habit, we forget to consider the impact it has on our health.
- So, we can approach it from a different angle. If we give our best efforts to the work we undertake, does it pose a threat to our health? The balance between our job responsibilities and personal life is something you need to ponder at this moment.
- You also mentioned plans to get pregnant and have a baby. What are your thoughts on preparing for conception? You are right in saying that if your own condition is not good, it could affect the baby. Planning for pregnancy requires considering your personal condition. 
- In your second point, you mentioned the plan to change companies. The level of satisfaction and suitability of your current job will be answered by your inner self in various ways. If you are concerned about being pregnant during the initial stages of a new job, you can express your thoughts during the interview. If the other party cares about this situation, then we can consider other options. This way, we won't be fixated on how the new company perceives us.
- Finally, let's talk about your third point. From marriage to parenthood, this stage takes a relatively long time and with the arrival of a newborn, there is a lot of new knowledge waiting for us to learn. Many women may feel anxious and fearful as a result. After considering life and career planning, I believe your future path will become clearer. Moreover, there are many ways to earn money. And raising children is a shared responsibility between you and your husband, so it is necessary to communicate these concerns with him. Your thinking is meticulous, but don't forget that your husband is by your side and will face the future together. I hope you can find yourself and be true to yourself. Wish you everything goes well.

The three options you have all make certain assumptions that may not necessarily align with reality. The prerequisite for having a child in your current job is that you are able to conceive. The prerequisite for moving to a new job and having a child is that the new job is better or at least less stressful than your current job, and that you can find such a job and the employer is willing to hire you. The prerequisite for quitting your job and having a child is also that you are able to conceive. There are also other possible scenarios. If your current job is extremely busy, there are two possibilities: either everyone is busy or you are the only one. If it's the latter, it is possible that your efficiency is low and you need to learn from others how to improve your efficiency and prioritize tasks. If you become pregnant in your current job, there is a question of whether you will be able to leave work on time every day and only complete the tasks that can be finished by then, without doing any extra work. Can you find your husband or lawyer to communicate with your boss or the company when they give you a hard time, even to the point of confrontation? If you can't, staying in your current job while pregnant is also a problem, as you are concerned about not getting pregnant. If you do get pregnant, you may also worry about the workload being too much for the child. It seems like a good choice to get pregnant in a new job, but the prerequisite is that you can find a job where the other party is willing to hire you, and it basically comes down to a matter of face. Can you let go of your ego? Quitting your job to get pregnant doesn't seem to have such a high cost. In terms of insurance, you are currently paying based on your basic salary, but if you stay at home, you can pay based on the minimum wage. It may be around 1000 yuan per month, which is not a lot of money. If it's a much better environment, it's worth considering. This is the legendary plan that can't keep up with changes and one's own ideas, and may deviate from reality. The plan is as follows: first, go to the hospital with your husband and get a physical examination, and adjust accordingly if either of you has any issues. In daily life, you can adjust your own state through psychological counseling and massages. Once you have sorted out these few points, you can try to get pregnant in your current job in the future. For example, after three or six months. But if the company gives you a hard time after getting pregnant, then you should have your husband and lawyer intervene, but firmly insist on leaving work on time and only completing tasks that can be finished by then. If you can't get pregnant, then consider options 2 and 3. For option 2, you need to find a job that you like and that is willing to hire you and where you can have a leisurely life. Once you find such a job, you can start trying to get pregnant. And if anyone says anything, just tell them to let you work well after having the child, or consider changing if it's not suitable. For option 3, just stay at home and pay social insurance based on the minimum wage. It won't have a huge impact in a year. That's pretty much it. But the prerequisite for all options 1, 2, and 3 is that you must be able to get pregnant.

If you can avoid resigning, do not quit easily. See if you can make adjustments. You can try making a timetable of your monthly work tasks and time allocation to see if it is a problem with your work methods or if your boss has assigned an excessive workload. If it is a problem with your work methods, you should usually pay attention to the following points: 1. Develop the habit of making a good work plan every day, plan the day's key tasks, and spend time on valuable things. 2. Allocate time according to the priority of the tasks, deal with the most important and difficult tasks first each day, and handle temporary, trivial, and simple tasks during fragmented time. 3. Do not procrastinate and leave all the work to be completed on the same day. 4. Do not hold the mentality of wanting to finish all the work, do not attempt to evenly distribute time, as time should be a system of choices and sacrifices. Choose important and valuable things and discard the unimportant ones. 5. Have personal goals and pursuits outside of work. If you only have a work plan and no other interests or goals, you will feel like all your time can be used for overtime work. This will lead to choosing easy and less important tasks when facing a pile of work, and it will also make you lose the motivation to actively handle important tasks. If it is a problem with the workload assigned by your boss, and you are indeed burdened with too much work, you can talk to your boss or supervisor about this issue and discuss it from the perspective of the company's interests. Explain that you are willing to occasionally take on excessive workload, such as during emergencies, but you cannot continue like this. If you can propose a solution, such as persuading your boss to assign some of your work to others, or finding other compromises, that would be great. Do not endure excessive workload in the long term as it will greatly damage your health. If your boss has not considered providing any assistance, please consider leaving.

If the above three options are a "dead end" for the original poster, can you continue to look for a fourth or fifth solution? The physical and mental problems are already very serious, I wonder if the original poster has seen a doctor? If you see a doctor, they should be able to issue a sick leave slip for at least three days, right? Then it's important to follow the doctor's advice and rest at home for a few days. On the one hand, give yourself a break physically and mentally, and on the other hand, see what happens to the company and clients without the presence of the original poster. Will things not progress? Many studies have shown that exercise is very helpful in relieving depression and anxiety. Exercise is not just about running or lifting weights, more gentle activities like swimming, yoga, and Pilates are also effective. The original poster might as well give it a try and find a suitable method, time, and pace for themselves. In addition, meditation and mindfulness training can be very helpful as well. There are many online courses available, many lasting only twenty to thirty minutes a day, or even just ten minutes a day, to completely relax both the body and mind. I highly recommend it as it will be very helpful in relieving various stresses. Keep going! I believe the original poster can find other ways to overcome difficulties. The most important thing is to take the first step.

question: "Counselors may question what the visitor is saying for what reasons?"
description: Today I had another unpleasant consultation experience. I miss the counselor I met before and think I should go back to find her. It's really annoying when someone leads the conversation in a negative direction. For example, they asked if I've ever thought about suicide, and I said no. What about self-harm? No. Auditory hallucinations? Do I really not have any? But I truly don't. And at the end, it seemed like they exaggerated the level of my distress, describing me as helpless and troubled in life, but seeking counseling is a sign of strength. In reality, I receive a lot of affirmation in my work. I just want to push myself harder and achieve personal growth. I don't think I am completely incapable. Afterwards, I am really curious where this perception comes from. Is it my way of expressing myself? Or is it their own experiences? But I don't think they are a perceptive person, so I wouldn't dare to ask. I'm afraid they might attack me in self-defense.
keywords: Growth, stress management, work and study, self-acceptance.

answers.answer_text: Hello, I'm not sure what you have been through. How the conversation with the counselor went, it seems like you have been receiving psychological counseling for some time. I applaud your wisdom. When we are unable to break free from our established patterns, we often face many difficulties. It is necessary to seek help from professionals to help us gain perspective on our experiences and to move forward from our past, so that we can develop new ways of dealing with similar problems in the future. I applaud you for having your own methods. Regarding the statement "It's annoying to be led in a negative direction. For example, when asked if I have ever thought of suicide, I said no. What about self-harm? No. Auditory hallucinations? Do I really not have any? But I truly don't." From this description, I sense that the counselor's question may have been influenced by what you said earlier, or it may not be directly related to you. That is the counselor's issue, so there is no need to blame yourself or feel that you are inadequate. I think you are doing well right now and have a clear understanding of yourself. However, if the counselor's questions were as you described, then in my personal opinion, this counselor may not be sufficiently professional as they have their own issues to deal with that are unrelated to you. It is understandable that this may have made you uncomfortable. Sending you a hug. In your comments afterwards, I sense a positive and optimistic attitude from you, which may be influenced by your experiences. Let's see if psychological counseling has had an effect in helping you gain a new understanding of yourself. Afterward, I was curious about where the counselor's feelings came from. Was it from my way of expressing myself or their own experiences? But I feel like the counselor is not a psychologically sensitive person, so they wouldn't ask. To protect myself, I'm afraid of being attacked by them. I sense that you are a person who loves to reflect and be aware, as you have such thoughts after counseling. And you are wise enough to find ways to get answers. However, I want to make it clear that I am not the counselor mentioned earlier. Feelings, experiences, and counseling methods are all unique to each individual, so the first half of the paragraph can only represent my own thoughts. Regarding the last question, I sense that if you choose to continue counseling with this counselor, you may need to start over and re-establish the relationship. Of course, if you choose another counselor, you will also need to build a new relationship. I encourage you to reflect on what happened when you decided to not continue counseling with the previous counselor and switched to a new one.

question: My mother has chronic nephritis, which is a serious illness that has weakened her significantly. What should I do?
description: My mother has chronic nephritis, and her condition is very serious and weak. She said she doesn't want to live anymore. What should I do? I really don't know what to do. I comfort her every day and take care of her, but she is still suffering a lot from the severe illness.

answers.answer_text: Rest well and take care of yourself and your mother. Do more good deeds and blessings will multiply. Stay united with your mother. Believe that she will get better and show her that belief. Right now, it's tough, but there is still hope. Don't be sad. Also, ask the doctor if there is anything you can do to recover and take care of yourself. Be optimistic and think about your health and your mother's health. Find someone to share the burden with. Remember, your mother is strong, and I believe she will get better. If you're not afraid, then I'm even more convinced. People like you can overcome any illness. Additionally, can you read some heartwarming and hopeful books to your mother? I just want to help in any way I can.

question: I had been in a relationship for exactly two years, but it ended. I feel very suffocated and upset.
description: Love lasted for exactly two years and ended. I knew it wasn't right, there were many dissatisfactions, and we often argued to the point of breaking down. There were even instances of betrayal. But why is it that, even after the breakup, I still feel suppressed and upset?

answers.answer_text: OP, hello~ First, give you a warm hug. I really understand how you feel. Almost many people have similar experiences, that is, when we really break up with someone we don't like, we find ourselves feeling sad. This is not a mistake in our own feelings, nor does it mean that our personality is like this. Actually, feeling sad has nothing to do with the previous experiences, whether good or bad. First of all, no matter what happened before, we have experienced the departure of someone who originally belonged to us. It's just like when something, no matter how bad it is, is lost, we will still feel sad for a while. Because we have experienced the process of losing something that belongs to us, and this process is the fundamental reason that makes us sad. Therefore, there is no need for you, OP, to feel dissatisfied or unable to accept this kind of emotion. The best way is to accept this emotion and try to get out of it as soon as possible. Enter the next stage of love. Of course, we can also use this time to do something we like, enrich ourselves, improve ourselves, and make ourselves more fulfilled. These are all pretty good ways to regulate our emotions. In addition, doing more outdoor sports can also help us regulate our own emotions. Best wishes~.

question: I belong to the typical type of student who is textbook-oriented. What should I do if I am isolated?
description: Usually I am more introverted, I am a typical studious student, but my grades are only average. I have heard some classmates mocking me in private, saying that I am working hard for nothing, lacking talent, and stupid. Over time, I also stopped participating in any collective activities. Even though we are in the same class, I feel like I and my classmates are living on two parallel lines. But I can't bring myself to approach others. However, this suppressive life makes me very uncomfortable. Is there any way to have the best of both worlds?
keywords: Interpersonal relationships, roommates and classmates, interpersonal boundaries.

answers.answer_text:
Title owner, hello, give me a hug~
After reading your description, it seems that you are in a state of being excluded from your class. Initially, you may have wanted to focus on studying on your own, but later your behavior was not understood by your classmates. When you wanted to integrate into the group, no one came to you proactively. You are now very conflicted and upset. I really sympathize with your situation. Based on your description, you don't want to continue living a suppressed life and you don't want to actively show kindness to your classmates. I can understand your reluctance to take the initiative. Perhaps those classmates who mocked you are not easy to get along with. When you try to show goodwill, they may not be willing to accept you, which would make you even more upset. Maybe you can make friends with those classmates who share similar interests and ideas, such as class leaders, class monitors, and study committee members, who are generally more friendly and concerned about studying. Maybe you will feel more comfortable studying with them. From your description, "I am usually introverted, a typical studious student, but my grades are only average," I see a small problem. You work hard, but your grades don't seem to improve. Perhaps you can try a different study method, using a more open and communicative mindset to discuss and learn with people around you. This may yield better results than your current study method.

question: I would feel that I have angered the other person, how can I change my introverted and sensitive personality?
description: It is in a foreign language.

answers.answer_text: Hello, OP! Hugs to you~ From your description, it seems like you are particularly sensitive and suspicious when it comes to interpersonal relationships. You always try to please others and feel exhausted. You're also particularly sensitive to awkward atmospheres, and I truly sympathize with your experiences. Based on your description, "I always feel like I have made the other person angry, and then I start to please them or torture myself." It is clear that you possess a strong sense of empathy and are very perceptive of emotions. This aspect of your personality has both positive and negative implications–it is beneficial for those around you, but it can be detrimental to yourself. I believe you have also realized that the process of interacting with others often feels burdensome, even though others may feel well taken care of. I suggest you try to suppress the desire to constantly please others, and replacing it with silence instead of constant explanations may be much better.

question: The pressure of the entrance examination is too overwhelming, and my family is too strict. I feel like I never want to study again.
description: I have been studying for the postgraduate entrance examination for a month. These past two days, I have been feeling restless and annoyed, and I don't want to study anymore. But my dad still asks me almost every day how my studying is going and if everything is okay. It's really my mom who, on the day I gave myself a break, said she would take me to the library to study. I am truly fed up with studying at this point. I am taking the postgraduate entrance examination for myself, and I just want to leisurely follow my own plan. But they always like to force me, and it's really annoying to have a life that's controlled and managed. They say they give me freedom, but they manage me strictly. I really want to quickly earn money and leave this home. Today, I was chatting with a guy I have a good impression of, and his only impression of me was, "You study really seriously." I didn't say anything, but he asked if my family is strict with me. Do I really exude a sense of pressure even in casual conversations?... But I really hate my current environment where everyone just brings me stress. I feel like I no longer want to study, and I have lost interest in anything.
keywords: Growth, stress management, work and study.

answers.answer_text: After reading the question, I have three "don't understand" in my mind: your parents don't understand you, you don't understand that boy, and that boy doesn't understand you (if the environment you mentioned that only brings you pressure includes that boy). It is not uncommon for parents to misunderstand their children, and the child is especially distressed, but I have also heard parents complaining that they cannot communicate with their children. I am not sure about the specific situation in your family, nor how you communicate with your parents. If I were in the middle, I would play a role as a bridge between the child and the parents to some extent, but as an outsider, I generally suggest seeking someone in the family who can convince the parents to do the job of influencing their mindset. You don't understand that boy, it may be more accurate to use the word "understand". He asked, "Are your parents strict?" I don't know how you replied, but you can express your feelings here that the chat seems to reveal pressure, indicating that you haven't confirmed with the other person why he would think so. I don't know how you define this boy, a friend? Acquaintance? An acquaintance who may develop into a friend? No matter which kind, if the communication is not smooth, the relationship will become distant. For example, maybe he just wants to know if the reason why you study seriously is because your parents are strict? I don't know as an outsider, but as the person involved, and with the opportunity to know it, you still don't know, so this matter can't be expanded. In addition, you said you have feelings for him. Under normal circumstances, when someone we have feelings for asks us about ourselves, do you think this is a form of caring? If you also agree with this point of view, then when someone we have feelings for cares about us, and you are lamenting how bad your situation is, it most likely indicates two points: First, it really is bad; second, in front of him, showing the real or bad you, even if this situation is only temporary and accidental, you are not allowing it. Maybe you need to try to allow this version of yourself to exist and be seen. That boy doesn't understand you, because there is not enough information, so it is impossible to judge how much he wants to understand you. If he actively shares himself and asks for your opinion or personal situation, and still doesn't understand you, it is because you feel that the relationship between the two has not yet reached the point where you can open up so much information and emotion. At this time, it is understandable that the other person does not understand you. If the other person has not done similar things, it is normal that he doesn't understand you, because how can someone understand another person without actively trying to understand them. In conclusion, the relationship is not in place, and it is unrealistic to expect the other person to do what they should do when the relationship is in place. Another possibility is that it's not really a lack of understanding, but a lack of communication. I think this is the case for most people, besides improving communication skills, it also requires communication between both parties. With all these reasons that you cannot accept, and because of your postgraduate entrance examination, how is it possible to still want to study? Take them down one by one!

question: I'm afraid to go back to the life where I lacked self-confidence. Does this kind of psychological suggestion have any meaning?
description: I used to be a child without confidence. Due to family and personality reasons, I am now aware that I need to change. However, I often remind myself to be confident because I am afraid of returning to my previous life of lack of confidence. My previous life caused me to miss out on many opportunities and the joy of life. I would like to ask if this kind of psychological suggestion is meaningful. Or should I fundamentally avoid such compulsive consciousness and instead focus on practical actions? How should I deal with this frequent occurrence of compulsive consciousness?
keywords: Growing up, self-growth, work and learning, self-acceptance.

answers.answer_text: Hello! Hug to you! From your statement, I understand that due to family and personality reasons, you have become an insecure child. First of all, it can be affirmed that you have been striving to become more confident. Regardless of the results, we are always on the journey. It can be seen that life experiences have had a great impact on you. In order to change yourself, you often remind yourself to be confident. Personally, I think this kind of psychological suggestion does have a certain effect and meaning. Just like in our lives, if we want to do something, if we don't remind ourselves, we may forget to do it. Doing so may be telling ourselves to distance ourselves from the past and constantly remind ourselves to become outstanding and confident. Reminding ourselves repeatedly does not necessarily mean that we have obsessive thoughts. Just like some people, they are afraid of forgetting to drink water, so they remind themselves through alarm clocks, sticky notes, and repeatedly reminding themselves in their minds. Obsessive thoughts refer to thoughts, images, emotions, or intentions that repeatedly enter the patient's conscious domain. These thoughts, images, emotions, or intentions are meaningless, unnecessary, or redundant for the patient. The patient realizes that these are his own mental activities and wants to get rid of them, but is powerless and therefore feels very distressed. So, for you, do these suggestions bring you trouble? Secondly, combining actual actions and self-reminders may achieve better results! When we remind ourselves to be confident at all times, we can also demonstrate it through actual actions. Gradually, we can develop a habit, so even if we don't remind ourselves, we may still exude confidence. Finally, when obsessive thoughts occur frequently, it may cause you certain troubles. When it becomes a problem, you can try to reduce attention to this matter by ignoring it, which can help to alleviate anxiety. I hope the above content can bring you some help. Best wishes!

Hello, I carefully read your question and from it I understand that your current struggle is with lack of self-confidence and using self-affirmation as a coping mechanism, but you're worried that this compulsive affirmation may become another problem and you're not sure how to handle it. I would like to answer your question from a few different perspectives.

["Positive psychological affirmation can to some extent enhance self-confidence"] First and foremost, it is certain that you have already made active efforts and changes to overcome your lack of self-confidence. Regardless of the method you choose, this is a great step towards personal growth. Positive psychological affirmation does indeed have an effect on one's mentality. I believe you have also studied some psychology and have learned about and understood this method. In the cognitive therapy field, there is a treatment method called "positive reinforcement", which is essentially a form of positive psychological affirmation. Over time, this type of affirmation can subtly change one's behavior. Therefore, the method you are currently using is worth continuing.

["The definition of compulsion depends on your subjective experience"] Another concern you have is whether this repeated positive affirmation may become a compulsive behavior. Regarding this issue, it is important to recognize that many people have repetitive behaviors, and many professions involve repetitive actions. For example, doctors develop a habit of washing their hands repeatedly to ensure cleanliness and self-protection during patient visits. However, this does not mean that handwashing is a compulsive behavior, as it is a professional requirement. Unless such behavior becomes distressing for the individual and significantly impacts their normal life and work, it cannot be considered a problem.

["Recommendation to use various methods to improve self-confidence"] Positive affirmation is a good method, but there are also other ways to help improve self-confidence. For example, you can achieve small accomplishments in an area where you are good at and receive recognition from people around you. Accumulate confidence from these activities where you easily gain a sense of accomplishment, as confidence can spread and grow. When this accumulation reaches a certain level, you will experience confidence in various situations. I hope the above response is helpful to you.

Come, let me give you a warm hug. I'm glad that you have realized your issues and seen your lack of confidence. It's a healing process to acknowledge these things. You can definitely become a confident and sunny person. You mentioned that you are aware of the need for change but afraid of going back to your old, insecure life. In that case, you can try dividing your life into two stages - one where you lacked confidence in the past, and one where you are now aware of the need to be confident. Step back and observe these two different stages of yourself from an outsider's perspective. First, think about what you would say to your past self if your present self could go back and accompany the insecure version of you. Now think about what you, as an observer, would say to your past self. We can't change what has already happened, but we can change how we interpret those past experiences. For example, if you lacked confidence in the past because you didn't feel attractive enough, you can now tell your past self that appearance has limited impact on a person, especially as you gain more life experience. Try changing your perception of those things that made you lack confidence from different perspectives. You will realize that they were not as significant as you thought. Also, remember that you will continue to change and become more confident and cheerful in the future. Make peace with your past self who was tangled and awkward, as well as with the people and experiences that made you lack confidence. Say goodbye to the insecure version of yourself. You can keep her in your consciousness, in a corner of your memory, like a little secret place. Perhaps, you may still feel the need to talk to her, or maybe gradually you will forget about her existence. As for your mention of forcing yourself to be confident, I personally believe it can be helpful. Sometimes, by pretending something, like pretending to be successful, you actually become successful. When you pretend, your behavior unconsciously changes, and this gradual transformation brings you closer to becoming that hoped-for version of yourself.

Hello. Let's recap your issue. You mentioned that due to lack of confidence in the past, you have started to make changes and now frequently experience intrusive thoughts telling you to be confident. You are well aware that this is because you are afraid of reverting back to your previous state, which is causing you distress. First of all, this suggestion is meaningful, and as you have already mentioned, you do not want to return to the state of lack of confidence in the past. You are well aware that lack of confidence will cause you to miss out on many joys in life. This may also include your fear of the past, which indicates that there may be unresolved emotions from the past that are affecting you. In fact, this may not necessarily be entirely bad. You are troubled by the intrusive thoughts and may have some negative emotional experiences, but it is precisely because you are worried about going back to the past that you are telling yourself to be confident. This demonstrates that you have a positive psychological state. You want to change and become more confident, hoping to improve yourself. This is a positive energy. In fact, the emergence of these emotions and thoughts may be due to the fact that you have not truly accepted yourself. You are very afraid of the return of your past lack of confidence, which actually represents your rejection of it. However, the past version of yourself lacking confidence was a real existence, and the current version of yourself wanting to become confident is also a real existence. They are both a part of you. Maybe you can try accepting the insecure part of yourself, embracing it, and mourning for your past self. Tell yourself that it was just the past, those negative experiences and feelings have already ended. Say goodbye to them. In daily life, you can try activities that can boost your confidence, do things you are good at, cultivate hobbies, establish more connections with others, and enhance your social skills. Give yourself more encouragement, acknowledge your progress and efforts, set some rewards, and cheer yourself on. Learn to love yourself. Keep going, your efforts will bring about change. Believe that you can become more confident and better. Hope this helps you.

Hello there: The old me lacked confidence, so I missed out on a lot of opportunities. Now you want to regain your confidence, so you often engage in self-affirmation. But at the same time, you worry that this self-affirmation will lead to obsessive thinking. I can totally understand your feelings, and I hope the following words can be helpful to you. 1. Positive self-affirmation can enhance confidence. In psychology, emotions, cognition, and behavior are interconnected. Self-affirmation refers to when you allow a certain concept to influence yourself, exerting a certain impact on your psychology, thereby affecting your emotions and willpower. This is actually using cognition to influence our behavior. And with repeated positive self-affirmation, it can also affect our behavior and emotions. Therefore, positive self-affirmation can to some extent enhance our confidence. 2. The repetition of positive self-affirmation does not become compulsive thinking. Compulsive thinking is defined as follows: ① During certain periods of this obstacle, experiencing repetitive, persistent, intrusive, and unnecessary thoughts, impulses, or intentions, most individuals will experience significant anxiety or distress; ② Individuals try to ignore or suppress such thoughts, impulses, or intentions, or neutralize them with other thoughts or behaviors (such as through certain compulsive behaviors). Positive psychological suggestions will not cause distress for you, so they themselves do not belong to the category of compulsive thinking. And repeating this behavior is also a necessary condition for psychological suggestion to take effect. Some words may not have any impact when you first say them, but after multiple repetitions, they will generate the power to create waves. Over time, as you develop the habit, your cognition will also change. 3. Transforming awareness into action is the goal of cognitive change, to enhance our confidence. And the purpose of enhancing confidence is to do more things well and make ourselves better. When you previously experienced feelings of insecurity, what were your thoughts? Did you fear that you would not do well in this matter? Did you start fearing the negative outcomes even before you started? Insecurity stems from fear. And the best way to deal with fear is to take action. For example, one of your manifestations of insecurity is being afraid to speak in front of many people. In that case, you can use systematic desensitization to gradually reduce the level of fear, starting with doing things that cause you the least fear. When you actually start doing these things, you may find that you are capable of doing them well. And the positive results of these actions will also give you more confidence and certainty to do other things. While changing your cognition, bravely do these things, and you will become better and better. Best wishes.
Sorry, but I can't help with that request.

Hello, thank you for your trust and invitation to answer your question. In your question, you mentioned that "past life has caused me to miss many opportunities and joys of life. Is this kind of self-suggestion meaningful?" This is a thought-provoking question and I am not sure how to answer it right away. I recalled a lyric from a song I heard long ago - What you think is what you are! I don't know if this can help you find the answer to your question. Meanwhile, in hypnotherapy, suggestions are used to facilitate personal change. Your thoughts are similar to "self-hypnosis". Usually, both positive suggestions and negative suggestions can have an impact. So, I believe if you keep feeling that you are not good enough, you might actually become worse. Conversely, if you focus on your good and positive qualities, you can become a better version of yourself! When the thought of "I am not good enough" arises, quickly activate the second thought - I may not be the best, but I am already good. Between being good and being the best lies the space where I can grow! Take good care of yourself.

Hello, OP! I understand your frustrations very well. You want to change your lack of confidence and have been trying to suggest to yourself to be confident. However, you are unsure if this psychological suggestion actually works and you don't know how to deal with your intrusive thoughts. I can feel your distress and dilemma. Psychological suggestion is actually a very common phenomenon, and positive suggestions can unlock a person's potential. When you are about to do something, confidently tell yourself, "I can do it!" This will make you more engaged and motivated, and your performance will be better. Positive suggestions can guide things in a positive direction, allowing you to face upcoming challenges with a more positive mindset. Psychological suggestion needs to be repeated constantly, letting those encouraging expressions, words, and actions appear repeatedly. This will continuously reinforce positive attitudes and firm emotions, leading to determination and belief in overcoming all obstacles. When you enter this state and your perception of yourself changes, you will no longer feel that these suggestions are compulsive behaviors, but rather normal and optimistic thoughts. Accepting your imperfect self is the first step. OP, you must accept yourself first. Everyone is imperfect, so there's no need to put too much pressure on yourself. Recognize your strengths and weaknesses, and make targeted changes and improvements in your life. Record your achievements to enhance self-confidence. While psychological suggestion is important, it also needs to be put into action. Start by completing things you are good at, and afterwards, record your achievements and feelings in a diary. This direct manifestation is more helpful in boosting self-confidence. In conclusion, positive psychological suggestion is helpful, but it also needs to be combined with specific actions to enhance confidence. I wish you the best in overcoming your troubles and gradually becoming a confident person.

Hello, dear questioner. I send you greetings and a big hug as if we were face to face. I can truly feel your current emotions, and I sincerely hope that my words can be of help to you. First, let me briefly summarize your problem: in the past, you were a child lacking confidence due to family and personality reasons. Now, you have realized the need for change and often suggest to yourself the need for confidence. You are unsure whether this psychological suggestion is correct and whether this sense of compulsion is fundamentally something you should be thinking about. Psychologist Pavlov believed that suggestion is the simplest and most typical conditioned reflex in humans. Actually, the two questions you raise are a bit contradictory, but they do not necessarily oppose each other. Should we not think about repetitive compulsions fundamentally? Should we instead focus on taking practical actions? We can engage in positive psychological suggestions while practicing actions. In the medical field, there is a theory that states, "The human brain automatically produces endorphins and sedatives, which have very good effects on pain relief and sleep induction. When a person receives positive psychological suggestions, the pituitary gland and hypothalamus in the brain are greatly stimulated, increasing the secretion of the aforementioned substances, finally allowing the person to smoothly fall asleep." This mainly refers to the fact that patients always believe that doctors are reliable. Even if the doctor prescribes vitamins instead of sleeping pills, the patient can still sleep soundly. Therefore, we can also see the importance of positive psychological suggestions. Regarding improving self-confidence, I believe that first, we need to understand why we lack confidence and what we are afraid of. "The right remedy" can only be applied when we understand ourselves, so that we can better improve ourselves, identify areas where we are lacking, and work on enhancing ourselves. I recommend that you read the book "Inferiority and Propose" which discusses the influence of family and some emotional and social issues, in the hope that it will be helpful to you. Take care!

Hello, after reading your question, I can feel your desire to become a confident person and your continuous efforts to become one. I want to give you a thumbs up because we all know that confident people can bravely showcase their abilities, express their opinions, and genuinely believe in themselves, which often exudes a charm that attracts the attention and praise of others. We all want to be confident people, but how can we achieve that? The upbringing and education from our families of origin, the praise and encouragement given by our parents, can build the initial foundation of self-confidence in children. You mentioned that due to your family and parents, you missed the first "confidence" train. Although I don't know what you have been through in your growth process, I believe that parents always want their children to become better and more outstanding, they just don't know what methods to use to cultivate a confident child. So let's start by putting aside any prejudices we may have against our parents and try to see another possibility~ Not having confidence doesn't mean that we are not good enough, but because we have forgotten our innate excellence as "chosen children" in the expectations of our parents. The training and learning we receive later can help us become more confident. A great start is that you are already on the second "confidence" train! Even though you may still have doubts and uncertainties on the train, wondering if it will take you to the destination of "confidence," believe in yourself. The training and learning we receive later can effectively enhance our self-confidence. If you are willing, there are many great books on confidence. Choose one that resonates with you the most, follow the teachings of classic books, and combine them with your own practice and experience to come up with methods that suit you. It will definitely be a good approach. The reason why you always doubt yourself, and even have the presence of obsessive thoughts, is because you are still oscillating, unsure if your current methods are effective. Confidence is a form of self-affirmation after success, and success may not necessarily require us to achieve earth-shattering feats in order to gain confidence and a sense of accomplishment. Starting with small things may be a great beginning. No matter what it is, as long as you do it well, give yourself encouragement and gradually accumulate, the feeling of confidence will definitely become better and better. It is important to note that "confidence" also has its limits, crossing those limits becomes "arrogance," so it is important to grasp the right "degree". "Confidence" is not something that is deliberately displayed, but radiates from within. In addition to practicing confidence, it is also essential to cultivate one's character and abilities internally. The universe always favors those who have goals and strive hard, just like you. Believe that you will definitely become a better version of yourself!

question: I am constantly troubled by money issues, how can I solve them?
description: I am sensitive to colleagues who owe money because it is normal in the workplace for people to borrow money and sometimes forget to pay it back. Lately, I have become extremely petty, feeling very uncomfortable whenever someone owes me a few dollars. I can see her body tensing up inexplicably, and it's really torturing me deep down. Please, how can I alleviate this?
keywords: Interpersonal relationships, deception and trust, interpersonal boundaries.

answers.answer_text: Hello, thank you for inviting. I understand your sensitivity to money and the emotions and interpersonal reactions that may arise from it—times are tough, and not repaying debts is a form of interpersonal violation. Wealthy people are not obligated to bear this burden, and those of us who are financially restricted feel even more pressure. Additionally, if someone who borrows money selfishly ignores their obligation to repay, the creditor should not bear that burden for free. You mentioned that sometimes forgetting to repay debts is normal, which demonstrates your tolerance. However, if your financial situation does not allow for such tolerance, you also cannot force yourself. After all, money does not come out of thin air. Another factor is how one feels about the attitude of the other party—some people act as if nothing happened after borrowing money, which can make the lender feel uncomfortable. Of course, another factor is the amount borrowed. The feelings differ depending on the amount borrowed, and this feeling is quite personal—everyone's financial circumstances are different. Your "unexplained nervousness" may be the subconscious struggle between your financial stress and the mindset of "should be understanding"? It is more likely that, although the benefit is small, you feel resentful at being taken advantage of for no reason. As for how to alleviate this, I have a few suggestions: combine your own values and views on friendship to set a standard for lending money to others—for whom to lend and for whom not to lend. Perhaps it would be better not to lend to those who make you worry about repayment. Helping others by lending money is a good thing, but if it also brings you stress, then it's not so good. Combine it with your own financial situation to set a standard for the amount of money to lend to others—for whom and how much to lend. With this, you can have a clear basis for making lending decisions, and it will prevent you from feeling out of control. Another suggestion, for situations where the person has some financial ability but is "stingy," is to regularly donate and do acts of kindness. After doing this a few times, you will experience a different mindset when facing the inevitable small financial transactions in life, because you will have the feeling of helping others without expecting anything in return.

OP, hello ~~~ First, give OP a hug. You are very sensitive about money, especially when it comes to lending money to others, even if it's a small amount, it makes you uncomfortable. You keep thinking about it and can't forget. When you see the other person, you feel tense all over. OP has realized that this is not quite right, but not sure how to make a change. OP can start by carefully recalling the root cause of the problem. Did you suffer losses due to money issues in the past? Or did you feel upset and aggrieved due to a shortage of funds when you were young? Or has someone borrowed money from you and not returned it? Generally speaking, it is normal to feel uncomfortable when someone owes you money and think of that when you see them, but usually it's for larger amounts. If you are bothered by small amounts of money, it may give others the impression that you are petty, which is not good for your image and relationships. One piece of advice to try is to set a specific amount that you cannot accept as a loss. If it exceeds that amount, remind the person to repay it. If it is below that amount, mentally consider it as a gift to the person when lending, so even if they don't repay it, you won't feel upset. If they do repay it, you can be happy about it. Of course, if this issue persists and affects your normal work and study, it is recommended to seek professional counseling to explore the root cause of the problem and make more fundamental changes.

question: I am a freshman in veterinary medicine. Why don't I find dissecting classes bloody and disgusting?
description: Recently, I attended my first anatomy lab class. A few people in a group dissected a rabbit. First, we administered anesthesia, then made an incision in the abdomen and removed the small intestine for experimentation. We then placed it back and waited for half an hour before taking it out for observation. However, it seemed like the anesthesia wasn't enough, as the rabbit woke up as soon as we made the initial incision. It struggled and one of my classmates started crying, but I didn't feel anything in my heart. Other classmates kept telling the person performing the dissection to be gentle and slow. After finishing the experiment, some of us wanted to sew the rabbit back together instead of using an empty syringe to make it die faster. I felt like we didn't know what we were doing, and the rabbit was definitely going to die anyway. We didn't even administer antibiotics at the end, so the rabbit wouldn't have survived. Why not just let it die directly? Trying to sew it back together wouldn't have worked, and none of us knew how to do it properly. However, I didn't dare say anything because I was afraid they would think there was something wrong with me. Another group finished their dissection quickly. They just used an empty syringe to kill the rabbit, then skinned it and dissected each organ one by one. In order to show that I had sympathy, I told our group about their method, saying that it was too bloody and cruel. But in reality, I just wanted to appear sympathetic. Is it abnormal for me to think this way?

answers.answer_text: Title, hello, give you a hug~ After reading your description, you are a medical student. During the experiment, the scene of dissection shocked your soul. I sympathize with your experience. According to your description, you found that your behavior was different from others during the experiment. You may be confused about whether you have psychological problems, but I think this is a normal behavior and does not mean that you lack compassion. On the contrary, I think this is a very rational behavior. I completely agree with your viewpoint. If you truly pity the rabbits being experimented on, you should let them suffer less pain when they leave, instead of leaving in agonizing struggle. However, I also believe that there is nothing majorly wrong with your group members' actions. It's just that the impact of this experiment on them was too great. Perhaps this is a growth process that medical students must go through.

question: If we don't argue, will my girlfriend have a period of time when she doesn't want to talk to me or meet up with me?
description: I and my girlfriend didn't have an argument, and nothing happened. She just suddenly went through a period of time where she didn't want to talk to me or see me. I don't know why. Can anyone help me?
keywords: Love, sense of security, love management, good feeling

answers.answer_text: You and your girlfriend didn't have any arguments, nothing happened at all, but suddenly there was a period of time when she didn't want to talk to you or see you. You feel confused, not knowing why. Why doesn't she want to talk to you or see you when everything was fine? You must be very sad at this time. You rack your brains but can't figure out why things turned out this way. There are several possibilities for this: 1. You did something unintentionally that made her angry, and she is sulking. You can try to communicate with her to find out what's wrong. 2. You failed to meet her expectations in some way. Girls like surprises, especially during the dating phase. 3. Everyone goes through periods of low emotions, and it will naturally get better after a few days. I don't know how long you've been together, but getting to know each other takes time. As you get to know her better, you will also understand her thoughts and feelings better. Best wishes.

question: Sometimes I feel very troubled, I dislike myself, and it's difficult to deal with this feeling.
description: When I bought a phone case at a physical store, I thought it was good at the time. But then I saw a better-looking one online and I really liked it! I regretted buying the one at the physical store. When I mustered up the courage to say I wanted to return it, the shopkeeper's attitude immediately turned sour. They aggressively grabbed the case and said, "The packaging is gone, how can I sell it? You'll have to keep it for yourself!" My heart sank like a knife, and I instantly regretted it. I felt like I was causing trouble. But if I didn't return it, I would feel even worse. So, it's really difficult to deal with this kind of feeling. Many things can be like this, and I even hate myself for acting like this.

answers.answer_text: Desire, when reaching out its tentacles, gets bitten by reality. When dealing with desires and needs, it's only necessary to sift and differentiate. Reasonable needs are what safeguard rights and interests. Comparing prices from three different stores is a way of assessing the situation; making hasty decisions and then regretting them is being fickle-minded; feeling heartache after being rejected, lacking a strong sense of responsibility and defense awareness. Feeling lost is also a rare opportunity for self-examination. If anything is lacking, pay attention to making up for it or avoiding it in the future. Looking at it from a different perspective will make it easier to bear. Everyone grows through exploration, that's why one gains wisdom from one's mistakes. Besides, some lessons can't be bought with money.

question: A 5-year-old boy refuses to write and always says he doesn't know how to write. What methods can be used to motivate him?
description: A five-year-old boy only knows how to write the number 1. He always says he can't write the homework assigned by the teacher. His family patiently teaches him to write, but he still can't do it, and more often than not, he doesn't want to write and just wants to play. The teacher also tells the parents that the child is the last one in the class and needs to practice writing more, otherwise he won't be able to keep up.
