Since he started kindergarten, he has been more active and can't sit still for long on a chair. He has a cheerful personality and many classmates like to play with him. He is polite, hygienic, and likes to share, but he does not like to study. When he doesn't want to write his homework, I tell him that he can go out and play after finishing it, but he says he won't go out then. He even says he doesn't want to go to kindergarten anymore. I don't know what methods can motivate such a young child. Do any teachers have any good ideas?

answers.answer_text: Hello. You are too anxious... Of course, what the kindergarten teacher said is also a source of pressure for you. And you are worried about the fear of your child "falling behind others". This layer upon layer of pressure and anxiety, when conveyed to the child, the child will instinctively resist. And the "I just can't write, I'm always last" and other labels, evaluations from others (especially from you), internalize into his own cognition and evaluation, this is the most worrying. So, what needs to change is your mindset. I suggest you read children's picture books: "Little Seed," "An's Seed," the poem "Take a Snail for a Walk," read books like "Good Mothers are Better than Good Teachers" by Yin Jianli, and "Positive Discipline," etc. Calm down your comparison, anxiety, and worry, and then learn the wisdom of being a parent. For example, don't label children, shield them from external pressures and evaluations (such as from teachers). Oh, the attitude of the mother of Little Bean in "Little Bean by the Window" and Mr. Ba in the Baidu Academy is worth learning from. Finally, only when your mindset is good, not "utilitarian," not impatient, can you "teach children". The so-called education should be fun, taking your child to nature, a twig that he picks up is like a 1, the little duck swimming in the lake is like a 2, the handcuffs opened in the boy's police uniform is like a 3, two round cakes put together is like 8. When he eats a bag of snacks, goes up stairs, you can teach him to count. The buttons on a straight elevator, the license plate of a parked car on the roadside, you can read them together. Why do you have to make him sit there and write stroke by stroke, so boring and tiring? Give him the impression that learning is boring and uninteresting, and even if he remembers and learns, will the result be good without interest? I personally am not an advocate of advanced education, my husband and I are ordinary people, and our child cannot have exceptional intelligence. My child only started holding a pen and learning to write in first grade. Before that, her hands were just used to play casually... Everything is difficult at the beginning, in first grade, she adapted to school slower than the kids who started practicing writing in kindergarten and wrote worse. Naturally, the homeroom teacher took the initiative to call me after the mid-term exam, gently and patiently complaining that my child was dragging down the class, had many "bad study habits," etc. As a qualified parent in modern society, of course, I didn't forget to smile and hurriedly thank the teacher for her concern, promising to cooperate with the school to urge the child to make progress. However, after hanging up the phone, I still adjusted my mindset and respected the child's development law. I did what I needed to do. Now, in second grade, the gap between her and those "early mature" children is no longer very obvious. This is what I think, if even I, as a mother, don't trust and appreciate my child, just blindly conform to the world's constant urging for her to fly high, fly fast, and fly far, then when she gets tired of flying, where can she find a place to rest? Where is the shelter for her to seek refuge? Look further ahead, when she turns 30, will you still care, and be entangled in whether she could write numbers from 1 to 10 at 5 years old or write numbers at 7 years old? Is such a trivial matter important? At that time, what ability will you care about the most? In the marathon of education, grasping the child's general direction is the right approach. You have to believe that sometimes being "slow" is really "fast".
